Maximilian, by the favor of divine clemency elected Emperor of the Romans, ever august, and King of Germany, Hungary, Dalmatia, Croatia, etc., Archduke of Austria, Duke of Burgundy, Brabant, etc., to the honorable and devout John Trithemius, Abbot of St. James the Greater at Würzburg, beloved to us: imperial grace and every good thing.

Since you have humbly explained to us that you have composed various editions of both ancient and modern authors, collected not without great labor, wakefulness, and diligence, which you desired with all your mind to have brought into the light; and since Master Johannes Haselberg of Constance, beloved to us and to the Holy Roman Empire, has offered himself with a most ready mind to be the agent of this matter, and for that reason has procured at great expense the formes by which he may print the aforesaid works: We therefore, desiring that provision be made for the indemnity of the aforesaid Master Johannes and for the adornment of your honor, lest your works, composed by you with great labors and wakefulness, lie hidden as if covered with rust, but rather that they shine forth more and more day by day, have therefore given and granted to the aforesaid Master Johannes Haselberg of Constance full power and authority in every respect, just as by the tenor of these presents we give and grant it.

We decree that he may print, and sell when printed, wherever he pleases and according to his will, whatever of treatises and little works has been published by you, the aforesaid Trithemius, Abbot of St. James the Greater at Würzburg, and has been reviewed and approved by the honorable Conrad Peutinger, doctor and our councillor, faithful and beloved to us. And we forbid all and singular chalcographers and printers of books, of whatever condition, under the penalty written below, strictly commanding them not to dare or presume, throughout the whole Roman Empire and in our hereditary lands, to print, publish, or, when printed by others, publish, buy, and sell such works, or similar ones, for ten years after they have been published by the said Master Johannes.

Moreover, we command all and singular our faithful subjects, and those of the Holy Roman Empire, beloved to us, of whatever estate, condition, dignity, or office they may be, whether ecclesiastical or secular, under the penalty of our most grave indignation and that of the Holy Roman Empire, and of ten marks of pure gold, to be applied, as often as action is taken contrary to this, one part to our fisc and the other part to the aforesaid Master Johannes Haselberg, that they assist the same Master Johannes of Constance with their favor and aid in their places and lands, and not permit the said works and treatises to be printed, or those printed elsewhere to be sold. Rather, they shall immediately declare in our name that all persons presuming to do anything against this our grace and prohibition have incurred the sentence of such indignation of ours and of the Holy Roman Empire, and shall execute our will expressly stated in this matter.

In witness whereof these letters have been furnished with the impression of our seal on the back. Given in our town of Innsbruck on the tenth day of the month of November, in the year of the Lord one thousand five hundred fourteen, in the twenty-ninth year of our Roman reign, and the twenty-fifth of Hungary.

By the king himself.

At the command of the lord Emperor himself.

N. Ziegler,

[unclear], by Paulus Oberstainer.

The Letter of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St James, formerly of Sponheim, to the most reverend father in Christ and prince, lord Laurence, from the noble and most ancient family of the Bibra, bishop of the distinguished church of Würzburg and sole duke of Eastern Francia, concerning the compendium of the first volume of the annals on the origin of the Franks

To the most reverend father in Christ and most excellent prince, lord Laurence, bishop of the noble church of Würzburg, sole duke of Eastern Francia, Johannes Trithemius, unprofitable, abbot in name only of the poor little monastery of St James the Apostle in the suburbs of the aforesaid city of Würzburg, offers ready service in all things, no less voluntary than owed by right. Most reverend father, illustrious prince, gracious lord, I have written, as your most reverend lordship knows, three large volumes, of no small labor, on the origin, progress, and particular deeds of the kings and princes of the people of the Franks, taking the beginning of the narrative of the succession of kings from the four hundred fortieth year before the birth of Christ, at which time, after Antenor, the great king of the nation, had been killed by enemies, his son Marcomer succeeded to the kingdom and led his people, namely our forebears, from the borders of Scythia into the borders of Germany and Saxony, to the mouths of the Rhine, where Guelders now is. In these three volumes I have encompassed a period of one thousand nine hundred fifty-four years, in which the kings of the Franks are numbered, succeeding one another in proper order, from that same Marcomer already mentioned down to the twenty-ninth year of the emperor Caesar Maximilian Augustus: one hundred and three. There are many collateral kings, outside the direct genealogical line, who are excluded from this number of kings. Through the whole first volume, however, I have continued the successions and deeds of the kings of the Franks down to King Pippin exclusively, through one thousand one hundred ninety years, in which there were sixty-one kings succeeding one another in a direct line. To Pippin succeeded Charles, surnamed the Great, his son; then Louis the Pious. When he died, his sons divided the kingdom of the Franks into several parts. When they too had departed this life, their grandsons again divided the kingdom of the Franks in such a way principally into two kingdoms, of which one is called, is, and shall forever remain Germanic, while the other is Gallic, and neither is subject to the other. And this division is as follows.

Johannes Trithemius wrote three volumes of annals.

Et propterea reges ambo, in diuisione regni pristinam libertatē Francorum ubiqƺ altérri alter illaesam seruirent. Rex uero Gallicanae. Ius regni frācię gallicanae cũ terminis suis. Solius regni germanici scriptor gesta ꝓsequitur. Verum in tam longo decursu annorum, primo ab introitu gentis in Germaniam, prolixior euasit historia, operę preciū fore arbitratus sum, si ex tribus ip̄sis ānalium uoluminibus, totidem libros extraherem breuiores, qui nomina, successiones, gestam memoratu digniora, regum Francorum Germanie continerent, per compendium. Scio enim quod reuerendissima dominatio vestra, vetustis delectatur in historijs, ratione administrandi principatus continue occupatur in młtis. Cum ergo princeps hodie nullus uiuat inter mortales, cui post deum, ad seruiendum complacendum pro uiribus, amplius, iure sim debitor, subiectissima uoluntate paratior, quam uestrae prestantissimae reuerendissimaeqƺ dominationi neminem iudico digniorem, cuius nominibus de Frācorum origine lucubrationes meas aut debeam, aut uelim dedicare. Reuere dīdissimus do minus epūs historia rum amator est. Finis eplē penulti ma februarij. An no M D XV. Anno. M. D. XV.

The kings of both Frances were always utterly free.

The aforesaid territories fell to it, namely the whole kingdom of Germany, with the Saxons, Thuringians, Marcomanni, Danes, Frisians, Hessians, Westphalians, Eastern Franks, Bavarians, Swabians, Bohemians, Sorbs, Austrians, Germans, and all the nations, peoples, and races that lie among those named above.

¶ The whole kingdom of Austrasia also, with these cities: of the people of Metz, which is now called all Lotharingia; Trier, with the Mosellani, Eufalii, and [Cynonoti?]; Cologne, Aachen, Liège, and Maastricht, both lower and upper, with Holland, Zeeland, Brabant, Hainaut, the whole region from the river Rhine westward as far as the sea, with the Tongrians, Flemings, Morini, and all the land that either adjoins or lies among the regions and cities mentioned. Finally, the kingdom of Arles, with its eight counties in Gaul, is counted by ancient right as subject under the dominion of the king of the Germans; by reason of this each archbishop of Trier in office for the time being is recognized as having afterwards been appointed archchancellor of the German kingdom throughout Gaul, the aforesaid kingdom of Arles. The kingdom of Burgundy also, with all its counties, was assigned in the same division to the kingdom of the Germans. All Alemannia too, with its cities and peoples, in which are the cities of Chur, Sion, and Valais, fell by lot to the kingdom of the Germans, together with the Helvetians, Alsatians, [Caurici?], Savoyards, the people of Constance, Basel, Strasbourg, Speyer, Worms, Mainz, and all the peoples from the source of the river Rhine as far as the sea, into which it finally flows by three mouths.

¶ But the Roman Empire, together with Italy, Lombardy, and all territories subject to it by ancient right, except Greece, the eastern empire, was then, and remains today, annexed and subject to the kingdom of the Germans. Nevertheless, in the course of time many disputes, invasions, and changes arose between the kings of the Germans and of the Gauls over certain boundaries of the kingdom; these have been written about more fully in the second volume.

¶ The kingdom of the Franks of Gaul also, separated from ours already mentioned, should in like manner, as the constitution states, have its own free king, who is no less free than the king of Germany, subject to absolutely no one. For it is manifest that the Franks were always utterly free from their origin. They never served the Romans, nor any other nation, nor were they subject to them. Rather, they themselves destroyed the empire of the Romans and made it subject to themselves. And therefore both kings, in the division of the kingdom, were to preserve everywhere unharmed for one another the ancient freedom of the Franks.

But the king of Gallic Francia, in the division of the monarchy, received as his portion the kingdom of Neustria, or Paris, the kingdom of Orléans, the kingdom of Aquitaine, the kingdom of Lausanne, the Armorican kingdom, or of New Brittany, with all the provinces, regions, and peoples of inner Gaul as far as Spain, from the river Rhône to the western sea.

The jurisdiction of the kingdom of Gallic Francia with its boundaries.

The writer pursues the deeds of the German kingdom alone.

After that division of the kingdom of the Franks I compressed the history; and, now omitting thereafter the Gallic Franks, in the second and third volumes of the annals I continue the narrative concerning the German Franks alone. But since, in so long a course of years, first from the entrance of the people into Germany, the history has become rather lengthy, I thought it would be worthwhile if from those three volumes of annals themselves I extracted the same number of shorter books, which would contain in brief the names, successions, and deeds more worthy of remembrance of the kings of the Franks of Germany. For I know that your most reverend lordship delights in ancient histories, and by reason of administering a principality is continually occupied in many affairs. Since, therefore, no prince lives today among mortals to whom, after God, I am by right more indebted, with all my powers, for service and pleasing obedience, nor am I readier with a most submissive will, than to your most excellent and most reverend lordship, I judge no one more worthy in whose name I either ought or wish to dedicate my studies on the origin of the Franks.

The most reverend lord bishop is a lover of histories.

End of the letter, the last day of February. In the year 1515.

In the year 1515.

Here begins the compendium or breviary of the first volume of the Chronicles or Annals of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James the Greater, Apostle, in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, concerning the origin of the people and kings of the Franks.

Compendium on the origin of the Franks

With the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have written, not without very great labors, three volumes of our annals, of no small size, in which, from the origin of the race of the Franks down to the twenty-eighth year of Caesar Maximilian Augustus, we have arranged a fuller history, distinguished, that is, by the following sequence of division. In the first volume, indeed, we described both the origin of the aforesaid race of the Franks and their kings, beginning from Marcomirus, who began to reign in the four hundred thirty-ninth year before the birth of Christ; and after the death of his father, whom the Goths had killed in war, he reigned for twenty-eight years, and was the first to lead the people from the mouths of the Danube into Germany, to the mouths of the Rhine. This people, sprung from the offspring of Trojans once fugitive from captured Troy, while it was still among its own fellow citizens, had the Trojan name; after this, dispersed among various nations and wandering, it often changed both its settlements and its name.

For at first, with the Trojans, they were called Trojans; afterward, among the Scythians, they were also named Scythians. But when they came into the borders of Germany, for a time they were called Sicambri; most recently they were called Franks from Francus their king. Yet the Sicambri could not at once obtain from the neighboring peoples, and especially from the Romans and Gauls, to whom their power was always suspect, that they should be called Franks, until at last, enlarging their kingdom and their name, they powerfully subjected to themselves the Romans, together with Italy and all Gaul. And because they lived with the Germans, they were more frequently named Germans than Franks by writers of deeds done. Thus the whole period of the first volume of our annals contains one thousand one hundred eighty-nine years, from Marcomirus down to King Pippin.

The second volume of our annals takes its beginning from German affairs, from the seven hundred fiftieth year of the Lord’s birth, when Pippin, mayor of the palace, was elected king of the Franks, Childeric having been shorn as a monk. And it contains the period of years from that point down to the eighth year of Richard, king of Germany, who succeeded William amid the dissension of the princes: five hundred fifteen years, as is clear to one counting the sequence of the order, in which the history of the German kingdom is woven.

The third volume of our annals takes the beginning of its annotations from the eighth year of King Richard, which was the one thousand two hundred sixty-sixth year of the Lord’s birth. We continue it to the twenty-eighth year of King Maximilian, that is, the one thousand five hundred fourth year of the Lord’s birth.

Trithemius wrote three volumes of annals.

The Franks received their name while with the Germans. The period of the first volume.

Epitome of the first volume of the Annals

Many have written on the origin of the Franks

Hunibald, historiographer of the Franks

The first six books contain 750 years. The second six books contain 840 years. The last six books contain about 100 years.

King Antenor is slain by the Goths.

In the year before the birth of Christ 460.

The war of the Scythian Franks with the Goths.

the tenth, containing two hundred forty-eight years. And thus the whole span of these three volumes amounts to one thousand nine hundred fifty-three years, whose deeds we have embraced.

Therefore, as we are about to write the epitome of the first volume of our Annals, a compendium or breviary from the sure consideration of our mind, we warn the reader not to carp at the work before he has prudently examined it. It is the manifest mark of a rash man to judge what he does not know, and to suppose that no one can know what he himself perhaps does not know. I know that many have written various and diverse things on the origin of the Franks; some of them contend that the people was indigenous, while others say that it came from some city of the Sicambri, I know not what. We believe that no one can either distinguish or reconcile their diverse opinions unless Hunibald’s compilation has illuminated him. For he flourished as a sound historiographer of the Franks in the times of King [Clovis?], whom Saint Remigius, bishop of the Romans, baptized, in the five-hundredth year of the Lord’s nativity; and after Doracus the philosopher, Wasthald the historian, and many other very ancient writers of deeds, he wrote a distinguished work, which he divided into eighteen books. In the first six he traces the earliest origin of the Frankish people from the destruction of Troy down to the death of King Antenor, whom the Scanzians, Goths, and Suevi or Suedi killed near the mouths of the Danube, namely in the four-hundred-fortieth year before Christ’s nativity. In the other six books he includes the period from the death of the aforesaid King Antenor down to Faramund, king of the Franks, the forty-third of the second order. From Faramund the remaining six books continue down to the last year of [Clovis?], the first Christian among the kings of the Franks, who died in the five-hundred-fourteenth year of the Lord’s nativity. And because we have written more fully about all these matters in the first volume of our Annals, the nature of the name “breviary” demands that here we aim at brevity. Here ends the prologue.

The first book of the compendium begins.

The breviary of the first volume of the Annals of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James of Würzburg, of the Order of Saint Benedict, begins succinctly.

In the four-hundred-fortieth year before the nativity of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ from Mary, the ever-undefiled virgin, when the peoples who were afterward called Franks, but before that Scythians, and still earlier Trojans, were settled at the maritime borders of Scythia, not far from the mouths of the Danube, King Antenor ruled. Against him a most savage nation, numerous beyond number, coming out of the Scanzian islands, which are now called Gothic, wore down his people by frequent incursion.

Joining weapons with weapons and hands with hands, Antenor, now defeated, now victor, was at last killed by the Goths in battle, together with many of his men, in the aforesaid year, as we have said, 440 before the birth of Christ. His son Marcomer succeeded him in the kingdom.

Marcomir, the elder son of the slain King Antenor, appointed in his father’s place, reigned for twenty-eight years. He began almost in the same year in which his father was killed. He was a high-spirited, brave, bold, and warlike man, who avenged his father’s death upon the neighboring Goths by frequent incursions, although he seemed far inferior to the Goths in number of fighters and in strength. Moreover, in the fourth year of his reign he held counsel with the chief men of the kingdom as to how either the Goths might be kept from the kingdom, or, if this could not be done, how he might otherwise provide for the people, lest it perish.

At last it pleased all who were rightly wise, since they could in no way withstand so immense a multitude of Goths, to change their dwelling-places by the will of the gods. Therefore, when the ministers of their gods had been summoned, the elders commanded that they should be stirred up by the divine powers as to which direction they were ordered to go. They prepare rites suited to prophecies; they offer sacrifices, composed by art, for summoning infernal powers. A priest stands in the midst, raving before the altar of Jupiter; he twists his head, utters verses in a murmur, gnashes artfully with his teeth, bent out of the ordinary manner, with his fingers he twists his arms together with his hands, brandishes them, and, flying about, bends himself back in like manner; to one seeing him sane he seems foolish, and more like a madman than a man. At last, when the divine power had been summoned by the chant, it gave back a prophecy to Menolpus as he prayed, and, beginning thus, thundered forth:

“Marcomer, prince of Jupiter, the divine power bids you be calm, and not to fear the chances of the long journey, which stretches toward the west after your brothers to the mouths of the Rhine, where Brutus holds the back, the Trojans the face, [exulrophaea] at rest. Each is your brother by nature, by nation a faithful friend. Go, with swift course take possession of the dwellings prepared, to be extended by the will of the father’s divinity into a third part of the world.”

That same night King Marcomir, in his fatherland’s incantation, called upon the divine power, singing beforehand with a murmur the one whom from her sagacity they named Aliruna as she prophesied. He compared the monster. He confirmed by the authority of the Sibyl the prophecy of the priest, and ordered the people immediately to be led across to the place where, the offspring having multiplied exceedingly, by the foretokening vision it would remain stronger.

Marcomir beheld a three-headed divine power standing before him, of one [unclear] in eternity. He heard the particular prediction of each head, and saw a distinct [unclear] set above each one. The first head was that of a toad; the second, of a lion; the third, of an eagle, in form as if standing over it with wings spread, touching with fostering care the lion on the right and the toad on the left. And the eagle said: “Your progeny, Marcomir, will subject my head to itself. It will trample the lion; [silꝰ] will kill the toad.” And the toad itself, being subject, [unclear].

It marks Gaul as first to be overcome. The lion marks Germany as to be conquered. Interpretation to Alruna of the monster seen. The varied change of the kingdom of the Franks. Alruna in Gothic is a wise woman. By the lion, the Saxons; by the toad, the Gauls. The land of the toad is Gallic; the lion is Germanic. Prophecy concerning the victory of the Franks.

me, because I appear foul, fair king, you should not think to be despised; my appearance and form are suited to future things. Your race will first destroy me; long after this it will keep the lion captive by the sword. Take care to hear from its mouth what remains further. The lion-like head then said to King Marcomirus: Strongest king, stranger who will come into my [unclear] with your people, soon you will conquer the toad with toil, over much time; then my rights will yield everywhere and of their own accord to yours, by wars and by craft. Afterwards the Eagle will crown me, the right-hand victim, having on the left the toad bound by your seed. But what will be afterward, our conjecture shows you. When this lion-like apparition had uttered these things, the three heads were suddenly turned into one, and the three-headed monster stood transformed into the image of a man, and not of a simple condition, but of a king crowned with a golden diadem, holding a scepter in his left hand and a sword in his right; and, murmuring in a shrill voice, it said in the Scythian tongue:

Alruna, taught by songs to raise the shades and to bring down the highest gods from heaven, so that they may bring responses to your incantations, hear what we foreannounce is to be for the people of King Marcomirus, and understand, lest we speak in vain. As the transformation of our image confirms the form and makes certain this very voice of the prophecy, so to this people a varied and broad kingdom is promised for the future, which long time and the multitude of the ruling lineage will vary, so that it will neither always be one nor divided among many. Now one, then two, now three, then four and beyond. Now it returns into one. At last it will stand divided in two, when the eagle has been joined as a friend to the lion, and the toad has held the left-hand part of the eagle in ambush. When all these things had been said, the vision disappeared.

King Marcomirus asked Alruna what the meaning of the prophecy was. She said to him: It is the ancestral god, O king, who accompanies you and your people; informed by his predictions concerning the future for your people and for the kings who will be born from you, you should know from this that you must migrate as quickly as possible toward the farthest lands of the lion, toward the west. The lion designates the people who dwell on this side of the river Rhine, sprung from the ancient stock of the Trojans.

On the other side of the river, however, dwells the people of the toad, inhabiting a wide and fruitful region. The other, third people, designated by the eagle, are the Romans, whose pride labors to subject the whole world to its dominion. Therefore go with your people toward the west, and you will dwell between those two peoples, of the lion and of the toad, between the sea and the Rhine. For it is to come to pass that many battles will be fought between your people and the people of the toad, and many on both sides will fall, slain by the sword.

But after many years, at last your seed and your people will take by arms the whole land of the toad, and they will possess it for many years, after the toad has been killed.

Then they will also subject to themselves the land of the lion, from the western river as far as the great eastern river of many nations. And finally they will possess the kingdom of the eagle with many nations, and there will be one king of several kingdoms from your seed, until after the third generation unity will be thrown into confusion by division.

Marcomir the king, therefore, after richly rewarding Aliruna, commanded her to keep silence about the secrets, and ordered her to depart. On the next day, having again summoned the nobles to him, he praises the counsel, and by public edict warns that their settlements must by all means be transferred. And so, an embassy having been sent to the Saxons in Germany, who themselves too are said to have been born from the Trojans, they asked them as brothers to grant the Scythians dwelling-places in some corner of their land. The Saxons readily gave consent to their request, promising that they would give them excellent settlements, and adding nonetheless that they should hasten to come as quickly as possible. A reason pressed the Saxons, on account of which they gladly consented to their Scythian brothers: namely, because they greatly desired to set them between themselves and the Gauls as a wall and bulwark.

Concerning the arrival of the Scythians within the borders of Germany, in the regions on this side of the Rhine, with their king Marcomir; they were first Trojans, then Scythians, afterward Sicambri, and in the final generation were called Franks.

Therefore in the four hundred and third year before the birth of Christ, which was the beginning of the seventh year of King Marcomir, around the middle of the month Hecatombaeon, which we call April, King Marcomir himself, with Sunno, Panthenor, and Priam his brothers, having left dukes beyond the Danube and the sea of Scythia within the borders, returning on their journey and circling northward, and then turning their road toward the region of the Teutons, began their migration westward with the whole people of the kingdom, with wives, children, and all their household goods, with great labor, difficult and long-lasting.

There were, apart from women and little children, one hundred seventy-five thousand six hundred fifty-eight men most ready for war. And the names of the princes who were with Marcomir and had descended from his lineage were: Duke Nicanor, paternal uncle of King Marcomir; Sunno, Panthenor, and Priam, brothers of Marcomir, now said to be king; Duke Helenus; Duke Antenor; Duke Menander; Duke Edrasius; Duke Gethenus; Duke Priam; Duke Marenus; Duke Ermo; Duke Nicanor; Duke Pyndar; Duke Helan; Duke Marcomir; Duke Colan; Duke Masan; Duke Antenor; Duke Ancrasius; Duke Bengoth; Duke Calomer; Duke Rodanus; Duke Malda; Duke Kylan; Duke Solas; Duke Colo; Duke Bremus; Duke Sunno; Duke Melanus; Duke Nicamor; Duke Thaphon; Duke Salon.

Number of Franks coming: 175,658 fighters. Dukes of the Franks under the king: 24.

The number of the whole people of the Franks was 489,360, and Meodarus duke.

Now the number of the whole people, as Humibaldus testifies, of men, women, and also little children of both sexes, was 489,360, apart from slaves and attendants. But if anyone desires to know fully what great difficulties they had on the journey, what wars they waged with the peoples resisting them, and into what great dangers they either fell or escaped, let him read the aforementioned writer in the book of histories of the race of the Franks. Its beginnings, just as they are remarkable, so they seem to me, saving the peace of those who judge better, to be fabulous in many respects.

At last, after many labors and innumerable difficulties, King Marcomirus, with his dukes and the whole people, came into Germany; and they were received kindly by the Saxons as brothers, and received the dwellings they desired between them and the Rhine, namely that province in which those now dwelling there are called the Western Frisians, and also the Guelders and the Hollanders: around that region, namely, where the Rhine flows into the sea by three mouths. And although those settlements received them at first rather narrowly, they soon made them wider by strength and arms, to the derision of the westerners.

Indeed, in the twentieth year of his reign, King Marcomirus, provoked by an injury from the Gauls across the Rhine, gathered an army, crossed the river, and subjected to his dominion that land which, enclosed by the islands of the Rhine, is nearest the sea, after expelling its inhabitants. He entrusted it to his brother Sunno to guard, and he brought in by ship peoples of his own race who would inhabit and cultivate it.

But when the Gauls were taking ill the incursion of a new and newly arrived people into the borders of the Hollanders, and were harassing it with various attempts, King Marcomirus, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, gathered a great army, both of his own men and of Saxons, crossed the Rhine by ship, entered western Gaul, and, devastating everything with sword and fire, came as far as the Meuse. Thereafter he fought many battles with the Gauls, victorious and triumphing everywhere; and his name was fearsome to all the Gallic peoples, and all who heard of Marcomirus were afraid. He made a treaty with the Britons inhabiting the island.

From that time, for nearly nine hundred years, the aforementioned kings of the race of the Scythians never ceased from harrying the Romans and Gauls, sometimes defeated, but more often victorious, until at last by arms they forced under their power not only all Gaul, but also all Germany, Swabia, Bavaria, Burgundy, Lombardy, Italy, Slavonia, Thuringia, Austria, Saxony, the Teutons, the Cimbri, the Danes, those on this side of the Rhine, the Mosellans, the Treveri, the people of Metz, the Austrasians, the people of Liege, the Morini, the people of Tournai, the Tungri, the people of the Meuse, the Atrebates, the people of Cologne, the people of Mainz, the Vangiones, the Nemetes, the people of Strasbourg, the Helvetii, the Rauraci, and the Bohemians, [unclear] together with the Spaniards and all the Germans, and almost all Europe.

[unclear] being completed, he died, namely in the year 412 before the birth of Christ, in the twenty-first year from the entrance of the people into the Saxon borders at the Rhine. He left three sons as leaders: Antenor, Priam, Nicanor, and twelve daughters.

Up to this year Vuasthald the Scythian, or Sicamber in his native tongue, brought down the historical work of his own people, over more or less 758 years, beginning from the destruction of Troy. In it he describes the various dwellings and settlements of his race, and also its leaders and wars, kings, and their various deeds in order. After him Hunibald the Frank, from the songs and writings of the priests of the Franks, continued the history for 1,426 years, down to the last year of King Clovis, who was the first of the kings of the Franks to receive the faith of Christ, baptized by Saint Remigius in the year of the Lord 499.

Antenor, the eldest son of King Marcomir, was raised to the kingship in the same year, and after his father reigned thirty years. He was held in the greatest honor among his people; he secured for himself a very firm friendship with the Saxons, with whose aid he victoriously fought many battles with the Romans and Gauls. Priam and Nicanor, his brothers, assisted him with the other leaders in faithful continuity; after crossing the river, they often inflicted many troubles upon the Gauls. Sunno also, the king’s paternal uncle, with his sons, always adhered to Antenor himself in all things with the greatest fidelity, and trained him in government as his own son, yet revered him no less as his lord.

King Antenor had a wife named Cambra, who was the daughter of Belinus, king of Britain. She was a woman more beautiful than the daughters of the whole kingdom, and of such prudence that the king and the princes of the Franks were always accustomed in all things to obey her counsel no less than that of some divine power. The customs of the people, still excessively rough with Scythian savagery, she rendered more cultivated by laws; she taught the nobles to build cities and castles. There she instituted the adornment of the forehead; she gave women the knowledge of sowing flax and committing hemp to the earth, and of weaving and preparing them for clothing and varied use. She composed laws; she pronounced justice. She presented herself as a seer, a priestess of Diana, and an Aliruna.

And since she was a woman in sex, but bore the mind of a king and priest, she became a laughing-stock among the Saxons in a proverb: whenever they heard anyone, beyond the ordinary, doing or saying something rather prudent, as though he wished to imitate the prudence of Cambra, they would rebuke him and say, “Look, camer.” In their language this is said: “Si camer,” as though they were saying, “Do you too know the prudence of Cambra?” Thus with time the proverb took root, so that the two latest words, that is, the adverb and the noun, “si” and “camber,” yielded a single word, which as a whole makes Sicamber.

The Sicambri were formerly called Neomagi.

The Franks changed their name together with their settlements.

Sunno the duke, the king’s paternal uncle, dies.

Groningen, a town of Frisia, is built.

The Third.

Priamus reigned twenty-six years.

The Sicambri began to use the language of the Germans.

Theocalus, pontiff and historiographer of the Sicambri.

But after some years, when the queen was dead, the Sicambri enrolled her among the goddesses, in her memory by decree of the kings and nobles. They, who previously were called Novimagi, that is Neumagi, as though “new kinsmen,” by their Saxon friends, were thereafter called Sicambri for about four hundred years, until at last from a certain king of theirs, Francus, as we shall say, they were named Franks, down to the present day, though with an admixture of peoples.

Meanwhile, because they were with their Trojans, they were also called Trojans; with Armenians, Armenians; with Scythians, Scythians; with Germans, Germans; with Gauls, Gauls. They often received a different name from others, and frequently changed customs, language, idiom of speech, and name together with their settlements.

In the twelfth year of Antenor, his paternal uncle Sunno dies, leaving two sons, Marcomir and Hector. The first of these, afterward racing with a horse over the ice, was drowned in the Rhine; the younger governed his father’s duchy in Holland under the authority of the king. He left four other sons, begotten from four other concubines, who are not counted among the dukes by the law of the Sicambri, which forbade, while children of the first wife survived, the sons of later women either to be princes or to be so named. Queen Cambra enacted this law so that the kingdom would not be thrown into confusion.

Priamus, moreover, brother of King Antenor, held the duchy among the Grunes, namely in that region bordering the sea which is now called Frisia, in which the son of Priamus the duke, in the three hundred seventy-seventh year before the birth of Christ, [built?] a new town, which from his own name is called Groningen down to the present day. For the duke’s name was Grunus, from whom the people too, although Franks by origin, were for a time called Grunes.

But Antenor, after many deeds bravely performed, dies in the thirtieth year of his reign, and in the year 382 of the Lord’s birth. The Sicambri, following him with great pomp according to the custom of the gentiles, enrolled him among the gods by order of the queen.

The only son of King Antenor by Queen Cambra reigned after his father over the Sicambri, who were afterward called Franks, for twenty-six years. In his time, entirely from the use of the old speech, there were among them many words which seem to sound more of Greek origin than of the character of the Teutonic or German language, as anyone who has full knowledge of both languages will easily discern. Nor was the change of the ancient speech among the people sudden; what began with time at last passed through usage into nature.

In the sixth year of King Priamus, Duke Marcomir died; he was the grandson of the first Sunno, concerning whom it was said above that, with the other dukes, he had led the people into Germany. Among many children he had a son

one named Theocalus, a man most outstanding in all the wisdom of the Greeks, Scythians, and Germans, whom the Sicambri appointed great priest of Jupiter. And he was their prelate, father, augur, and prophet.

The priests, moreover, used the Greek language in sacred rites for a long time, and did not admit any mixing of another language. Until that time they had no temples of the gods, but sacrificed to their divinities under certain leafy trees, which the priests had consecrated after prior judgment.

Therefore in the eighth year of Priamus, king of the Franks, his mother Cambra and the queen, at the command of Theocalus the pontiff, [unclear], of which they called one Neopagus and the other Neomagus, in memory of their newly acquired name. In these two cities, and especially in Neopagus, the residence of the king of the Franks was for a long time.

They also built in the same city of Neomagus a great and very strong temple to Jupiter, in which Theocalus the pontiff, dwelling with the priests, instructed the sons of princes and nobles in morals and knowledge. He pronounced prophecies to the people. He wrote in songs the brave deeds of kings, which the youth, compelled to learn by heart, was accustomed to sing on feast days at [unclear]. At certain times of the year, however, the priests stayed not in cities but in solitude; their food was sparse, and their exercise of mind in learning the courses of the stars, songs, and the histories of the ancients was continual.

King Priamus, after many incursions made against the Gauls, after battles and victories, at last died in the twenty-sixth year of his reign, in the year 356 before the birth of Christ from the Virgin Mary, leaving several sons and daughters from the four wives whom [unclear] had had.

Helenus, the elder-born son of King Priamus, succeeding his father, reigned among the Sicambri for nineteen years, a man severe toward enemies, who also sacrificed infants, as often as he was able to capture them, to Pallas and other demons. Toward his own people, however, he was not cruel but gentle and very humane, burdensome or troublesome to no one and therefore pleasing to all.

In the first year of his reign he had a war with the Transmosan Gauls and the Tungri, in which he laid low more than sixty thousand of the enemy and turned the rest to flight. He also killed with his own hand the firstborn of the king of the Morini, named Guedenus, and subjected to his rule a great part of the land beyond the Meuse, which he entrusted to his dukes to defend. Very often thereafter he fought with the Gauls with varying fortune, now defeated [unclear]. Concerning his battles and deeds, we have written more in the first volume of the Annals.

At last, after many brave deeds performed against the Gauls and other enemies round about, Helenus, king of the Sicambri, died in the nineteenth year of his reign, 338 years before the birth of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

Diocles, the elder-born son of King Helenus, after his father reigned thirty-nine years. He was a man tall in bodily stature, harsh in character, and severe with excessive maturity, bold, brave, and most warlike, who [unclear].

The Goths devastate the borders of the Saxons.

Five German kings with 260,000 men.

One hundred thousand of the Goths are killed.

Twenty-five thousand Saxons are killed.

The Gauls make war on the Franks while their king is far away.

The Gauls are defeated by the Sicambri through cunning and courage.

Many thousands of the Gauls are slain.

Three leaders of the Franks were killed.

Diocles, king of the Sicambri, dies.

In the twelfth year of his reign, a multitude of the people of the Goths came forth from the Scanzian islands, which are now called Gothic, and, pouring into the borders of the Saxons, began to carry out a very grievous devastation, consuming with sword and fire whatever it could find. Against this most savage people, which was accustomed to spare no one, five kings went forth to war, namely the king of the Doringi, the king of the Teutons, the king of the Rugii, and Diocles himself, king of the Sicambri, with many princes, commanders, and warriors; their army was numbered at 260,000 men.

War is waged; a fierce battle is joined with the enemy, in which more than one hundred thousand fighters from the army of the Goths were said to have been slain. On the side of the five kings, twenty-five thousand fell, among whom Heriman also, king of the Doringi, perished. But the Saxons, having gained the victory, divided the spoils of the enemy among the allies with an equal balance; and, when the enemy had been driven far off in flight, the kings returned to their own territories.

Meanwhile, when the Gauls dwelling beyond the Meuse learned that King Diocles had gone out of the country with his army, they gathered in a great multitude and hastened to make war against the Sicambri. When the commanders of the Sicambri, to whom the region had been entrusted, had learned this through scouts, they gathered the whole army of the remaining soldiery of the people and, leading it against the enemy, divided it into three parts. Two of these they arranged as separate battle-lines, and the third they placed in hiding-places for ambush. But as the Gauls approached and brought forward one battle-line, when they saw that the forces were being ordered otherwise, with their opponents hastening to close combat.

For as soon as the Gauls came into sight of the Sicambri, the Sicambri, impatient of delay, directed one line against the enemy formation. When the battle had now begun, the second line, circling around from Nijmegen against the enemy on the flank, threw their order into confusion. And when the fighting was fierce on both sides and the army of the Gauls was already inclining toward flight, suddenly the Sicambri burst forth from the ambushes and, making an attack, held the Gauls enclosed among them, so that no place of flight lay open to those preparing to flee. Thus the wretched Gauls, enclosed in the midst of the Sicambri, were slaughtered to death like cattle, and they suffered so great a massacre that, out of their eighty-eight thousand who had assembled for war, scarcely ten thousand, saved by flight through the benefit of night, escaped.

From the Sicambri, Duke Marcomir, Duke Helenus, and Duke Antenor perished, along with almost four thousand. Nevertheless, the victory, together with the spoils of the enemy, fell to the Sicambri.

King Diocles, however, throughout all the days of his reign, stood vigorously in conflict with the Gauls; meanwhile there was scarcely a year in which he did not harass them with some incursion or battle.

He finally died in the thirty-ninth year of his reign, 298 before the birth of the Lord. By the queen he had four sons, Helenus, Priamus, Nicanor, and Basanus; by other wives, however, he had several sons.

The Sixth King. Helenus reigned for fourteen years.

Helenus, the elder son of the aforesaid King Diocles, succeeding his father, reigned for fourteen years: an idle, wanton man, memorable for no exercise of virtue. In his time the Gauls, making repeated incursions, stirred up no small [unclear] among the Sicambri. Against them his brothers, with the nobles of the kingdom, often led out an army; fighting with varying fortune, they came forth sometimes defeated, sometimes victorious. But the king sat idle at home among gatherings of concubines, dissolving in lust, neither useful to the kingdom nor pleasing to the people: foolish in peace and unfit for war.

Therefore, when the fourteenth year of his reign had not yet been completed, the nobles of the kingdom, assembling at Neopagus with the whole soldiery of the army, by the common decree of all deposed him from the kingship as useless and harmful to the people, in the year 284 before the birth of the Lord.

Helenus reigned for fourteen years.

Helenus was deposed from the kingship because of his idleness, in the year 283 before Christ.

Basanus reigned for twenty-six years.

Basanus, the younger son of the above-mentioned King Diocles, after the deposition of his brother Helenus from the kingship, was raised to the kingdom of the Sicambri by the common guidance, and by the election, of the nobles and soldiers, and reigned for thirty-six years: a man most prudent in his generation, strong, bold, and exceedingly warlike.

The very greatest vanity. Basanus the pontiff. Because of the greatness of his prudence and the deeds magnificently accomplished by him, they called him Basanus the Great. The Sicambri held him in such reverence that they showed him honors not only royal, but almost divine. No one was ever permitted to contradict his commands with impunity, whether in a small matter or a great one, under the certain penalty of a bitter death. For he was exceedingly desirous of divine esteem; for that reason he both did and said great things.

Basanus reigned for twenty-six years.

Basanus, king of the Franks, philosopher and supreme pontiff.

The very greatest vanity. King Basanus wished to be regarded as justice and as a god.

King Basanus kills his son for the sake of justice. Hence, wherever he went, he ordered a [rod?] and a sword to be carried before him, as a manifest sign of justice. He was accustomed to observe it so steadfastly that he spared neither his own son, nor his brother, nor any one of the princes, if anyone knowingly offended even a little against the law of equity which he had established. He had a son named Sedanus, who, accused of adultery, was soon judged by his father to death according to the law that he had established for the Sicambri. But when the nobles pleaded for the young man, the father replied

How steadfast he wished to be esteemed in justice. Hedanus is beheaded by his own father. Thereafter they named the king Just Basan.

[unclear], Basangot.

Fear of King Basan terrified everyone.

The king of the Orchades vainly declared war on the Sicambri.

The Sicambri advanced against the enemies. The war and victory of the Sicambri against the Gauls.

The castle Basanburg is built.

King Basan, pontiff of the idols, restored the sacred rites. What sort of men the Sicambrian priests were.

He said: “Do not, noble men, fight against justice, and against the laws which I decreed with your mature consent, because it is easier to bind with the hand the wind blowing in the air than to turn the mind of King Basan away from the execution of equity.” Having heard this, the princes were silent; but the father himself said to his son: “It is not I, son, who kill you, but the law of the fatherland, which you knowingly transgressed”; and, having seized him, he beheaded him with his own hand.

From that time the Sicambri began to fear their king Basan to such a degree that no one among them, great or small, presumed either to say or to do anything evil against the law. Hence the priests of the gods called the king by the Greek word [unclear], that is, Just Basan. But the common people called him Theobasan, which in the German tongue signifies Basangoth, because all venerated him as a friend of the gods, afterwards to be deified.

From this a proverb arose among the Sicambri, so that whenever one person saw or heard from another anything contrary to the law, he would say: “Hort opp lieffman, kent gy nit dy grote kunig Basan.” As if he had said: “Cease from such things, good man; do you not know how just the great king Basanus is? If he perceived anyone saying or doing unlawful things, without doubt he would kill him as a transgressor.”

In the fifth year of King Basan, the king of the Orchades, having several island chieftains as auxiliaries, declared war on the Sicambri because of the rejection of his daughter, whom King Basanus, having taken as wife, had repudiated and sent back to her father; the cause of this repudiation we described in the first volume of the Annals. But King Basanus, learning of the arrival of his adversaries, advanced against them with a great multitude of fighters to the seashore, not far from the place where the Franks afterwards built Mesoburg. When the Orchades saw from their ships so great an army of the Sicambri, they did not dare to advance onto land.

When the Gauls and Morini again broke in toward the east, where the Sicambri had placed colonies in the region of the Tungri, King Basanus met them with a strong force of his men, and laid them low with so great a slaughter that scarcely a few out of many escaped. Having obtained victory, he built several castles, very strong fortifications, on both sides of the river Meuse, in which he stationed garrisons of the Sicambri.

But on the upper part of the river he built a very strong castle, which he named Basanburg after his own name; in it the kings of the Sicambrian Franks after him dwelt for a long time, on account of the pleasantness and strength of the place.

In the twenty-sixth year of his reign, King Basanus, after many battles bravely fought with various nations round about, wishing to show himself pontiff to the gods, renewed their sacred rites with much superstition. He appointed several priests, highly skilled in the worship of the divine powers, curious in the courses of the stars, in prophecies, in foreknowledges, in the interpretation of dreams, educated in ethical and physical doctrines after the manner of the ancients, and also in songs, in the histories of ancient kings and heroes, and of the race

only of his own, very well practiced in composing and singing in both languages. Among them Heligastus, son of Theocalus the priest, once surpassed the rest in talent and practice in writing. He was in charge of educating the sons of dukes and nobles, and described the deeds of heroes in verse.

Hunibaldus, historiographer of the Franks, writes many marvelous things about this man. Unless they are granted to have been performed by the artifice of some demon, they should be judged to have been fabricated by some writer rather than carried out by a man devoted to idols. He foretold many future things to the Sicambri. He made Jupiter visible to the priests, brought men’s secret plans into public view, and disclosed to King Basanus the hidden counsels of enemies in difficult causes and affairs. Nothing at all seemed to escape him, even what the enemies had discussed against the Sicambri in the most secret counsel. This matter instilled security in his friends, but despair in his enemies.

For King Basanus, together with all the princes of the kingdom, depended wholly on the counsel of Heligastus; and what he ordered, all did, but whatever he forbade, no one dared to attempt. At his command the Sicambri met the enemy, and if he commanded the contrary, they remained peacefully at home. As often as he foretold victory for the Sicambri, they conquered; as often as he foretold otherwise, they were conquered. While he lived the Sicambri prospered in all things; whenever their name was heard, it terrified their enemies and made them fearsome to all round about.

But afterward, when he had completed thirty-two years in his office, and on a certain solemn Thursday, standing in the midst of the priests, hurling thunderbolts in the temple and troubling the upper air with his voice, he was resounding with frenzies in the manner of one prophesying, he suddenly disappeared; and, vanishing completely, no one was ever found who could know where he had gone. The Sicambri, thinking that he had thus become a god, proclaimed that he had been taken into marriage with Diana, and decree sacred rites for him every year.

In the thirty-third year of his reign Basanus moved his army to the upper parts of the river Rhine, against the people called Tegarania, which dwelt toward the south between the Saxons and the Mainz people on this side of the Rhine, under the protection of the Treveri, having its own petty king named Thaborinus. King Basanus killed him together with many others, and subjected his whole region to his dominion. These things happened 251 years before the birth of Christ. The place in which the aforesaid King Thaborinus of the Tegarania fell was called Mount Thabor from his name; it is about four miles from the confluence. There Basanus, king of the Franks, built a very strong castle, which, in perpetual memory of the victory, he called Mount Thaborinus; but by a corrupted word it is today called Montabaur by the inhabitants.

In the thirty-sixth year of his reign Basanus, very great king of the Sicambri, on the solemnity of his birthday at Nijmegen, summoned his sons, brothers, dukes, nobles, and the distinguished men of the families to a banquet. With them for seven days [unclear], they performed sacred rites to their ancestral gods, and he showed Jupiter in the air above the temple, visible to all.

Clodomer, son of Basanus, is made king by his father. King Basanus suddenly disappeared in the assembly. King Basanus, most eager for divinity. In the year 248 before the birth of Christ. The eighth. Clodomirus reigned eighteen years. Envoys of the Gauls sent to the Sicambri. The Saxons and Doringi, allies of the Sicambri. The Saxons with the Doringi came to the aid of the Sicambri.

On one day he designated his son Clodomirus, with the consent of all the nobles, as king over the Sicambri. He foretold many future events to the people in his native song. He commended his sons and the kingdom to the princes. He enjoined justice, and, having entered the chapel of the temple, appeared nowhere again.

I do not know what I should bestow on these little tales: indignation or laughter? Whether he was taken away by trickery or by art remains uncertain. But I think this one thing was the cause: the desire, in a man undoubtedly removed either by his own wit or by the spontaneous will of a demon, of obtaining the estimation of divinity. For, as Amerodagus, philosopher of the Sicambri, writes, King Basanus was most eager for divinity. He cultivated justice. He loved his people. He laid low the enemy. He was most dutiful to good men, always cruel and severe to the wicked.

But he vanished, or, as I should more correctly say, withdrew himself, as Amerodagus is the authority, from the public assembly of the nobles, as we have said, in the thirty-sixth year of his reign, and in the year 248 before the birth of the Lord. The Sicambri, judging that he had been transferred into the fellowship of the gods, worshipped him under the name Basangot.

The elder son of Basanus, succeeding in the kingdom, just as his father had ordained with the consent of the princes, reigned eighteen years. In the first year of his reign, as soon as the Gauls learned that Basanus had vanished, whom they themselves did not doubt was dead, they sent envoys to Clodomirus and demanded back from him all the land between the Meuse and the Rhine, and all around in the circuit, which the Sicambri, at their first entry into the territories on this side of the Rhine, had violently usurped for themselves against justice. If he should scorn to restore it, they threatened that they were prepared to recover everything by the sword, whether he sent back a negative reply through the appointed envoys, or answered nothing at all.

But King Clodomirus, as though he were going to hold counsel with his princes about the urgent matter, prudently and carefully delayed the envoys of the Gauls and kept them with him for a rather long time; and, taking the greatest care that no secret of the design in his mind should come to their knowledge, he ordered his servants to feed them abundantly and arrange for them to have pleasant days. Meanwhile King Clodomirus, sending messengers to the kings of the Saxons and Doringi, very urgently asked that they quickly and secretly send forces in aid to the Sicambri, their friends, against the Gauls, their common adversaries. The Saxons came with the Doringi in support of their friends, as they were asked, bringing forth an army of one hundred thousand fighters. When matters had been arranged very secretly at his nod, King Clodomirus allowed the envoys of the Gauls, given gifts, to depart; and, lest anything on the way about the foregoing matters could come to their knowledge, he assigned escorts for the journey to them as they set out safely, who should accompany them and more cautiously observe them as they went with letters of this sort.

Clodomir, great king, to the satraps and Gallic peoples. We marvel at your rashness, in that you demand back from us the land which our forefathers long ago, by right of war, most justly vindicated with the sword from yours, as from unjust neighbors and their manifest enemies. Consider that our forces are far superior to yours, and cease from this wrongful rashness of folly. Remember the disasters which you formerly suffered, as you deserved, at the hands of our divine father, numbered among the gods, and of his parents, and be quiet, hiding in your holes with the foxes. It is ours to command you, and yours humbly to obey our commands. But if you presume to come against us, we have determined to meet you with power and to defend with the sword what our ancestors handed down to us.

When the Gauls had received these letters and messengers, they were stirred to anger, and resolved to take vengeance on the Sequanians for the Sicambri. After a bridge had been skillfully built over the Meuse, they led across a huge army of fighters. King Clodomir met them powerfully with 264,000 men, and, having divided the army into parts, placed one in ambush, sent another [unclear] in the region [unclear], and led the third part, which was the greater in number of soldiers, against the enemy.

The Sicambri engaged with the Gauls in a place not far from the river Meuse, which is called Delon, and for some time the battle was fought with doubtful fortune. At last the Sicambri, feigning flight, began gradually to retreat until they had finally drawn the Gauls rather far from the river Meuse to the place of ambush. There the Sicambri then stood immovable, and those who had earlier pretended flight fought back most bravely, like giants. Meanwhile the soldiers, going around, came to the crossing of the river and, after the enemy guards had been killed or driven far off, seized the bridge first. The rest at once burst out from the ambush and, attacking the enemy fiercely, cut them down from behind, slaughtered them, and killed them without pity. Finally those who could, seeking safety in flight, since they did not know that the bridge had been seized in advance by the Sicambri, were enclosed on every side and cut down by the enemy; nor was there any place to escape death, since those lying hidden pressed upon them. With night coming on, few out of many escaped alive, those who were able to flee into the dark groves and woods.

Thereafter the kingdom of the Sicambri rested from the tumult of wars for a few years; but afterward, when peace was broken, the people often took up mighty arms again. The other deeds and wars of King Clodomir, which he had with [exterminations?], we have written, following Hunibald, in the first volume of our Annals. King Clodomir died in the eighteenth year of his reign, 230 years before the birth of the Lord, leaving three sons by Queen Ermedrude, who had been the daughter of the king of the Teutons: Nicanor, Helianus, [unclear]. Clodomir’s eldest son [Helenus?], succeeding his father, reigned thirty-four years, a stern man, just among his own nation, and warlike, who [unclear].

The king was a man utterly unable to endure any injuries from enemies, especially from the Gauls, and he was fierce against enemies. For this reason he often fought against them savagely, with varying fortune.

For from that time when that people, sprung from Trojan stock, first came from the borders of the Scythians into Germany, to the mouths of the Rhine, it never ceased from the harassment of the Gauls, until at last, not without [unclear], nor always victorious, with much bloodshed of its own men, it powerfully subjected all Gaul to itself.

No one was ever able fully to overcome the Franks, or Sicambri; no one imposed upon their ferocity the bridle of subjection. Rather, they did not lay aside the desire for ruling, which they had once imbibed, before they had brought all Gaul, Germany, and at the same time Italy under their power, the Roman empire having been annihilated and many kings destroyed.

For, as was said above, it is clear from the reckoning of times that nine hundred and thirty years elapsed from the entry of the Franks, as they are now called, into the districts of Germany on this side of the Rhine, down to Clodio the Great, who, as the first victor over the Alamanni, believed in Christ. During these years the Sicambri fought with the Gauls, never ceasing to wage war against them, although they were often partly routed, until at last they overcame them all. The Franks fought against the Gauls for 930 years. Many of the Franks were also called Germans.

It should be known, however, that they were not always named Franks, nor Sicambri, but frequently changed their names together with their settlements. For indeed, as Hunibald testifies, when after the destruction of Troy they wandered for many years among various nations and did not long have stable settlements in one place, among the Scythians [unclear], among the Armenians they were called Armenians. When they dwelt at the mouths of the Danube, they were called neither Franks nor Sicambri; but because they bordered on the Scythians, they acquired the speech and name of the Scythians. Amerodacus, historian of the Franks. Afterwards, driven by the Goths through the envy of the Romans, as Amerodacus is the authority, they descended into the territories of Germany; and, having established their settlements, as was said above, at the mouths of the Rhine, they learned the language of the German Saxons, and were first called Neomagi, afterwards also Germans. Then, named Sicambri from Cambra, they changed even that name in time, stirred by love for King Francus, from whom the name of the Franks, as will be said later in its proper order, took its beginning. Hence it came about that the writers of other peoples, whenever in the accounts of their histories they introduce the memory of the deeds of this people, more often call them Germans than Sicambri or Franks; and this has usually brought no small occasion of error to those who do not know the true origin of the Franks, while they believe that the Franks were either indigenous or had begun from a conspiracy of a few men.

But King Nicanor, joined with the Saxons and Thuringians, in the fourteenth year of his reign, marched with a great multitude to war against the Goths, who had again burst into the territories of the Teutons and Saxons. War of the Franks against [unclear]. In the first encounter the Goths were superior and crushed the Germans with a great slaughter. But soon, when the army had been restored, the Goths were defeated; many thousands of them perished both by the edge of the sword and submerged in the waters. The rest sought safety in flight. In the twenty-first year of his reign he waged a naval war against the king of the Orkneys, in support of the king of Britain, whose sister Constantia,

XXVIII.Laudabilis ī principe consuetudo. Marcomer regnumduxit sicambrorū Marcomet rex franCorum moriturVNDECIMVS,Clodius regnauitannis undecim Clodius rex in bellop̄rim moritur a gallisB iij

by name, he had as his wife. But he waged war not very successfully, because many of his men, through inexperience in naval combat, perished at sea. He was also always in conflict with the Gauls, and fought many battles with them; and often, fighting most bravely with his men, he triumphed gloriously.

At length he died in the thirty-fourth year of his reign, in the one hundred ninety-sixth year before the birth of Christ, leaving five sons: Marcomirus, who succeeded to the kingdom; Antenor, who ruled the maritime regions; Priam, who died at his maternal uncle's in Britain; Helenus, who held the duchy on this side of the Rhine, between Saxony and the Rhine, over the Tegarani; and Clodius, duke of the [Mosanorum?]. Son of Nicanor, the elder by birth of the king's [unclear], succeeding his father, he reigned twenty-eight years. A foremost man in his genealogy, an augur, a seer, an interpreter of dreams and of events, he [unclear]. He ordered the great deeds of his people, whenever leisure allowed, to be sung before him, both in the palace and in the temples, so that their spirit, stirred by the example of these men, might be directed to the defense of his nation and always to the enlargement of the kingdom. This was the custom among the elders and the Germans: that the deeds or sayings of heroes worthy of remembrance should be entrusted by the priests of the temples to native songs; and, after the youth had been instructed in learning, remembering, and singing these, [unclear] failed at last.

King Marcomirus, however, ruled the people of the Sicambri at all times prudently and with the greatest moderation; he increased the worship of the tutelary gods; he fought many battles with the Romans, the Gauls, and the other nations round about; and in his time he enlarged the borders of the first kingdom not a little. On these matters Hunibald composed a fuller history, which here, out of love of brevity, we pass over.

King Marcomirus died in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, which was the one hundred sixty-eighth year before the incarnation of our Savior Jesus Christ. The first-born son of King Marcomirus of the Sicambri after his father, reigned eleven years. In his time the sword of the Romans, directed into Gaul, the Sicambri by no small [unclear] repelled.

After many battles fought with the Gauls, in the last year of his reign King Clodius, having gathered a huge army both of his own men and of Saxons, again fought with them not far from the fortress of Basanburg. In this battle, while looking about with too little caution in the battle-line, he was killed by his adversaries. But the Sicambri, emboldened, notwithstanding the death of the king, continued the war; and, fighting bravely, at length defeated the Gauls, and after killing many of them, put others to flight. And many Franks perished. The Franks always pursued the Gauls in war. Nicanor, king of the Sicambri, dies.

Tenth. Marcomer reigned twenty-eight years. A praiseworthy custom in a prince. Marcomer held the kingdom of the Sicambri. Marcomer, king of the Franks, dies. Eleventh. Clodius reigned eleven years. King Clodius dies in battle, first, at the hands of the Gauls.

Before the birth of the Lord, in the year 57.

The twelfth: Antenor reigned sixteen years. Truces are made between the Sicambri and the Gauls. The priests of the Sicambri were of great power. King Antenor dies.

The thirteenth: Clodomer reigned twenty years. When the truces had ended, the Gauls declare war on the Sicambri. War of the Sicambri with the Gauls. The Gauls are overcome by the Sicambri. Clodomir, king of the Franks, died.

The thirteenth king: Merodacus reigned twenty-eight years. The Franks, with 220,000, laid waste Italy.

But King Clodius dies, slain in the Gallic war, as has been said, in the eleventh year of his reign, but in the 157th year before the birth of Christ.

The elder son of King Clodius reigned after his father for sixteen years. He made with the Gauls truces for ten years, which our people, with faith interposed, call treugas; this also pleased the Romans, who were always on the side of the Gauls, enemies and foes, as was said, of the nation of the Sicambri. For the king was thirty-six years old when he began to reign, more a lover of peace than of war, and he did little worthy of memory except this one thing: being more humane than the rest, he forbade men to be sacrificed to the divine powers. This displeased many nobles of the Sicambri, who thought that fear of themselves among foreign nations was being diminished. But because this act of piety was decreed by the counsel and assent of the priests, the constitution itself remained inviolable. For priestly authority among them was always greater and more excellent than that of all leaders and princes. King Antenor dies in the sixteenth year of his reign, but in the 141st year before the birth of the Lord.

The son of Antenor reigned after his father for twenty years. In his first year the Romans, through Scipio, overthrew the Numantines and brought them under their own power. In his sixth year the Gauls, the truces which they had made with his father now ended, determined, after assembling a great army of their men, to move against the Sicambri; and, crossing the river Meuse, they were the first to declare war on the enemy. Clodomir, surrounded by the aid of the Germans, without delay confidently met the Gauls and fought most bravely for his people and kingdom. A very fierce battle was joined there for a long time, and many fell on both sides. At last the Gauls turned their backs; the Sicambri pursued them as far as the river and laid low the greater part of the army with the edge of the sword. If they had either thrown down or seized the bridge, as King Clodomirus, son of great Basanus, had once done, not even one of the Gauls could have escaped. After the Gauls had suffered that disaster, as long as Clodomir survived they no longer crossed the Meuse with an army, though in their usual manner they often carried out raids.

But King Clodomer, after many battles had been fought with the Romans, the Gauls, and the peoples higher up around the Rhine and the Moselle, dies in the twentieth year of his reign, which was the 121st year before the birth of Christ.

The son of Clodomir, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-eight years, a high-minded, vigorous, and most daring prince. How warlike he was, both the Romans and the Gauls were able to feel, with whom he fought many times bravely, even with his own hand. For when the Saxons, Thuringians, and Germans were bringing aid, he led against the Romans into Italy an army of 220,000 fighting men, and, laying waste...

all the places round about. He came with his forces as far as Ravenna and, enriched with much spoil, returned victorious.

He also, on his return, grievously afflicted many colonies of the Romans, subjected them to still heavier hardships, and made his name formidable to all. Greatly moved by these events, the Romans, having joined many nations to themselves, declared war on the Sicambri; when the necessities for the expedition had been prepared, they assembled for battle. And lest the Saxons or the Thuringians should bring aid to the Sicambri, the Romans had first induced the Goths and Slavs by promised gifts, so that at one and the same time [the former] would subdue the Saxons, and [the Romans] themselves the Sicambri. King Merodacus, therefore, being of necessity deserted by the Saxons and Thuringians, called upon the king of the northern island, whose people we today call Danes; he came with a hundred thousand and brought aid to the Sicambri.

And so, in the twenty-second year of his reign, he perceived that auxiliary troops, an immense army, were coming against him. For Marius, leader of the Romans, sent the Roman legions with the Gauls, under Theodomenus as commander, beyond the Meuse against the Sicambri, whom they themselves called Germans. They joined battle fiercely, and many thousands of men fell on both sides; the Sicambri fled, having lost more than twenty thousand fighters. After this, Merodacus, having restored his army and become stronger than the Gauls and Romans, inflicted much slaughter upon them, as, following Hunibald, we have said more fully in the first volume of our histories or annals.

Afterward, when he had joined many battles with the Gauls and Romans and had considerably enlarged the borders of his nation, King Merodacus died in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, but in the ninety-third year before the birth of Christ.

Cassander, the elder son of King Merodacus, succeeded his father and reigned twenty-one years. He was a very warlike man; in his time the Gauls, with the aid of the Romans, often crossed the river Meuse and invaded the territories of the Sicambri as enemies. Cassander, meeting them in the strength of his men, forbade the enemies the devastation of his nation. For all the days in which he ruled over the Sicambri, he was in conflict with the Gauls and Romans.

In these times Borbista, king of the Goths, entered the borders of Saxony with a countless multitude of fighters, devastating the region with fire and sword. Against him three very powerful kings, namely Arthari, king of the Saxons, Hamer, king of the Thuringians, and the aforesaid Cassander, king of the Sicambri, united their armies into one and advanced to battle. When the encounter had been made, the fighting was fierce for a long time; many fell on both sides. At last King Borbista turned his back, and the Germans obtained the victory.

On another occasion after this, King Borbista again entered Saxony with a very great multitude of Goths, cruelly devastated the region with fire and sword as far as the river Vistula, and, having seized much spoil from the Germans, withdrew; nor did he presume to advance farther that day.

The Romans declared war on the Sicambri. Expedition of the Romans against the Sicambri. Marius the Roman came against the Franks. Merodacus, king of the Sicambri, died. The fifteenth. Cassander reigned twenty-one years. Borbista, king of the Goths, devastates the Saxons. The Sicambri and Saxons with the Thuringians. The Goths are overcome by the Germans. Again the Goths enter Saxony.

For he had known the unconquerable strength of the Germans, and how often the pressure of the Romans had tested it.

But King Cassander, after many battles bravely fought with the Gauls and Romans, died in the twenty-first year of his reign; before the birth of the Lord, however, in the year 72. He was buried at Neopagus with many treasures.

[Antharius?], the son of King Cassander. After his father he reigned for twenty-five years. Of him Hunibald writes that he crushed the Moguntines, Roman colonists, in a pitiable slaughter; he burned and overthrew the city, which afterward is seen to have been transferred and built in that place now [unclear], across the river Ciana and the valley, on the slope of the mountain by the bank of the Rhine. This lamentable desolation of the Moguntines took place in the sixteenth year of King Arthar, which was the fifty-sixth year before the birth of Christ, as is shown from the sequence of the times.

King Anthar, with the help of the Germans, entered Gaul, burned villages, and many times carried away limitless booty and spoils. He wrought great devastation throughout Gaul, burned cities, destroyed villages, overthrew castles, shattered the strength of the people, and reduced a region long fruitful to a wilderness.

But when King Antharius had grown old, in the last year of his reign, which was the seventh before the birth of Christ, when the Gauls again broke into the region of the Sicambri and crossed the Meuse, he met them with the army of his people to fight. There, when he engaged rather incautiously, he was surrounded by the enemy and perished with twenty thousand Sicambri in the twenty-fifth year of his reign. And the Gauls on that occasion brought great calamity upon the Sicambri.

[Francus?], the elder son of King Antharius, from whom the Sicambri were thereafter called Franks, as Hunibald is the authority, reigned after his father for twenty-eight years: a fierce, daring, and warlike man, a most vigorous defender of his people. He avenged the death of his father severely enough upon the Gauls, and waged many wars with foreign nations, always a victor and glorious triumphator. The people of the Franks rightly boast that he was the founder of both their name and their honor. This King Francus was accustomed to fight, not to flee; he was beloved by his own people and very mild, but to all his enemies always exceedingly to be feared.

In the first year of his reign he contracted a perpetual treaty with the Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians. With the consent of all the dukes and nobles of the Sicambri, confirming the friendship on silver tablets, according to the ancient custom of the people, they established the conditions of the agreements in this way: that the Sicambri and the Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians, under their distinct kings and princes, should thereafter be regarded as one people, like brothers and kinsmen, and should remain in it; and war
