that whatever threatened the kingdom of one of these, from whatever people, should concern all, and should be repelled with united arms and common expenses.

This confederation of kings terrified the senate and people of Rome more than can be said; they labored in various ways, with diverse ingenuity and manifold contrivance, to dissolve the compacted alliance of the Germans, and in every way in vain. From that time the courage and power of the Franks were always suspect to the Romans, since they feared, as afterward happened, that the Germans would gain possession of the monarchy of all Europe. And this was the reason why Octavian, Caesar of the Romans, at the birth of Christ had the whole world obedient to the Romans registered by heads, thinking that the Franks were to be destroyed by the multitude of peoples; at that time, as yet, the writers of the histories of nations called them Germans.

But in the third year of the reign of Francus, when the Romans saw that they could by no device break up the alliance of the German kings, they again sent the Goths into the borders of the Saxons; and these, settling for almost ten years in the borders of Germany, were gradually and successively thinking of spreading into the interior of the nation just mentioned. Meanwhile King Francus fought frequently with the Gauls, and avenged his father’s death upon them with harsh vicissitude, and during that time killed many thousands of them. But when the Goths too were daily breaking farther into the interior of Germany, the Saxons together with the Teutons, at last compelled by necessity, resolved to make war upon them. Having summoned their allies to their aid according to the agreements, the Sicambri and the Thuringians led out to battle an army of two hundred and thirty thousand men. But the Scanzians and the Goths too, having themselves summoned allies, opposed to the arriving Germans an almost innumerable multitude. A very savage battle was joined between the parties in the place called Colmasus; with many falling on both sides, they fought from morning until night with the issue of war uncertain.

On the following day the Germans divided the army into three parts and set individual commanders over them. But the Sicambri, fighting most boldly under their king Francus, cried out, repeatedly shouting the name of their commander Francus: “Here, Francus!” At last the Goths were defeated, and more than eighty thousand of them were slain; the rest, slipping away in flight, returned with their children and wives to their former hiding-places. Thus the Saxons, with the aid of the Franks and the Thuringians, recovered their borders, which for ten years had been devastated and occupied by foreigners.

From that time the Sicambri, laying aside the name they had had before, began, from love of their king, to call themselves Franks. Indeed, as Hunibald bears witness, not only the nobles, but also all the soldiers and the whole people of the entire nation were so delighted by the very novelty of the name that they prevailed upon the king by prayers to sanction by public edict that thereafter they were to be called forever not Sicambri but Franks. This the king established all the more willingly, because he more eagerly loved the immortality of his name. Therefore those who first by some were called Sicambri, by others Germans by reason of the alliance, were called Franks from Francus. And indeed, in a wondrous manner [unclear]

This confederation of kings did not please the Romans and Gauls.

Whence the Franks are called free, the free Franks, because they never served.

They gloried in the novelty of this name, since for many times thereafter, whenever they met one another, they greeted each other thus: “A good day, free Frank.” Nevertheless, not suddenly but only after much time did this name at last come into use, so that the people itself was called Franks even among other nations. For to the Romans, and especially to the Gauls, the name of the Franks was hateful. Hence among their writers they were more often called Germans than either Sicambri or Franks. But Hunnibald did not pass over in silence whence, or from whom, the name of the Sicambri had its origin.

That the Franks were formerly called Sicambri is attested not only by Hunnibald, but also by blessed Remigius, the archbishop, who, as Gregory, bishop of Tours, records, when he was to baptize Clovis, king of the Franks, the first of the Frankish kings converted to Christ, as we shall say in its proper place, said before the assembled nobles, as he laid aside the royal ornaments and humbled himself for the sacred laver, in the hearing of all: “Meekly bow your neck, Sicamber. Worship what you burned. Burn what you worshiped.” Of the history of this matter we have already spoken more fully, following Hunnibald, in the first volume of the Annals.

Therefore in the twenty-fourth year before the birth of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, which was the thirteenth year of King Frangus, the Sicambri changed their ancient name into a new one, although both before and afterward among writers they were more often called Germans or Sicambri. For although they themselves took for themselves the name Frank under the aforementioned king and always retained it, nevertheless it could not immediately come into use among foreign nations, especially hostile ones. From this the fact is most plainly established that the writers of histories who flourished in human letters among the Romans, the Gauls also, or other nations, at the time when the name was changed and nevertheless for many years after this as well, whether from ignorance or from detestation of the term, more often called this people German than Frankish. For it is certain that the Romans came to know the name of the Franks not through writings but through arms, not through love but through fear, not through adoption but through subjection.

But now, when the message had been received, in no way broken, he said to the soldiers: “If you are free, if you are worthy of the name of Frangus, now at once resume your strength and avenge so great an injury.” They, together with the nobles, said with one voice: “We are most ready, O most free Frankish king, either to conquer with you every people opposed to us, or to die fighting.” Gladdened by these words, the king immediately sent messengers to the Saxons, the Germans, and likewise the Thuringians, asking aid by right of alliance against the assault of the Gauls. All of them sent the requested contingents of soldiers with great eagerness: the Saxons, namely, 84,000 fighters; the Germans and Teutons, 60,000; and the Thuringians, 46,000.

Joined with these, the Franks, with great forces, very hastily led an army of three hundred thousand men against their adversaries. But when Francus the king saw the desolation of the region which the Gauls had wrought, moved by great indignation of spirit, he said: “See, my most valiant fellow-soldiers, you who rightly grieve that the blood of your fathers has been shed, what those most faithless Gauls have done. I swear by the head of my father Antharius, whom those most wicked men killed, that I shall give no rest to my head until I have notably avenged myself upon them.” And they all praised his purpose.

Therefore, when a bridge had been made with ships and much timber, in two days he brought the army across; and, leaving forty thousand men to guard the crossing, he advanced with the remaining multitude into Gaul. And he made such a slaughter as no one of the Sicambri before him either could have made or is believed to have conceived in his mind. For, entering as far as the river Tabul and both the western and the northern sea, he ravaged with fire and sword the Tungri, the Tarubani, the Legii, and whatever lies between or adjacent to these. When the Gauls joined battle with him, he overcame, routed, and destroyed them with such ease that he was thought to be not a man but some divine power sent from heaven. Hence all the nations round about, exceedingly terrified, feared any further to engage the Franks, as most savage monsters. In that encounter and devastation of the Gauls, more than two hundred thousand of them fell by the sword of the Franks, with children, infants, and women. For just as the Gauls had previously done when they devastated the Sicambri, sparing no one, so they received from the same.

Hence the Senate and people of Rome, moved with indignation, sent legions of soldiers against the Saxons into Germany, Marcus Julius being commander. For they did not think it would be safe to engage the Franks, whom they themselves called Germans, before they had first completely subdued the Saxons and the Dorings. When the Romans therefore entered Saxony, at first indeed they conquered, killing eighteen thousand Germans. But when Francus the king heard of the destruction of his allies, he sent his son Chlogio as commander, with a great army, to the aid of the confederates. They, having recovered their strength and again engaged the Romans, obtained the victory and put the enemy to flight, many of them being slain by the sword, in the twenty-fourth year of King Francus.

Finally King Francus, weighed down by labors and old age, after many battles conducted most victoriously against the Romans, Goths, and other nations, and after the kingdom of the Franks had been enlarged not a little and its settlements extended, died in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, precisely in the ninth year before the birth of the Lord. His wars, customs, institutions, laws, and victories were written by Clodomirus, the Frank, high priest, in German verse, and by Hunibald in prose, in the Latin language; under their guidance we have material both here and in the first volume of the annals of German and Frankish affairs which we have written.

Three hundred thousand Franks and Germans against the Gauls. The Franks, after making a bridge over the Meuse, devastate Gaul. A great part of Gaul is made desolate by the Franks. Fear of the Franks seized all nations. Expedition of the Romans against the Germans. The Romans are overcome by the Franks in battle. Francus king of the Franks dies in the year precisely the ninth before Christ. Clodomirus the Frank, writer.

The eighteenth, Clogio, reigned for 30 years.

Clogio, the elder son of Francus the king, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for 30 years: a man most cunning, versatile in intellect, an augur, magician, and most curious astrologer. Concerning him the aforementioned pontiff of the Franks, the counsellor and seer Clodomirus, set out many stupendous marvels in verse, of which we made mention in the first volume.

His mother, named Lothildis, daughter of the king of the Doringi, was the chief priestess or priest of the temple of Pallas, devoted to the magical arts, by the practice of which she did many marvels. For, as the aforesaid authors wrote, by her songs and incantations she destroyed whichever enemies of her son she wished, made them unfortunate, and, though absent however far away, killed them by the ministry of demons; by sorcery she procured victory for the Franks, and fear, terror, and flight for their enemies. Rains, thunders, flashes of lightning, and terrible storms in the air she brought on by her songs as often as, where, and upon whom she wished.

In the fourth year of his reign the Romans again launched an expedition into Germany; the allied kings, meeting them with no lack of energy, did not cease bravely to repel force with arms until they compelled the enemy to retreat and flee. For King Clogio, in the name of the Franks, having engaged in battle with the Roman army, fought most bravely for his people, and at last, after many had fallen on both sides, the Romans departed without victory.

In the eighteenth year of the reign of the aforementioned Clogio, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, there was born in Bethlehem of Judah the Lord, the savior of the whole universe, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, from the untouched ever-virgin Mary. In that year, according to Hunibald, by an edict of Caesar Augustus the world subject to Roman rule was enrolled head by head; this, besides the mystical reason, being done by divine providence, was not without literal meaning, the Franks providing the occasion.

In the same year also King Clogio, at his mother’s urging, made his son Phrisus, his second-born, duke of that region which lies by the German sea toward the north; and from the name of that duke it was called Phrisia, as Hunibald maintains, down to the present day. Again, after ten years, with the consent of the aforementioned King Clogio and of all the princes of the people of the Franks, the same son Phrisius was raised to kingship, on this condition, namely, that all kings of Phrisia, like the other dukes, should remain forever subject to the king of the Franks, should pay each year a tribute of 260 oxen, and should fight with the Franks, in the manner of the other allies, against whatsoever enemies.

But Clogio, king of the Franks, died after many brave deeds, in the thirtieth year of his reign, which was the twentieth year of the Lord’s nativity. Hunibald writes many things concerning his character, prophecies, and oracles.

VICESIMVS.Marcomer regnauit annis.XVIII.Treuerenfes.Mogũtinenses.Colonien̄.Iesus christus in iudea sub pontio patĩ Romanilegiones mittũt in britania.C iij

Herimer, the elder son of King Elogion, succeeding his father, reigned for twelve years, a warlike man and excessively bold. In the third year of his reign the Gauls made an incursion and came as far as the Meuse, laying waste with hostile rashness everything that belonged to the jurisdiction of the Franks, except fortifications and castles; and after this they hastily withdrew to their own territory with booty and spoils.

But afterward, when this incursion of the Gauls became known to King Herimer, he was moved to anger; and, having summoned to himself the dukes beyond the Meuse, through whose negligence the Gauls had broken in, he at once proceeded against them according to the laws of the Franks. For thus it was contained in the law: Let a prince established under the king of the Franks in ducal power diligently guard the province entrusted to him. But if through his negligence enemies enter the region, if they injure our people or despoil the inhabitants of the land of their goods, let him pay half of his possessions into the king’s purse, and let him be duke no longer, but live deprived of honor. If he willingly permitted entry to the enemies, let him be buried alive or punished by beheading; but let his wives, together with his children and all his goods, pass into the king’s service.

Then, having called to his aid his German, Teutonic, and [Doringian?] allies, King Herimer entered Gaul with a great multitude, and subdued them with such great slaughter that for many years they could not recover their former strength. Finally, however, in the last year of his reign, when he had again led an army into Gaul and, being too bold, not to say rash or presumptuous, fought rather incautiously, he was killed by them in battle, in the year of the Lord 32.

Marcomirus, brother of the aforesaid King Herimer, who had been slain by the Gauls, succeeding his brother in the kingdom of the Franks, reigned for eighteen years, a man tall in stature, but in his character feared and terrible. He engaged in many battles with the Romans and Gauls, and often grievously afflicted the people of Mainz and Trier, together with those of Cologne.

In the second year of his reign, the only-begotten Son of God, the Lord and Savior of the world, Jesus Christ, born as man of Mary, ever and most pure Virgin, without union with a man, according to that same humanity was crucified, suffered, and died for our salvation, and was buried, at Jerusalem, the city of the Jews, under Pontius Pilate, governor of the Romans. He descended to hell and rescued the righteous from there; on the third day he rose from the dead; and ascending into heaven, he sits at the right hand of the Father, to judge the living and the dead, and he lives forever.

In the tenth year of King Marcomirus, Clodius, Caesar of the Romans, led an army into Britain, which we now call England by the customary name, and made it, together with Armorica and the Orkney islands, tributary to the Romans.

Tenth. Ninth. Herimer reigned twelve years.

King Herimer was a most warlike man. Incursion of the Gauls into the Meuse of the Sicambri. The just law of the Sicambri.

The Sicambri devastated all Gaul. Herimer, king of the Sicambri, perished in battle.

Twentieth. Marcomer reigned eighteen years. People of Trier. People of Mainz. People of Cologne. Jesus Christ in Judea under Pontius Pilate. Roman legions are sent into Britain. C iij

Quibus auditis cōsternati sunt omnes qui erāt

On his going and returning he most grievously afflicted the Franks dwelling between the Meuse and the Rhine, although not without bloodshed among his own men.

At that time Guiderius, son of the late King Cymbeline, was reigning in Britain; when he had been slain in battle by the army of Claudius, his brother Arviragus soon rose up in his place. Setting the royal diadem upon himself, and after many Romans had been killed, he pursued Claudius all the way to the ships. Caesar, seeing that he could not overcome Arviragus, offered peace, gave him his daughter as wife, and recovered the tribute that had been denied to the Romans. With the help of his son-in-law he also carried his army over to the Orkney islands.

Marcomer, however, the aforesaid king of the Franks, died in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the fiftieth year of the Lord's Nativity, in the ninth Roman indiction.

Clodomir, son of the aforesaid King Marcomer, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for twelve years. He was a restless and very warlike man; of him Hunibald reports that he was most hostile to the Romans and the Gauls, and desired nothing more than to erase the memory of them. Scarcely a year passed in which he did not launch an expedition into Gaul at least once.

In the first year of his reign, three suns appeared at once, which gradually returned into one; and there followed throughout all Europe a great famine and an immense mortality not only of men, but also of beasts of burden.

In the ninth year, King Clodomir, with a great army of his men, crossed the Rhine and the Meuse, drove out the Gauls, and recovered everything that had previously been lost. He fought with the Romans near Mainz, with the aid of the Germans, but he could not prevent them from repairing the city. He died in the twelfth year of his reign, in the sixty-second year of the Lord's Nativity, in the fifth Roman indiction.

Antenor, son of King Clodomir, reigned after his father for six years. Throughout the whole time in which he reigned, he waged war with the Gauls and the Romans; and at last, on this account, he perished miserably with many nobles of the kingdom, when, as we shall say, the bridge broke on the river Meuse and he was drowned.

In the last year of his reign, after a bridge had been built of wood over boats in the ancient manner, he led his army across the river into Gaul; and, after ravaging the region, he hastened his return into Francia with much booty and many spoils. And when the greater part of the army had already crossed the river, while the king himself, with the nobles and the rest of those at the rear, was still waiting on the bank, suddenly the bridge, weighed down by the number of horsemen, fell; and the boats, loosed from one another when the ropes broke, presented a pitiable spectacle to those watching, as many fell into the river.

The king, thunderstruck and surely troubled in mind, began to take counsel with those who were present about repairing the bridge, when behold, they are soon told that the Gauls were coming behind them in a great multitude of fighters, ready for battle. When this was heard, all who were

with the king; for them time and place denied flight, while their smaller army forbade battle. Therefore, since no way of escape lay open except the way of swimming through the river, they threw into the water whatever arms could weigh them down, and tried for safety by swimming. The king also, having cast off his cuirass and girded over his tunic only with a sword-belt and sword, lowered himself with his horse into the waves. All the rest, compelled by necessity, lowered themselves into like danger.

They all began to swim at once, some on horses, others sustaining themselves against the force of the waters with hands and feet. Of these, many reached the bank by swimming; many also who had no skill in swimming, choked by the waters, perished in the midst of the waves. Among them King Antenor was submerged, with nine princes, whose names are these: Duke Priamus, Duke Walther, Duke Clogio, Duke Herimer, Duke Antenor, Duke Marcomerus, Duke Clodius, Duke Richimer, Duke Antenor, Duke [Ruutvuicus?], with sixty-three other nobles of the Franks. Thus, then, Antenor, king of the Franks, perished in the sixth year of his reign, in the sixty-eighth year from the Lord’s nativity, in the eleventh Roman indiction.

Ratherus, or, as another writes, Ratherius, the elder son of the aforementioned King Antenor, after his father’s death reigned over the Franks for twenty-one years. He was a magnanimous, daring, strong man, who with his sword always most bravely defended the people of the Franks from every incursion of the Gauls, fearing no one, dreading no one, but himself to be feared by all. In his second year, Nero, the wicked emperor of the Romans, stirred up the first persecution against the Christians; at Rome he killed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, and throughout the whole empire he cruelly destroyed many thousands of believers.

Ratherus, king of the Franks, however, wore down the Gauls in many ways; he avenged his father’s death with arms, fire, and iron; he restored the territories taken from his people; he built castles, cities, and fortifications; he renewed the treaty with the Germans, Saxons, and Doringian kings, which Francus the king had once concluded a hundred years before, as we said above; and he enlarged the boundaries of the kingdom of the Franks.

After these things at last he died in the twenty-first year of his reign, in the eighty-ninth year from the Lord’s nativity, in the second Roman indiction. He was buried in the city Ratherama, which he himself had built new from the foundations, dedicated to his own name. His magnificent deeds Arebaldus, bishop of the Franks and poet, described in verse after the manner of the ancients; these Hunibald later reduced to prose.

Richimerus, son of King Ratherus, succeeding his father, reigned for twenty-four years: a prince magnificent in all things, daring, warlike, and excessively superstitious in the worship of his people’s idols, since he wished not only to equal the Romans in the number of gods, but even to defeat and surpass them.

The king of the Franks committed himself to the waters with the dukes.

King Antenor perished in the river with nine dukes.

Nine dukes and sixty-three nobles perished.

Antenor perished in the year of the Lord 68.

Twenty-third. Ratherius reigned for twenty-one years.

Nero, the most faithless man among the reprobate.

He renews the treaty between Franks and Saxons; he dies.

Arebaldus, bishop and historiographer.

Twenty-fourth. Richimerus reigned for twenty-four years.

The man dies. Arebaldus, bishop and historiographer.

35
Arebaldus francoꝝ pontifex obijt Gothi fines saxonū denuo iuraserunt Qua propter multiplicatis per eū numinibns, mortuo Arebaldo summus agente francorum pontifex et facerdos constitutus fuit, quod et libenter admisit. ¶ Anno eius duodecimo, gothi dentio in fines saxonum effusi, regionem suo more deuastare coeperunt, Contra quorum incursus, Vuindekint. saxonū rex. Hermenfridt doringorum rex. & ipse ri chimer francorum rex cum germanis fratribus simul atque theutoni bus, iuxta foedus antiquum et annos ante paucos (ut diximus) re nouatum, celeriter magnum produxerunt exercitum, & facta con gressione plus qua uiginti millia gothorum peremerūt, ceteros uul neratos et spoliatos uerterunt in fugam. ¶ Fugatis denuo de saxonia gothis frangi cū germanis atque theu tonibus consilium habuerunt, inter se disquirentes quemadmodū gothis et scanzianis populis reditū in fines saxonū siue germanoꝝ deinceps possent iterdicere. Placuit postremo regibus et ꝓceribus cūctis, ut ex populo francorum, saxonū, dorīgorum, germanorū, & theutonum, qui circa mare dacis et gothis erant uiciniores, unā conducerent gentem. cum liberis uxoribus atque iumentis, quę ter ram post saxoniam ultimam et proximā scanzianis incoleret, ho stiumque incursiones prohiberet. ¶ Eo autem tractatu concluso, richimer rex francorum decem et octo millia uirorum cum liberis et uxoribus in regionem illam de stinauit, quibus sunnonem filium suum secundo genitum, ducem et principem constituit. Ad quem iuxta condictum plures deinde conuenerūt ex germanis saxonibus atque doringis, & facti sunt ex diuersis populis unus, breuique tempore creuerunt in gentē magnā, & scanzianos deuastare saxoniam deinceps non permiserunt. A romanis tamen sepius infestabantur. ¶ Hic sumno dux sedem gentis sire postust cum potentia in finibus saxonię. ab oriente habens sarmatas, a meridie sclauos boemie, ab occidente saxoniam et theutones, ab aquilone uero cimbros, ma re, dacos, & scamos gothos, hominesque insulanos et loca paludi nosa habitantes. ¶ Sunnone post hęc mortuo, Clodomercilius in ducatu cismari no succéssit, qui terminos accepte possessionis non parum adauxit Post hūc Sunno eius filius principatum gentis accepit, qui anno dominice natiuitatis, centesimo quadragesimo sexto, indictiōe ro manorum quartadecima, in memoriam patrie suę agentis franco rum, ad ripas fluminis Odere ciuitatem nouam construxit. quam progenitorū suorū amore Franckenfurt nuncupauit Aliā post hęc quoque urbem, ad ostium fluminis memorati haud procul amaricō didit, quam suo ex nomine Sundam siue ut Hunibaldus testat Sun noniam nuncupauit. ¶ Remansit aliquandiu in his terris nomen francorum, quousque tandem multiplicatis ducibus, regio in partes fuit diuisa plures. &

Arebaldus, bishop of the Franks, died. The Goths again invaded the borders of the Saxons. Therefore, after the [unclear] had been multiplied by him, when Arebaldus had died, he was appointed chief bishop and priest of the Franks [unclear], and this he gladly accepted.

In his twelfth year, the Goths, again pouring into the borders of the Saxons, began to lay waste the region in their accustomed manner. Against their attacks, Widukind, king of the Saxons, Hermenfrid, king of the Thuringians, and Richimer himself, king of the Franks, with the Germans, his brothers, together with the Teutons, according to the ancient treaty, renewed a few years before, as we have said, quickly led forth a great army; and, when battle had been joined, they killed more than twenty thousand of the Goths, and put the rest, wounded and stripped, to flight.

After the Goths had again been driven out of Saxony, the Franks, with the Germans and Teutons, held counsel, inquiring among themselves how they might thereafter bar the Goths and the Scanzian peoples from returning into the borders of the Saxons or Germans. Finally it pleased all the kings and nobles that, from the people of the Franks, Saxons, Thuringians, Germans, and Teutons, who around the sea were nearer neighbors to the Dacians and Goths, they should bring together one people, with children, wives, and beasts of burden, which would inhabit the land beyond furthest Saxony and nearest to the Scanzians, and would prevent the incursions of enemies.

When that agreement had been concluded, Richimer, king of the Franks, assigned eighteen thousand men with children and wives to that region, and set over them as duke and prince his second-born son, Sunno. To him, according to the agreement, many later came from the Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians; and from diverse peoples they became one, and in a short time they grew into a great nation, and thereafter did not permit the Scanzians to lay waste Saxony. Yet they were often harassed by the Romans.

This Duke Sunno established the seat of his people with power in the borders of Saxony, having to the east the Sarmatians, to the south the Slavs of Bohemia, to the west Saxony and the Teutons, and to the north the Cimbri, the sea, the Dacians, and the Scanzian Goths, and men living on islands and in marshy places.

After Sunno had died, Clodomercilius succeeded in the duchy across the sea; he enlarged the boundaries of the possession he had received by no small amount. After him his son Sunno received the leadership of the people; in the year of the Lord’s nativity 146, in the fourteenth indiction of the Romans, in memory of his homeland, [unclear] of the Franks, he built a new city on the banks of the river Oder, which, out of love for his forefathers, he called Frankfurt. After this he also founded another city, at the mouth of the aforesaid river, not far from the sea, which from his own name he called Sunden, or, as Hunibald attests, Sunnonia.

The name of the Franks remained for some time in these lands, until at last, when the dukes had multiplied, the region was divided into several parts, and

36
singule diuisiones nomen a singulis uel principibus uel euentibꝰ acceperūt. A marcomero etenim duce quidā postea dicti sunt marcomeri a brandone filio eius qui urbem brandenburg cōdidit alij nominati sunt brandenburgij, atque alij ab alijs alia noīa suscepērūt. ¶ Cōtriu̇rat ante hac anno Richimeri regis quinto, domicianus caesar sarmatas et dacos qui morabantur in finibus germanię uerfus orientem et eos ualde nimis afflixit. Addēsque sceleri peccatum, secundam in christianos post impijssimum Neronem, perfecutione nem suscitauit, seque primus omnium caesarum deum et dominum appellari omnibus pręcepit. ¶ Anno regni fui undecimo Richimerus rex frācorum, bellū habuit cum romanis et gallis non longe ab urbe basana cōmuni germaniorū suffragijs adiutus, in quo multi ab utraque parte ceciderunt Interea romanis legionibus ad coloniam agrippinā reuerfisis, Nerua caefar nunciatur mortuus in cuius locum milites traianū hispa¬nice nationis uirum, in cesarem sublimarunt, qui imperauit annis decem et nouem mensibus sex, & diebus quīdecim. ¶ Richimer autē rex francorum post multa fortiter gesta, postremo tandem moritur anno regni sui. XXIIII. Dominiceꝫ uero natiu̇tatis. C.XIII.in dictione romanorum. XI cuius uitā mores acta et cultum in deos ruthvuigus francorū vates carmine scripsit. Odemarus Richimeri sup̄dicti regis franccoru̇ natu maior filius, post patrem regnauitannis. VICESImus gntus Odemarus regnauitannis.XIIIII.Inter francos et gallos treuge fiunt.Odemarus rex pacem bello pretulit.Franci cū germanis fuerūt his adhuc teporibus gentiles.Vechtanus francoꝛum summus pontifex et uates.

The several divisions received their names from particular princes or events. For from Duke Marcomer some were afterwards called Marcomeri; from Brando, his son, who founded the city of Brandenburg, others were named Brandenburgers; and others received other names from other sources.

In the fifth year of King Richimer, Domitian Caesar had previously crushed the Sarmatians and Dacians, who dwelt in the borders of Germany toward the east, and afflicted them exceedingly. And, adding sin to crime, he stirred up the second persecution against the Christians after the most impious Nero, and was the first of all the Caesars to command everyone to call him god and lord.

In the eleventh year of his reign, Richimer, king of the Franks, had a war with the Romans and Gauls not far from the city of Basana, aided by the common support of the Germans; in it many fell on both sides. Meanwhile, when the Roman legions had returned to Cologne Agrippina, Nerva Caesar was announced dead; in his place the soldiers raised Trajan, a man of Spanish nation, to be Caesar. He ruled nineteen years, six months, and fifteen days.

But Richimer, king of the Franks, after many deeds bravely done, at last finally died in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, and in the year 113 of the Lord’s nativity, in the eleventh Roman indiction. Ruthvuigus, bard of the Franks, wrote his life, character, deeds, and worship of the gods in verse.

Odemar, the elder son by birth of the aforesaid Richimer, king of the Franks, reigned after his father for fourteen years. He was a prince of the Franks very beloved by the people, who refrained from wars as much as could be done without harm to the commonwealth. For he made truces with the Gauls and the Romans, which the Franks call treugae, as if “confidences,” because faith was pledged between them; and he showed himself so friendly to them thereafter that he compelled all to lament his death.

Thus, as long as he lived among men, he kept the peace he had promised, and expended all his effort on the honor and adornment of his people. He founded very many castles, cities, and fortifications throughout the kingdom; by the counsel of the priests he both enlarged and renewed the laws and rites of sacrifices. For all the Franks, Saxons, and Germans at that time were still subject to the vanity of idols and far removed from knowledge of the Christian faith. They worshipped Mars as the fierce god of war, from whose divine power they sought victory at all times. To each of their gods they dedicated not only individual altars and temples, but also individual cities and villages; nor was there any number to the insensible gods.

In these times the chief priest, pontiff, elder, and bard of the Franks was named Vechtanus, born from the ancient stock of kings, eloquent in Greek and Latin speech, and highly skilled in astronomy, music, medicine, and the philosophy of the Greeks, since he had devoted much time to study both at Rome and at Athens [unclear]

From Brando they were called Brandenburgers.

Domitian Caesar persecutes the Christians.

War of the Franks with the Romans.

Trajan becomes Caesar at Cologne.

Richimer, king of the Franks, dies. Ruthvuicus the historiographer.

The twenty-fifth: Odemar reigned fourteen years. Truces are made between the Franks and the Gauls. King Odemar preferred peace to war. The Franks, together with the Germans, were still pagans in these times. Vechtanus, chief pontiff and bard of the Franks.

Nicanor qui dux fuit insulanus ad ostia rheni Odemarus quem pater post mortē sacrorum cõstituerat, propterea quod in omni litteratura gentili doctissimus euaferat. ¶ Claruit eo tempore Doracus francorum confiliarius parens regum uates insignis Vechtani quondam auditor atqꝫ discipulus de regum nobili prosapia ortus, qui post haec sacerdotis obtinuit in tanta estimatione habitus est, ut quasi numen aliquod coleret̉ ab omnibus, imperaret non modo plebi que uellet sed etiam regibus francorum proceribus cunctis. Historias gentis carmine scribens continuauit. ¶ Pacem habuerunt frangi cunctis diebus quibus regnauit marcomirus multumqꝫ sub eius directione diuitijs potentia honore creuerunt. Scribit Doracus in annalibus ut Hunibaldus testat' qđ romani francoꝝ pace bello semp̄ habuere suspectos tanqͣ futuros imperij subuersores phedij oraculo dudum premoniti, acpropterea totis sepe uiribus in eorum interitum licet frusta cõspirarūt.

Vechtanus the pontiff wrote histories of the Franks. Vechtanus, pontiff of the Franks, perished in water. The town of Odemersheim is founded by the Franks. Odemarus, king of the Franks, dies. Twenty-sixth. Marcomer reigned twenty-one years. The city Marcaburg is founded among the Nitriones by the duke. The city Franckenfurt is founded beside the Main. Doracus, prophet and writer of the Franks. Doracus, of great authority among the Franks. The Franks were always suspect to the Romans, in peace and in war. Doracus in the annals.

of worldly things, with certain other fellow pupils of his. At last, having returned to his homeland, he taught the sons of kings and nobles, according to the ancient custom of the Franks, beneath an oak.

He wrote many things in Greek songs concerning the sacred rites of the gods, and put into German verse the histories of the ancient kings; with these he exercised the talents of the young and greatly raised up their memory. In the fifth year of King Odemarus, he perished in a small river, to which he gave its name when he was drowned, so that from Vechtanus it is called in German the Vecht down to the present day. Over his tomb King Odemarus founded a new city, which he named Odemarsheim after himself; it still stands at present within the borders of the diocese of the church of Utrecht.

But Odemarus, the peaceable king of the Franks, at last, after the founding of many cities, died in the fourteenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 127, in the tenth indiction of the Romans. His body was buried beneath a pyramid in Odemarsheim, as he had ordained while alive.

Marcomerus, son of King Odemarus, succeeding his father, reigned for twenty-one years. He had a wife named Athildem, daughter of Marius, king of Britain, by whom he begot seven sons, whose names were these: Clodomir, the firstborn, who succeeded his father in the kingdom; Marcomer, who held the duchy among the Nitriones, where he founded a city named after himself, called Marcoburg; Clogio, who perished in Britain; Franc, who was duke on this side of the Rhine among the Hogii, from the Confluence as far as the mouth of the river Main toward the east, among the Moguntiaci, Xones, and Germans, and who restored the old city Helenopolis and named it Franckenfurt; Merodac, who was struck by a boar while hunting and perished; Nicanor, who was duke of the islands at the mouths of the Rhine; Odemarus, whom his father had appointed to the sacred rites after his death, because he had become most learned in all gentile literature.

At that time Doracus flourished, counsellor of the Franks, kinsman of kings, an eminent prophet, formerly hearer and disciple of Vechtanus, born from the noble lineage of kings. After this he obtained the priesthood, and was held in such high esteem that he was worshipped by all almost as some divinity, and commanded not only the common people whatever he wished, but even the kings of the Franks and all the nobles. Writing the histories of the people in verse, he continued them.

The Franks had peace during all the days in which Marcomirus reigned, and under his direction they greatly increased in riches, power, and honor. Doracus writes in the annals, as Hunibaldus bears witness, that the Romans always regarded the Franks as suspect, in peace and in war, as future overthrowers of the empire, having long before been warned by the oracle of Phedius; and for that reason they often conspired with all their forces for their destruction, though in vain.

38

For under King Faramund afterward, and under his successors, they obtained all Gaul by their own forces and overcame the Roman Empire.

But Marcomir, the aforesaid king of the Franks, died in the twenty-first year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 148, in the first indiction.

Clodomer, the elder son of the already-mentioned king of the Franks, reigned after his father for seventeen years: a man of singular prudence, modest toward his own people, most humane. He had a wife named Hasildis, daughter of the duke of the Rugians, by whom he begot three sons, Farabert, Nicanor, and Roric. The first of these, as we shall say, succeeded his father in the kingdom. The second was king of Frisia. The third, drowned in water not far from Novesium, at his death left his name to the river which is called Rora down to the present day. The place of Roric’s drowning was between [Neocum?], a castle on this side of the Rhine, and the old city which the inhabitants called Moradunum; in those times all Francia was alien to the knowledge of the Christian faith.

Clodomer, king of the Franks, died in peace in the seventeenth year of his reign, in the third Roman indiction. In his time the Gauls were considering an incursion against the Franks. But King Clodomer himself, wisely anticipating their movement, restrained them from doing it.

Farabert, the elder son of Clodomer, king of the Franks, succeeding his father, reigned for twenty years, beginning in the previously noted 165th year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the third Roman indiction. He renewed and again ratified the treaty of friendship, long before contracted through the Frankish king, as we said above, then confirmed by other kings, renewed, and often strengthened by a new enactment, with the Germans, Saxons, Teutons, Marcomanni, and Cimbri; this greatly displeased the Romans and stirred them to arms.

For in the sixth year of this King Farabert, which was the 171st year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the times of Lucius Aurelius Commodus Caesar, the Romans, not bearing with calm minds so great a concord of the Franks, brought forth a great army of their men. And so, when legions had been sent through Sarmatia into Germany against the Dacians, Marcomanni, Teutons, Saxons, and [unclear] Franks, they brought forth a great army of their men. Against their incursion the kings of the aforesaid peoples sent out such great forces of fighters that the Romans, defeated, were compelled to return without victory, with loss and disgrace.

In the eleventh year of King Farabert, under the emperor Antoninus Pius, the Romans again led an army through the Sarmatians into Germany, and for a long time

Marcomir, king of the Franks, dies. Twenty-seventh. Clodomer reigned for seventeen years.

Roric, duke of the Franks, is drowned in the Rora, where now is the town and monastery of Werden.

Clodomer, king of the Franks, dies.

There was fierce fighting, and many on both sides fell, wounded by the sword. Concerning the manner, outcome, and miracles of rains in this war, which were then said to have occurred on behalf of the Roman army, following Hunibald we set out a sufficient account in the first volume of the Annals; we judge it superfluous to repeat it here.

Farabert, king of the Franks, after many brave deeds, died in the twentieth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 185, in the eighth indiction.

In the times of this king Farabert, namely in the 182nd year of the Lord’s nativity, Eleutherius, the Roman pope, at the request of Lucius, king of Britain, son of Coillus, sent into that Britain which is now called England the bishops Faganus and Duvianus, so that they might announce the word of salvation to the aforesaid king and also to the nobles and the whole people of the British kingdom or island, and baptize those converted to the faith of Christ in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. When they came to the appointed place, in a short time they converted not only King Lucius but the people of the whole island to the faith of Christ.

At that time there were in Britain several pontiffs, priests of idols, among whom the flamens were preeminent in authority, twenty-eight in number; and there were three archflamens: of London, of York, and in the City of Legions, which the ancient walls and buildings testify to have been situated on the river Usk in Glamorgan. When the aforesaid flamens were converted to the faith of Christ, the preachers consecrated their temples of idols to the honor of the one God, the almighty Father, appointing the same number of bishops in place of the flamens, and archbishops in place of the archflamens. Gildas wrote of these matters more fully in the book which he entitled On the Victory of Aurelius Ambrosius, king of the Britons; after him, Geoffrey of Monmouth, the Briton, who for Robert, duke of Gloucester, completed the history of the Britons and the successions of all their kings in order from the first entry of the people with Brutus from Troy into that island down to the year of the Lord’s nativity 689, in ten books. His contemporary Caradoc of Llancarfan also described the successions, years, times, and deeds of the kings of the Franks in lucid language.

The elder son of Farabert, king of the Franks, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-eight years: a strong, vigorous, bold prince, who fought many battles with the Romans, likewise with the Gauls. In his time, as we said, King Lucius first most humbly received the Christian faith; after he died without children, the Romans sent Severus, a senator, into Britain with two legions. He fought many battles with Fulgenius, by whom at last, in the siege of the city of York, he was killed along with many Romans; they received his son, named Bassanus, as king. In the same year in which Severus was slain in Britain by Fulgenius, Sunno, king of the Franks, with the Germans and Saxons bringing aid, crossed the river near the castle

Suno

[Unclear] laid waste to the Gauls, and, after the region round about had been plundered, enriched with spoils, he returned victorious. But the remaining things which he magnificently accomplished in peace and in war, Hildegast, philosopher of the Franks and an eminent seer, described after him in a German poem, and Hunibald in prose in the Latin tongue; concerning these matters we have spoken in the first book of the Annals.

Sunno, king of the Franks, died in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, and in the year 213 of the Lord’s Nativity, in the sixth Roman indiction.

Hilderic, the elder son of King Sunno, reigned after his father for forty years, a magnanimous, prudent, bold, warlike man, who at all times defended his people bravely no less by prudence than by arms, and powerfully extended the boundaries of the kingdom far and wide. For he was of such great virtue and power that he was a considerable object of fear not only to the Gauls but also to the Romans; to them the Frankish name was so hateful and odious that they were accustomed never to write or name that people otherwise than as German.

The Franks gloried in their name; but the Romans, troubled by hatred of them, begrudged them the word. Nor did the writers of histories among the neighboring peoples, especially the Romans and Gauls, by common agreement grant the Frankish name to the people of Sicambria before, by Frankish arms and virtues, they had subjected almost all Europe to their dominion. For earlier, as we have said, the Romans, the Gauls, and the remaining nations hostile to the Franks, as Hunibald bears witness, moved by envy, called them by no other name than Germans. For thus says the author already mentioned:

“Our ancestors had no less common concern for the name of their people, which they had once received from Franco their king, than for the kingdom, because they thought it would be glorious for them not thereafter to change the Frankish name into another, once it had been taken up by their forebears with the highest honor.”

In these times Hildegast, philosopher, counselor, seer, kinsman of kings, and elder, most learned of all, flourished in great esteem among King Hilderic, the nobles, and also the whole multitude of the Frankish people. In his own age he said, did, and wrote marvelous things. And he was of such great estimation and authority among his people that all always obeyed his command.

On the birthday of Hilderic, king of the Franks, while standing in the temple of Jupiter at Neopagus before the image of that god, after prayers had been poured out for the obtaining of a prophecy, he suddenly began to rage, as is the custom in madness, with a song of the alrunae; and, shaking his head and with his hands bent back, he prophesied thus, not using verses composed by the rule of meters, but rhythms without measure, uttered in fury and in great confusion. Hunibald made their interpretation thus:

“Victory will come to the Franks from the western god, whom the ancient Dardanian ancestors worshiped.”

The final acquisition of all Europe by the Franks

Whatever the Gaul possesses, whatever all Germany possesses, all will yield to your right, warlike Sicamber, when it shall have given you this man, the first king by name, whom the princes, leaders now without a king, will appoint; then, when he is victorious, the Frank will reign [without end?].

Concerning the empire of the Romans also he added as follows:

Behold, the great God will give brothel-camps to the Frank, and the lion will break the eagle, dashed against by the serpent.

Hunibald explains this meaning concerning the standards of the Franks which they used in battles, which we call among the emblems of princes.

What the emblems or arms of the ancient Franks were

They depicted a lion, with the forepart of its body, on a fleece of blue color, its feet stretched out for seizing and its mouth open in the manner of one roaring; the lower part of its body ended in a serpent’s tail, with which it seemed to press and suffocate the neck of an eagle, depicted beneath on a golden fleece with wings spread, and most strongly bound.

The Romans had the eagle as their standard when fighting. Desiring to suppress and annihilate its proud and arrogant power by strength and prudence together, the Franks took the lion for the one and the serpent for the other. For by the lion the Franks wished mystically to signify their strength, and by the serpent wisdom and prudence, by which they undoubtedly hoped that they would at last overcome [unclear]. All subsequent kings of the Franks used these emblems or arms, though they are improperly so called, down to Clodoneus the Christian, who is read to have taken up, in place of the lion, three lilies sent down from heaven, as will be said in its place.

Interpretation of the arms of the Franks. The arms of the Franks down to Clodoneus.

When and why the ancient emblems of the Franks disappeared.

Hildegast, a noble teacher of the Franks in all knowledge.

The Franks began to be more refined in manners and in building.

Hildegast also, the wise man of the Franks already mentioned, taught the sons of the nobles to sing in their mother tongue the deeds of their ancestors in songs, with lyres and various other musical instruments. He admonished the people to live by civilized customs, to build houses, and to go about more refined in dress, and he ordered them to put aside savagery. For indeed up to that time the Franks cared little for cultivation or adornment, either in buildings or in clothing. Hildegast established all these things in a more refined form, and most wisely instructed them to crush and subdue the pride of the Romans not only by arms, but also in possessions and manners. From that time the Franks began to build houses both larger and more beautiful, and distinguished by various dwellings. For whatever they had constructed in earlier times, with excessive sim

by reason of its simplicity it was contemptible and rustic, since, on account of their frequent changes of settlements, they had been accustomed to live in fields rather than in cities. Hence the Germans, taking up a proverb, whenever they saw something made or painted with ancient simplicity, were accustomed, praising its antiquity, to say: "That is a good old Frankish work."

The Franks from their origin rude and uncultivated.

That is an old Frankish work.

Hunibald records the other things wonderfully said, written, or done by Hildegast. In the twenty-fourth year of Hilderic, king of the Franks, Alexander, the son of Mammaea, Caesar Augustus of the Romans, was killed at Mainz, a city of Germany, in a military mutiny, in the thirteenth year of his reign.

Alexander Caesar is killed at Mainz.

Hilderic, moreover, king of the Franks, the first of that name, after many deeds bravely and magnificently performed, died at last in the fortieth year of his reign, and in the two hundred fifty-third year of the Lord's Nativity, in the first Roman indiction.

The Thirty-First.

Bartherus, son of King Hilderic, succeeding his father, reigned eighteen years. In his time the Romans waged war with the Goths, who [unclear] the river Ister [unclear] killed [unclear] thousand, under the leadership of Decius Caesar, his son. Many of the Romans also fell, among them his sons. But Decius Caesar, a most wicked persecutor of Christians, while fleeing, was submerged in the whirlpool of a certain marsh; his corpse could never be found by his men.

Bartherus reigned eighteen years.

In the tenth year of King Bartherus, when the Romans under the wanton rule of Gallienus were sluggish with idleness, the Franks, thinking that a suitable time was at hand to avenge their insults against them, with the Germans, Saxons, Bavarians, and Thuringians assisting, gathered a great army of warriors, entered the borders of the enemy, and, devastating everything with fire, advanced by hostile incursion with the sword as far as Ravenna; enriched with plunder, they returned to their own lands.

The Franks launch an expedition against the Romans.

Franks, Germans, Saxons, Bavarians, Thuringians.

In the following year, which was the eleventh of King Bartherus, the Alemanni, after mustering their forces, led a strong army into Gaul; and after the region had been laid waste by sword and fire, they returned to their own lands with spoils and much plunder. In the same year also they launched an expedition into Italy against the Romans, inflicted much damage on them, and avenged the injuries, many in number, that they had received from them.

The Alemanni laid waste Gaul and Italy.

In the [thirteenth?] year of King Bartherus, which was the two hundred sixty-sixth year of the Lord's Nativity, in the fourteenth Roman indiction, the Franks, with the aid of the German Saxons, mustered a huge army; after crossing the Rhine and the Meuse, under the leaders Antharius and Luther they entered Gaul, despoiling everything in hostile fashion. Duke Antharius was the son of Bartherus, the aforesaid king of the Franks; Luther was the son of Marbod, king in Saxony.

The Franks again moved into Gaul.

The Franks reached as far as Spain.

Beginning from the region nearest to the Tungri and proceeding thence hostilely through the Bellovaci beyond the Seine, they came as far as Spain, surrounding the noble city of Tarraco with a siege and utterly destroying it.

But Bartherus, king of the Franks, at last died in the eighteenth year of his reign, namely in the year of the Lord's Nativity 271, in the fourth Roman indiction; Hunibald sufficiently sets forth his many deeds.

Clodius, the elder son of King Bartherus, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for twenty-seven years. In his third year the Romans, sending legions into Alemannia and mindful of the earlier injury, sought it in war. Against their incursion the Alemanni advanced armed, having in their army thirty thousand fighters. A very hard battle was joined not far from Lake Benacus, in which nearly fifteen thousand of the Alemanni were slain.

In the twelfth year of King Clodius the Franks, under their leaders, invaded Gaul, and killed many thousands of the Roman guards and also of the Gauls; and, occupying a great part of inner Gaul, they dwelt there for seven years.

But King Clodius of the Franks died after this, in the twenty-[seventh?] year of his reign, [in the year] 298, in the first Roman indiction.

Walther, son of King Clodius, after his father reigned over the Franks for eight years, a magnanimous, strong, and warlike prince. In the time of his reign, when persecution had been proclaimed everywhere, Diocletian in the East and Maximian in the West overthrew the churches of Christ, burned the divine books in fires, and miserably afflicted the Christians in the tenth persecution after Nero. And Diocletian, in the first year of the aforementioned King Walther, ordered himself to be worshipped as a god; he also at the same time subjected Alexandria, with all Egypt, to the Romans.

In the first, second, and third years of Walther, king of the Franks, there were great disturbances in Britain, which is now called England. For after King Lucius had died some years before, he who, with his people, was the first to receive the faith of Christ from Pope Eleutherius, as we said above, in the one hundred eighty-fifth year, in the times of Farabert king of the Franks, the Romans sent the senator Senerus into Britain to take up the kingdom. When he too had been killed at York by Fulgenius, Basianus, son of that same Senerus, was admitted as king. When he also had been killed, Carausius seized the kingdom and despised the commands of the Romans. When he too died in the second year of Walther king of the Franks, the Romans sent Allectus to take up the kingdom.

Against him Asclepiodotus, a warlike, strong, and bold man, rising up, killed him with two Roman legions, set the diadem of the kingdom upon himself, and, against the will of the Caesars and the senate, reigned for ten years; he cultivated justice and, after the Romans had been excluded, kept the province in peace.

Walter, king of the Franks, in these times rested from wars, and at last finally died in the eighth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 306, in the ninth Roman indiction, in which year there was an earthquake.

Dagobert, the elder son of Walter, king of the Franks, succeeded his father and reigned for eleven years. He was a man pious toward his subjects, gentle, most humane; and while they held him in singular love and great reverence, they feared him. In the administration of justice according to the laws of the Franks he was most equitable, and, preserving each man’s right unimpaired, he did injury to no one, nor did he permit it to be done by another.

In his fourth year Coelus, duke of Gloucester, rising up against his lord Asclepiadotus, king of Britain, killed him by the counsel of the Romans. Rejoicing at this news, the Romans sent the senator Constantius to Britain with legions, a man no less prudent than warlike. When Coelus, who had already occupied the kingdom, learned that he had landed on the shore, he did not dare to engage him; he sent messengers to him, asked for peace, and obtained it, on condition that the tribute should be paid firmly to the Romans each year according to the ancient custom.

When peace had been confirmed, however, King Coelus died not long afterward, within the fortieth day. Constantius took as wife his daughter, named Helena, a virgin second to none in beauty, wisdom, Christian religion, and piety toward God; by her he begot Constantine, afterward the great emperor, and obtained with her the kingdom of Britain, with all the nobles consenting.

But Dagobert, the above-mentioned king of the Franks, died in the eleventh year of his reign, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 317, in the fifth Roman indiction.

Clogio, the son of King Dagobert, succeeded his father and reigned for only two years. For in the second year of his reign the Romans and Gauls, fiercely invading the kingdom of the Franks in the regions on this side of the mountains, began to lay everything waste with fire and sword. But King Clogio, having gathered forces as best he could, met the enemy with the help of the Germans; when he fought too incautiously, he was killed. Yet the Franks for that reason did not desist from the conflict, but fought bravely.

For Clodomer, the brother of the slain king, having drawn his body back from the battle-line, put on his arms, so that he might be thought by everyone to be the king himself, and so that neither his friends, once the king’s death was known, should lose heart, nor the enemies, exulting, should presume a certain hope of victory. And so Duke Clodomer, clad in the king’s arms and having returned to the battle-line, since he was thought by all to be the king himself, struck constancy into his own men and fear into the enemy.

Walter, king of the Franks, dies.

Thirty-fourth.

Dagobert reigned eleven years.

Asclepiadotus, king of Britain, is killed by the duke.

The Roman Constantius comes into Britain.

Helena, daughter of Coelus, becomes the wife of Constantius and the mother of Constantine.

Dagobert, king of the Franks, dies.

Thirty-fifth.

Clogio reigned only two years.

War of the Romans and Gauls with the Franks.

Duke Clodomer defeated the enemies by stratagem.

Eranteo tempore magni gentium motus in bri¬ tania, & in cunctis adiacentibus infulis, francorum regno uicinis, quorum consideratione rex Clodomirus anguftiabatur, metuens Romanorum insidias, ne absente pugnatorum exercitu nouā ali¬ quam inregnum molirentur incursionem. ¶ Habito autem cum proceribus regni consilio, rex Clodomirus doringor legatis incōtione magnato publica tale dedit respōsū. Conspiratio dorin¬ gorū in sueuū. Doringi cū sueuis sediciose cōfligūt. Plures ab utraqꝫ ꝑte ceciderrunt. Frāci cū saxonibus pro pace laborant. Triennales fiunt in ducie. The Romans and Gauls are overcome by the Franks. Clogio, king of the Franks, is killed in battle. Before the twenty-fourth year of age let no one be made king. The Thirty-Sixth. Clodomir reigned eighteen years. The Romans gravely afflicted the Sueves. The Franks came to the aid of the Sueves. The Franks, ancient enemies of the Romans. Genebaldus, commander of the army of the Franks. The Romans were turned to flight by the Germans. The cause of the dissension between the Thuringian and the Sueve. The Thuringian and the Sueve fight a duel. The Sueve killed the Thuringian in the duel.

By fighting so bravely he restored the battle, so that at last he turned the Gauls together with the Romans to flight, obtained the victory, gathered the spoils of the enemies, and freed the kingdom from destruction.

Accordingly Clogio, king of the Franks, fell in the second year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 319, in the seventh Roman indiction. He left two sons, of whom the elder by birth, Helenus, was then in his twentieth year, while the younger, Richimer, was in his eighteenth. But by law it was forbidden to the Franks that they should promote anyone to the kingship before he had completed the twenty-fourth year of his age. Hence it happened that neither of Clogio’s sons came to the kingdom, but their paternal uncle Clodomirus was elected king.

Clodomirus, brother of the slain king Clogio, was elected king by the common decree of the Franks. After him he reigned eighteen years, a distinguished, prudent, and brave prince, who kept his people in peace and enlarged the kingdom of the Franks.

For in these times, when the Sueves were being grievously afflicted by the Romans, they had resolved to call the Franks, Saxons, and Thuringians to their aid; they trusted that they would find them willing all the more readily because they knew that they had always hated the Romans. But the Franks, otherwise ancient enemies of the Romans, having held counsel among themselves, readily gave their consent to the request of the Sueves, thinking it healthier to fight with enemies in borders far away and belonging to others than in their own.

Therefore Clodomir, king of the Franks, appointed his brother Genebaldus commander of the army that was to go, and entrusted to him eighty thousand fighting men. The other kings called by the Sueves to their aid did likewise. The soldiers appointed, coming together into one body, formed a sufficiently large army. They joined battle with the Romans and fought very fiercely, killing many thousands of them, while the rest sought safety in flight; and so the Romans were driven from the borders of the Sueves.

When the Germans, having gained this victory, were dividing the spoils in the camp in the customary manner, a dangerous quarrel arose between two soldiers, of whom one, a Thuringian, was named Gunther, while the other was a Sueve named Adelbertus. This was the cause of the disturbance: that the Sueve soldier had accused the Thuringian of having secretly carried off something or other from the common booty. When he denied it, a serious sedition of the Thuringians arose, while the Sueves defended the Sueve. For each had many adherents from his own people, who were stirred up in spirit.

But when the Thuringian steadfastly denied the theft, the Sueve offered that he would prove the truth by duel. When the princes had permitted this, single combat was entered into between them on the appointed day; in it, at the second encounter, the Thuringian was killed by the Sueve. When his corpse had been stripped of clothes and arms, the very theft over which he had been accused was found hidden on him. After the Thuringians received this confusion, they were exceedingly angry,

But, concealing their anger, they afterwards held secret counsel among themselves as to how they might avenge Gunther’s fall upon Adelbert. And when the plan had been settled, namely that they should kill the Swabian that same night, one hundred and twenty of them conspired together to keep the matter secret.

Therefore on the following night they silently rushed upon the tent in which they suspected Adelbert to be, demanding that the murderer be handed over to them to be killed. Roused by these voices, the Swabians ran to arms, firmly resolving either to defend their innocent soldier from death or to die with him. An attack was at once made upon the Thuringians, and they slaughtered almost all those one hundred and twenty.

When this was announced in the camp of the Thuringians, they were greatly moved and, as though turned to fury, immediately seized their weapons; and, having formed a battle-line, they sprang upon the Swabians, who suspected no such thing, raising shouts on high like madmen. But the Swabians, not slow, when they could not call the Thuringians back from the tumult with fair words, themselves also put on arms and strove to resist bravely. A savage battle was joined between friends, in which more than two thousand men of each side perished. Yet the Thuringians lost more than the Swabians, and at last, overcome and compelled by necessity, they withdrew.

This contention had remained hidden from both the Franks and the Saxons until the struggle came to an end, since they had pitched their camps not in the same place but in different stations. Afterwards, however, when they learned the cause, they undertook many negotiations for peace and concord between the disputants; but since each side complained that it had been gravely and unjustly injured, they could not restore full concord between them. They did, however, establish truces, or an armistice, between them for three years, during which they ordered the parties to abstain from war, until anger should cool with time and the disturbance be calmed.

From that time the Thuringians always held the Swabians suspect for treachery, and up to the present day, as Hunibald says, they labor under a hidden and open hatred against them, although many do not know the cause of this mutual persecution.

But when the three years had passed and the end of the truces was at hand, the Swabians declared war on the Thuringians. The latter, having very little confidence in their own affairs, sent notable and [unclear] envoys to Clodomir, king of the Franks, and to the nobles of the kingdom, begging with great urgency that, in view of the former confederation, they would bring them the aid owed and friendly against the Swabians. At that time there were great movements of peoples in Britain and in all the adjacent islands neighboring the kingdom of the Franks; in consideration of these King Clodomir was distressed, fearing the stratagems of the Romans, lest, in the absence of the army of fighters, they should contrive some new incursion into the kingdom.

Having held counsel with the nobles of the kingdom, King Clodomir gave this reply to the envoys of the Thuringians in a public assembly of the magnates.

By the report of Duke Genebald, our very dear brother, we learned some time ago what the cause of the breach of trust was between you, friends, the Thuringians, and the Suevi, and the occasion of those disturbances which today stand at the gates. We acknowledge that we have been allied with you for a long time, and we neither wish in any way, nor indeed ought, to violate the right of the treaty that has been made. But you yourselves, excellent Thuringians, now see more clearly than daylight amid what great dangers the kingdom of the Franks is placed, since the Romans with the Gauls threaten us daily before our gates, watching most carefully our entrance, and likewise our departure, to see whether by any occasion they can overthrow our kingdom, which our ancestors, with the shedding of much blood, were scarcely at last able to acquire and establish.

Therefore it has by no means seemed prudent to the counsel of the Franks, especially in these perilous times, to divide the people and, neglecting our own affairs, to defend those of others, since, with the gods propitious, we may perhaps be able to suffice for one of the two, but to protect both, that is, our kingdom and yours, in these days from the incursion of enemies is not within our power. Finally, the very great distance of places hinders us very much from being able to bring you aid so often against the Suevi, since they hold the beginning and source of the river Rhine, while we hold its farthest mouths and setting. Nevertheless, lest we seem to have failed you altogether, as friends, it has pleased our counsel that we send our messengers and envoys to the Suevi, through whom we may again obtain for you three-year truces and armistices. Meanwhile let the Thuringians take counsel, so that they may be able either to obtain perpetual peace with their own people, or by some other means whatsoever set up the necessary wall of defense, that is, either from their own people or from foreign friendly nations.

When these things had been set forth by the king of the Franks, the envoys of the Thuringians answered: Your counsel, O king and you princes of the Franks, is excellent, if however you will be able to obtain three-year truces from the Suevi on our behalf. But as to your advice that we should set up a wall of defense between ourselves and the Suevi, either from ourselves or, if any necessity requires, from some foreign source, this is also the opinion of our king and of all the nobles of the people of the Thuringians; concerning this, we beg you, hear our counsel, and at the same time give aid as faithful friends.

We have a land broad in extent toward the south, and fertile with abundance of fruits, whose farthest borders mark the boundary between the Suevi and the Thuringians. If you are willing to place inhabitants there from among your people, and a duke, they will without doubt be for you and for the kingdom of the Franks a perpetual honor and advantage, and for the Thuringians a wall of defense, and for the Suevi a cause of fear. No difficulty concerning the gift can intervene to prevent it from being in your power by the voluntary offering of the princes and people of the Thuringians.

After consultation had first been held concerning these matters, the Franks gladly agreed, since nothing was more dear to their heart than to extend the Frankish name, and at the same time the kingdom. Therefore, first, with a letter and envoys sent to the Suevi, peace

from the Thuringians for three years, keeping secret their plan of undertaking a new possession. Then they sent their men, together with the envoys of the aforesaid friends, into Thuringia, so that, by the judgment of the king and the nobles, they might confirm the proposed business concerning the grant of the promised region. When all these things had been duly completed, what we are writing followed.

When and whence the Franks first came to Menigauium [unclear]. The sequel follows.

Therefore, in the seventh year of Clodomir, king of the Franks, and in the year 326 of the Lord’s nativity, in the thirteenth Roman indiction, on the ninth day of the month of April, by order of the aforesaid king, there went out from the mouths of the Rhine, where the Sicambri had formerly had their first settlements in Germany, thirty thousand armed men, with wives, children, household goods, and beasts of burden, and two thousand six hundred eighty-six farmers and craftsmen of various trades, intending to set out for the new settlements promised to the Franks by the Thuringians. They did not all go out together at one time, but successively by companies, beginning on the prescribed day, until at last in the month of September they completed the aforesaid number, as Hunibald, the historian of the Franks, testifies.

[Margin: Here began the duchy of the eastern Franks. Würzburg, the ducal city of Franconia. In the year 326. 32,686 Franks come to Würzburg.]

King Clodomir appointed his brother Genebald duke of the people of eastern Francia, and entrusted to him the army and also the administration of the whole duchy under these conditions, according to the custom of the Franks: namely, that both he himself and his sons, heirs, and successors should remain forever under subjection to the kings of the Franks, should faithfully obey their commands in all things, should go forth with them to war against any adversaries whatsoever, and, according to the custom of the other dukes of the kingdom of the Franks, should everywhere render to those kings the service and honor owed to them.

[Margin: Genebald, first duke of eastern Francia. The institution of the duchy of eastern Francia.]

When these conditions had been given and accepted, Genebald, duke of eastern Francia, set out for Menigau with the people assigned to him, and ruled for nearly thirty years over the principality offered to him. For he was a prudent, bold, and warlike man, who not only governed and distributed the land of the duchy of Francia prudently, but also greatly enlarged the boundaries of its possession.

[Margin: Menigau, the place where Würzburg now is.]

When the Suevi heard of the arrival of the Franks within the borders of Thuringia, they bore it with considerable displeasure, fearing what did in fact happen: that, once multiplied in number and strength, they would also extend the boundaries of the possession they had received to the Suevi’s ruin. But when they saw that they could in no way resist the undertakings of the Franks, they feigned rejoicing at their arrival and, sending envoys, asked for peace, more from necessity, as it seemed to many, than from intention. They also committed to the arbitration of the Franks the settlement of the whole cause of the disputes that they were alleging against the Thuringians. The Thuringians did the same. Thus the great discord between them was calmed by the prudence of Duke Genebald.

The Suevi make firm peace with the Franks.

Marcomer, duke of the eastern Franks.

In the same year, in the month of September, Marcomir, son of Duke Genebald, came with the remaining band of the Franks, which by King Clodomir’s command had already earlier been chosen for migration by families, households, and persons, into the southern borders of Thuringia, and around the river Main to receive with his brothers the dwellings promised to them, having on the east the Boii and Bohemians, on the south the Suevi, on the west the Rhenish people, the people of Mainz, and the Apodas, and on the north the Fagophagi and Thuringians.

At the entrance of the Franks, the Thuringians, by order of Heurolus their king, withdrew beyond the forest, leaving all the grain, sufficient for the new guests for the following year. Therefore the Franks, newly arrived, first settled in the borders of the Thuringians between the river Falanus, as it is now called from Falagastus, and the lower parts of the Neckar, around the banks of the river Main. In that district, which was formerly called Meingau and afterwards East Francia, in which over time they built no small number of villages and cities, and in a short while grew in wealth and power.

But Duke Genebald begot Marcomir and Dagobert, who ruled over the eastern Franks for twenty-one years. Dagobert begot Clodius, who ruled over the people for ten years. Clodius begot Marcomir, who ruled for sixteen years. Marcomir begot Faramund and Marcomir. Faramund, both with his father and alone, administered the duchy for fifteen years, and afterwards, having been elected, became king of the Franks, as we shall say in its proper order. He entrusted the duchy of eastern Francia to his brother Marcomir, who ruled it for eighteen years. Duke Marcomir begot Priam, who ruled for twelve years. Priam begot Genebald the second, who ruled for twenty years. Genebald begot Sunno, who ruled for twenty-three years. After him Clodus, brother of Clodoneus king of the Franks, ruled for sixteen years. When he was struck by a boar while hunting and killed, Clodomir, son of the aforesaid Duke Sunno, succeeded in the duchy and ruled for twenty-one years. Clodomir begot Hugbad, who ruled for twenty-six years. Hugbad begot Helenus, who ruled for thirty years. Helenus begot Gotfrid, who ruled for twenty-two years. Gotfrid begot Genebald the third, who ruled for thirty years. Genebald begot Clodomir, who ruled for nineteen years. After him Heribert, his nephew, succeeding in the duchy, ruled for thirty years. When he also died, Clodoneus, his brother’s son, ruled in the duchy for twelve years. Clodoneus begot Gosvuert, who ruled for [unclear] years.
