in the seven hundred and fortieth year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the eighth Roman indiction, the duchy of eastern Francia remained without a duke for twelve years, under the rule of Pippin, mayor of the palace and afterward king of the Franks, who entrusted it to his son Charles the Great.

Therefore there were in eastern Francia, succeeding one another for four hundred and fourteen years, twenty-one dukes in number, who constitute the sacred seven, tripled in order, and not foreign to mystery. But in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 752, in the fifth Roman indiction, Pippin, raised from mayor of the palace to king of the Franks, as was said above, handed over the oft-mentioned duchy of eastern Francia to Saint Burchard, first bishop of the church of Würzburg, and to his successors, as their perpetual property.

From that time, apart from the bishops of the church of Würzburg, down to the present day, no one has been able by right to claim for himself the duchy of the aforesaid Francia, although by the rashness, not the right, of certain kings and emperors, rebels against and excommunicates of the Roman Church, the contrary was sometimes attempted, as if in vengeance for themselves. Among these Conrad, the third of that name and afterward emperor, since he was a Swabian by nation, violently usurped for himself, by royal permission, the duchy of eastern Francia; nevertheless, after he had become Caesar, he restored it to the Church with manifold satisfaction.

Let these things, briefly touched upon by a necessary historical digression concerning the origin, genealogy, and succession of the dukes of the people of eastern Francia, suffice. Let us now return to the order of the kings of the Franks, from which we departed. But Clodomir, king of the Franks, after many deeds bravely performed, at last died in the eighteenth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord 337, in the tenth Roman indiction.

The last duke of Francia was Gosbert.

The duchy of eastern Francia is vacant for twelve years.

There were twenty-one dukes at Würzburg.

The duke of eastern Francia is now the bishop.

The duchy of eastern Francia belongs solely to the prelate of the church of Würzburg.

Conrad III was not duke of Francia but an invader.

Of these things a fuller mention is made in the Annals.

Clodomir, king of the Franks, dies.

The Thirty-Seventh.

Richimer, the eldest son of King Clodomir, succeeding his father, reigned thirteen years. Throughout all the days of his reign he was always in conflict with the Romans and the Gauls; and with the help of Genebald, his paternal uncle, namely duke of eastern Francia, residing at the city of [peapolitanam], and of the other princes of the Franks, and also of the Thuringians, Saxons, and fierce German friends, he often fought victoriously against them and afflicted them with great slaughter.

In the fourth year of his reign, after gathering the support of his friends, he entered Gaul with a very great multitude of fighters, and laid waste everything with fire and sword. Against him Tiberianus, prefect of the Romans, also moved a great army of his own men to war. When they joined battle, they fought for a long time with uncertain fortune, and many on both sides fell slain. Finally, however, the Gauls were defeated and compelled to seek safety by flight.

Richimer reigned thirteen years.

A war is undertaken between the Franks and the Romans.

The Romans again declared war on the Franks. The Franks stood bravely against the Romans. The Romans are defeated by the Franks in battle. Richimer, king of the Franks, is slain in battle. Thirty-eighth: Theodomer reigned ten years. The seat of the kings of the Franks was at Dispartum among the Tungri. The Franks were never at rest until they had conquered all. The eastern Franks cross the Rhine. The city of the Treveri is plundered by the Franks. King Theodomer is killed by the Romans together with his mother. Thirty-ninth: Clogio reigned eighteen years. Saint Antony dies.

In the sixth year of King Richimer, in the fourth indiction, the Romans, assembled troop by troop into one force with the Gauls under Constantius, son of Constantine, the great Caesar, declared war on the Franks. But King Richimer, since he was a high-spirited, strong, and bold prince, terrified by nothing, summoned to his aid, as was his custom, his friends the Teutons, Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians; and when these had been united with the Franks, he set against the Romans and Gauls an army of nearly two hundred thousand, with whom he fought spiritedly. In the first encounter the Romans were victors; in the second, defeated and overcome, they fled with loss to their own men.

In the last year of his reign Richimer, king of the Franks, when he was about to fight rashly again with the Romans, was slain in battle, namely in the thirteenth year of his reign and in the three hundred fiftieth year of the Lord's nativity, in the eighth indiction of the Romans.

Theodomirus, son of the aforesaid King Richimer, reigned after the death of his father for ten years. During all the days of his reign he lived in contention with the Romans and brought to completion many battles against them with varying outcome. His mother, named Hastila, daughter of the king of the Saxons, [unclear] the Gauls [unclear]. In antiquity the part of the Tungri was beyond the river Meuse, in the fortress which antiquity called Dispartum. From the boundary of the Franks as far as the river Loire the Gauls dwelt under the rule of the Romans; beyond the Loire were the Goths, mixed with peoples of diverse nations.

In these times the borders of the kingdom of the Franks were greatly enlarged beyond the Meuse, and they had occupied a great part of Gaul, though the Romans were unwilling. Nor did they desist from what they had begun until at last, reckoning from this time onward, within nearly seventy years, they subjected all Gaul to their dominion.

In the times of Theodomirus's reign, Dagobert, son of Genebald, the first duke of the eastern Franks, succeeding his father in the principate, gathered a multitude of fighters, crossed the Rhine, and devastated cis-Rhenane Gaul with plundered spoils, fire, and sword. He despoiled and burned the very ancient city of the Treveri, built in the times of Abraham, prince of the Jews.

But King Theodomirus at last was seized by the Romans inhabiting Gaul together with Hastila his mother, was beheaded, and perished in the tenth year of his reign, and in the 360th year of the Lord's nativity, in the third Roman indiction.

The son of King Theodomirus, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for eighteen years: a high-spirited prince, strong, and of singular prudence, who engaged in many battles with the Roman Gauls and harshly avenged the injury of his enemies. In his first year Saint Antony, abbot of the hermits, departed to the Lord, on the seventeenth day of the month of January

Maximus quō ueīt in britaniam rex. ¶ Hūc ante paucos annos britaniae rex Octauius, filio carens, de procerum consensu e roma uocauit in britaniam matre namqꝫ Bri to, patre autem Romanus erat et dedit ei filiam suam uxorem cū qua Octauio mortuo totius insulę regnum obtinuit. Maximus britaniae rex, cum ingenti multitudine suorum, na- vigio intrauit gallas, omnia per circuitum regionis hostiliter ua- stauit. ¶ Et primo quidē applicuit cū nauibus ad littus terrę armoricę, que ab illo tempore deinceps britania noua, siue minor dicta est usqꝫ in praesentem diem quam tunc inhabitabant frāci, sub mode ramine ducis Iubalhici, quem reges francorum uicarium regni illis in locis cōstituerāt. Dux aūt Iubalchus introitu tantę multitudinis gentiū haud mediocriter turbatus, copias ut potuit suoꝝ cōtraxit, ꝑcedēsqꝫ obuiā ueniētibus cū eis bellū cōmisit, in qͦ ip̄e cū ꝗndecim francoꝝ millibꝰ fuit occisus, cepteris fuga saluē que rentibus. ¶ Deniqꝫ ut nominis sui terrorẽr cunctis per gyrū incuteret, ma- gna crudelitate usus est, quippe qui mulieres, uirgines, senes iuuenes, paruulos infantes, quotquot reperit, sine misericordia trucidauit. Erant autem frāci reges, duces, nobiels, milites, po- pulus omnis, idolorū uana supsitione adhuc obcecati atqꝫ polluti Maximus uero, si Tyrannus, tamen cū omni militia, ppl̓o suo fuit christianus. ¶ Hac de iubalcho frācis obtenta victoria, maximus principa- tū illū armoricū cōtulit duci Conano, qui fuit ex fr̄e nepos Octauij regis britaniae supradicti, relictaqꝫ cū eo bona parte exercitus brita- norū ad custodiam ipse cū reliquas multitudine copiarū discedens in- de, per uniuersamqꝫ galliā discurrēs, contradicentes suo imꝑio nō minus crudeliter quā potēter bello armis fecit obedientes. ¶ Interea Gratianus romę cesar ītelligēs maxīmū sibi nomē dia

on the day, in the 105th year of his age.

At the same time also the Alemanni had a war with the Romans, not far from the Rhine, in the territory of the people of Strasbourg. In that battle many fell on both sides; more of the Alemanni were killed than of the Romans, whose commander of the army was Julian Caesar, despiser of God and apostate.

Clogio, king of the Franks, wishing to avenge his father’s death, gathered a huge army and, entering Gaul in force, stormed the city of Cambrai, where he slew without pity many Romans whom he found there.

Proceeding from there, he subjected Gaul to his kingdom as far as the river Saône. Against him the Romans, fighting more by stratagems than by strength, could do nothing.

In the thirteenth year of Clogio, king of the Franks, meanwhile, because the commanders with their armies were ravaging the Gauls, Valentinian, Caesar of the Romans, having secretly and swiftly led legions through [Sarmatia?] into the territories of the Germans, waged war with the Saxons in the territories of the Franks, on this side of the Oder, not far from the sea. In it many on both sides fell, slain by the sword. Yet in the end victory fell to the Romans, and the defeated Saxons took to flight.

King Clogio died in the eighteenth year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 378, in the sixth Roman indiction, leaving three sons by the queen: Marcomir, who first succeeded to the kingdom; Dagobert, who after the death of the aforesaid brother held the kingdom under the title of duke, as we shall say below in its place; and Hector, surnamed Degenbart, from whom Pippin and Charles, later the great emperor, drew their lineage, as we have said in the second volume.

Marcomir, the elder son of Clogio

Marcomir, Clogio’s elder son, succeeding first in the aforesaid year to the kingdom of the Franks, reigned sixteen years, a high-souled prince, strong and bold, who engaged in many battles with the Romans.

Indeed, in the first year of his reign the Romans, aided by troops of the Gauls, moved war against him. He, with the Franks and Saxons, met them in an undaunted encounter not far from the city of Cologne, fought bravely, laid low many thousands of the enemy, and distributed the spoils among his helpers and friends. This war lasted four years.

But the Franks, fierce in their inborn savagery, received the Romans for battle no otherwise than a lion is accustomed to tear apart a little dog with outstretched claws, destined at once for death and without mercy. At last, when four years had passed, the Romans, considering that they could not tame the Franks and subject them to themselves, recalled by edict the remnants of the legions that had remained, and assigned them to other places. The Franks, however, did not therefore cease from harassing the Gauls, but continued what they had begun.

In the ninth year of Marcomir, king of the Franks, in the fifteenth Roman indiction, Maximus, king of Britain, sprung from the lineage of the Caesars, received the name and diadem of the Roman Empire, being appointed by the soldiers in England.

How King Maximus came into Britain.

A few years earlier Octavius, king of Britain, having no son, with the consent of the nobles summoned this man from Rome into Britain; for on his mother’s side he was a Briton, but on his father’s a Roman. And he gave him his daughter as wife, with whom, after Octavius had died, he obtained the kingdom of the whole island. He had come, when summoned into Britain, with an army of Roman soldiery; the greater part of the soldiers remained with him, while a smaller number returned to Italy.

Then, after the death of the Caesars Valentinian and Valens, in the fifth year of his British reign, raised up in pride of mind and impatient of quiet, he caused himself to be made Caesar of the Romans by those soldiers who had remained with him, against Gratian, whom the Romans had set over themselves.

Soon, therefore, when he had been hailed as Caesar by the soldiers, he entrusted the kingdom of Britain to a vicar to administer, and, gathering into one place all the noble youth fit for war of the whole island of Britain, which is now called England, he sailed with them into Gaul, having this intention in mind: that, once the Gauls had been conquered, he would proceed to Rome and subject the empire to himself.

Therefore in the ninth year of Marcomir, king of the Franks, and in the year of the Lord’s birth 387, in the fifteenth indiction of the Romans, Maximus, king of Britain, with a huge multitude of his own men, entered Gaul by ship and ravaged everything round about the region in hostile fashion.

And first he came with his ships to the shore of the Armorican land, which from that time thereafter has been called New Britain, or Lesser Britain, down to the present day. At that time the Franks inhabited it, under the rule of Duke Iubalchus, whom the kings of the Franks had appointed vicar of the kingdom in those places. Duke Iubalchus, greatly disturbed by the arrival of so great a multitude of peoples, gathered his forces as best he could, and, advancing to meet those who were coming, joined battle with them; in that battle he himself was killed with fifteen thousand Franks, while the rest sought safety in flight.

Then, in order to strike terror of his name into all the surrounding peoples, he used great cruelty, since he slaughtered without mercy women, virgins, old men, young men, and little infants, as many as he found. Now the Frankish kings, dukes, nobles, soldiers, and all the people were still blinded and polluted by the empty superstition of idols; but Maximus, though a tyrant, was nevertheless a Christian, together with all his soldiery and his people.

After this victory over Iubalchus had been obtained from the Franks, Maximus conferred that Armorican principality upon Duke Conan, who was, through his brother, the nephew of Octavius, the aforesaid king of Britain. Having left with him a good part of the army of the Britons for protection, he himself departed thence with the remaining multitude of troops, and, ranging through all Gaul, by war and arms made those who resisted his command obedient, no less cruelly than powerfully.

that he had usurped the diadem of the Roman empire, and that, having gone out from Britain with a great army, he had begun to ravage the Gauls; he also gathered forces and moved against him into Gaul, and entered the city of Paris with his army. Afterwards, when he joined battle with Maximus, he was defeated through the treachery of Merobaldus, master of the soldiers, and, slipping away in flight, came to Lyons, where he was afterwards killed.

Conanus, however, whom Maximus had established as king in the region of Armorica, endured frequent attacks from the Gauls and Romans who were in Aquitaine. Meeting them bravely, he fought with them manfully, and, after very many of them had been killed, turned the rest to flight.

At last, having obtained peace and quiet possession of the Armorican kingdom, he began to take counsel with his nobles as to how they might as quickly as possible have their wives and children, whom they had left behind in Britain, brought to them with all their household goods, lest the propagation of their race should fail.

The number of soldiers who had come from Britain with Conanus into Armorica was thirty thousand fighting men. The common people and farmers, however, as Geoffrey is the authority, were one hundred thousand, all of whom, by order of Maximus, had sailed from Britain into Armorica. Of these, many did not have wives; the rest, who did have them, had left them in Britain with their little children when they were compelled to follow Maximus.

But Conanus and all his people, since they were Christians, in no way consented to take as wives the daughters of pagans who worshipped mute idols. Even if these women had been Christians, nevertheless it did not please them to have any traffic of marital union with the Gauls.

In those days there was in Britain, which is now called England, a certain sub-king named Dionotus, who, after the death of his brother Caradocus, held the principality of Cornwall; to him also King Maximus, when about to set out for Gaul, had entrusted the kingdom, as to a very prudent man. He had an only daughter named Ursula, by everyone’s judgment the most beautiful among all the virgins of Britain, and very devoted to Christ.

Therefore Conanus, the new king of the Armoricans from Britain, not only knew very well Ursula, the daughter of the aforesaid prince of Cornwall, Dionotus, but also loved her greatly. Hence, after messengers and letters had been sent to him, he asked that she be sent to him as his wife.

Secondly, he asked that the wives and children of the soldiers and common people, left behind in Britain when their husbands departed at the command of Maximus, be put on ships with their household goods and sent to him in the Armorican kingdom.

Thirdly, he instructed that, according to the number which he had specified in his letters, virgins should be sent: noble ones from noble lineage for the soldiers, and common ones also for the common people, whom each of those who then had no spouses might take as wives.

King Conanus of Armorica accomplished many things in war.

Erant autem cum hunis pictis scoti, daci, norviegij, quos Gratianus omnes facta cogref sione fugauit in hibernia. ¶ His temporibus Maximus rex britonum, romani usurpator imperij, superata iam uniuersa gallia, peremptoqꝫ apud Iugdunum Gratiano caesare, sedem regni sui collocauit in urbe Treuirorum ubi synodus conuocauit episcoporum, in qua sanctus Martinus pręsul Thuronensis personaliter comparuit, signifqꝫ miraculis pluribus corufcauit. Aderat Ambrosius episcopus mediolanus, ausonius quoqꝫ presul burdegalẽsis, qui de laudibus patrię urbifcꝫ Treuirorum, opus metricum scripsit, quod Mosellam, a pręter fluente fluuio, pręnotauit. Hieronimus etiam pręsbiter bethleemia nus librum beati Hilarij episcopi pictauienfis de synodis eodem tē pore apud treuiros rescripsit. ¶ Maximus autem cum maximo exercitu mouens a treueri, uictorem filium suum infantulum regem galliarum conftituit, eiꝙ tutores Quintinum Nanneum principes urbis Treuirorum deputauit. Ipse deinde cum exercitu profectus in italiam, a Theodosio per emptus est. anno Marcomiri regis francorum tertio decimo Nec diupostea etiam filius eius uictor, ingratiam fauorem Theodosij, gladio periit. ¶ Post Maximi autem inferitum. Marcomirus rex franco rum cōtractis copijs, magnum suorum exercitum transmifit in gallia sub ducibus Sunnone, Genebaldo, Priamo, Antenore, quatinus non folũ recuperaret amissa, sed omnẽ quoqꝫ gallia fraçis redderet subiectam. Et breui quidem tempore multa recuperantes, que Maximus abstulerat, etiam gallię partem non modicam regno franco addiderunt. Veruntamen armoricarum regnum, quod britones inhabitabant, utdiximus, sub Conano, illa uice obtinere non poterant quod tamen postea receperunt. ¶ Interim uero quod hi duces bello intendunt gallicano, romani francorum regnum duce Valentiniano caesare, qui cum Theodosio imperabat exercitu grandem miserunt in germaniam, fran cos (ut sperabant) penitus deleturi. Contra quos Marcomir rex france corum, cũ germanis atqꝫ saxonibus prooeffit ad bellum, facta cōgressione ab hostibus peremptus cecidit cum multis, alijs fuga la Dei perio comden tes ambo fracorum inimici. Gnauius Melga deuaftarũt britania. Gratianus comes latrones fugauit de britania Maximus caefar fe dem regni pofuit a pud Treuerim. Confiliũ episcopoBz celebratur Treueris Ambrofius. Ausoni us. Hieronymus. Maximus in italiam profectus occiditur. Franci mouerũt in galliaṁ, Franci pręter Armo rica om̃a recuparũt. Romani exercitum mittũt in germania. Marcomerrex a Va lentiniano perimit̃. F

Eleven thousand of the nobles. Of the common people, indeed, sixty thousand virgin women. The sum of the girls was seventy-one thousand. Seventy-one thousand girls, placed on ships, were endangered at sea. The greater part of the girls was drowned; the rest were captured by barbarians. Vuania and Melga, Huns and Picts, took them. The girls perished for love of chastity. Vanius, king of the Huns, and Melga, of the Picts. All seventy-one thousand girls were Christians. Geoffrey, writer of the history of Britain, [unclear]. Marcomer, king of the Franks, was prudent, and trusted neither Maximus nor the Romans.

When Dionotus had seen Conanus’s messenger, desiring to satisfy his wish, he gathered from the various provinces of Britain eleven thousand daughters of the nobles, and from the others, of lower rank, sixty thousand virgin women; all of them he ordered to assemble on a fixed day within the walls of London. He also ordered ships to be brought from all the coasts of Britain, sufficient for the transport of so great a multitude. Although this had pleased many in so great an assembly, nevertheless it displeased many, who loved their parents and homeland with greater affection. Nor perhaps were there lacking some who, preferring chastity to marriage, would rather have lost their life in any land than be married.

At last, when the things necessary for their transport had been prepared, the women who were to set out boarded the ships and passed through the River Thames into the seas. Finally, when they were turning their sails toward the Armoricans, that is, from north to south, suddenly a great storm arose at sea; the fleet was divided and the ships were separated from one another. Great danger threatened them all; the greater part of the ships was scattered into the deep sea and was drowned with the women.

Those, however, who escaped so great a danger were driven to barbarous nations, islands of the sea, and by an unknown people were either slain or consigned to perpetual servitude. For they had fallen into the army of the wicked princes Vuania and Melga, who, hired for pay by the emperor Gratian, were ravaging first Britain and then the maritime nations and surrounding islands, out of hatred for Maximus; by them they cruelly perished for love of chastity.

Now Vuania, or if you prefer, Gnavia, in the manner of the Gauls, was king of the Huns; Melga, however, was king of the Picts. The emperor Gratian had sent them, hired for pay, into the borders of Germany and also Gaul, so that they might afflict those who followed the party of Maximus. Therefore, raging through the coastal regions with both infantry and naval incursion, they encountered the aforesaid women and girls, cast by chance into those regions; and since they were beautiful Christians, they solicited them for intercourse with themselves. But when the women, faithful in Christ, refused to consent to the shameful lust of the wicked men, they were pitiably killed by the impious.

This lamentable history of seventy-one thousand holy virgins and women, apart from little children, Hunibald does not relate; but the aforementioned author Geoffrey of Monmouth does, at the end of the fourth book concerning the origin of the people and the deeds of the kings of the island of Britain, which was first called the island of giants, then from Brutus, the first king, was called Britain, afterward was named Albion, and finally obtained the name of England, which it retains to this day.

But the aforementioned Marcomirus, king of the Franks, because he was a prudent man, so governed the reins of his principate that he followed neither the party of Maximus nor that of Gratian, because the former had taken Armorica from the Franks, with many of them cruelly slain without cause, and the latter ruled the Romans, a people hostile to the Franks from their origin. Therefore he held himself pru-

[Unclear]ly within the borders of the kingdom, preferring that one enemy be consumed by another rather than to bestow favor on an enemy.

¶ After the slaughter of the maidens, the aforesaid two kings, [Guanius?] of the Huns and Melga of the Picts, to please Caesar Gratian, flooded Britain as enemies, stripped as it was of all soldiery by Maximus, as we have said, and with fire and sword wrought a great slaughter and cruelly killed an innumerable multitude of the people. When this had been announced to King Maximus, who was at that time staying at Trier, he sent a certain Gratianus, a citizen, with two legions into Britain, to drive the enemies from there. With the Huns and Picts there were Scots, Dacians, and Norwegians; after an engagement, Gratianus drove them all into Ireland.

¶ In these times Maximus, king of the Britons, usurper of the Roman empire, after all Gaul had now been overcome and Caesar Gratian slain at Lyons, placed the seat of his kingdom in the city of Trier, where he convoked a synod of bishops. At it Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, appeared in person and shone forth with many signs and miracles. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, was present, and also Ausonius, bishop of Bordeaux, who wrote a metrical work in praise of the country and the city of Trier, which he entitled Mosella from the river flowing past. Jerome also, the priest of Bethlehem, copied out anew the book of blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, On Synods, at Trier at the same time.

¶ But Maximus, setting out from Trier with a very great army, appointed his little son Victor king of the Gauls, and appointed Quintinus [and?] Nanneus, chief men of the city of Trier, as his guardians. Then he himself set out with the army into Italy and was slain by Theodosius, in the thirteenth year of Marcomir, king of the Franks. Not long afterward his son Victor also perished by the sword, to gain the grace and favor of Theodosius.

¶ But after the death of Maximus, Marcomir, king of the Franks, gathered troops and sent a great army of his men into Gaul under the leaders Sunno, Genebald, Priam, and Antenor, so that it might not only recover what had been lost, but might also render all Gaul subject to the Franks. And indeed, in a short time, recovering many things that Maximus had taken away, they also added no small part of Gaul to the Frankish kingdom. Nevertheless the kingdom of Armorica, which the Britons inhabited under Conan, as we have said, they could not obtain on that occasion; yet afterward they recovered it.

¶ Meanwhile, while these leaders were devoting themselves to the Gallic war, the Romans, under Caesar Valentinian, who was ruling with Theodosius, sent a great army into Germany against the kingdom of the Franks, intending, as they hoped, to destroy the Franks completely. Against them Marcomir, king of the Franks, advanced to battle with the Germans and Saxons; when an engagement had taken place, he was slain by the enemy and fell with many, while the others [entrusted themselves to the protection of flight?] [unclear], both enemies of the Franks.

[Guanius?] and Melga devastated Britain. Count Gratianus drove the robbers out of Britain.

Caesar Maximus placed the seat of his kingdom at Trier.

A council of bishops is held at Trier. Ambrose. Ausonius. Jerome.

Maximus, having set out for Italy, is killed.

The Franks moved into Gaul.

The Franks recovered everything except Armorica.

The Romans send an army into Germany.

King Marcomer is killed by Valentinian.

[unclear]. In the fifteenth year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord’s nativity 393, in the sixth Roman indiction. Valentinian, wishing to advance farther and desiring to subject to his rule the whole kingdom of the Franks that was in the regions on this side of the Rhine, was compelled, because of an incursion of the Lombards, to withdraw into Italy.

But, concealing by stratagem the necessity of going back, he sent messengers to those who had remained in the kingdom of the Franks, through whom he ordered that they should either choose war anew or pay tribute to the Romans. But the Franks, now deprived of their king, and with the strength of their soldiery and their dukes stationed in Gaul, since they did not know the emperor’s necessity for withdrawing, and thought that nothing other than war was imminent, and saw that they were unequal in strength, promised tribute to the Romans. Yet they could neither promise it without the consent and will of the princes, then, as we have said, far absent, nor pay it. When these matters had been concluded with the Franks as Valentinian the emperor wished, he set out against the Lombards.

Meanwhile all the things that the Romans, under the command of Valentinian, had done with the Franks were announced to the dukes of the Franks, Dagobert, Sunno, Genebald, Priam, Antenor, and the other elders who were directing the wars of the nation in the region of the Gauls: how they had condemned both the king to death and the nation to tribute, a nation which had always been free and had been subject to no one from its Trojan origin. They were angry, stirred up, and greatly troubled, and in many deliberations they considered how they might prudently avenge this injury.

After much and prolonged consultation, therefore, they at last came together into one opinion: that they ought rather to preserve their fatherland in its ancestral liberty than to press forward with affairs in Gaul. Leaving, therefore, Duke Priam in the territories of Gaul with a sufficient guard of soldiers, the other princes returned with the army into Germanic Francia. Thereafter, after the death of King Marcomir, the kingdom of the Franks remained vacant, without a king, under only two dukes, for nearly twenty-six years.

Dagobert, brother of Marcomir king of the Franks, who was killed by Valentinian, and son of the aforesaid King Clogio, after the death of his brother was, by the consent of the Franks, interrex, or governor of the kingdom, for about five years, as Hunibald indicates, a high-minded and warlike man. In his time Marcomir, son of Clodius, held the dukedom among the eastern Franks for sixteen years. Dagobert began the government of the kingdom under the name of duke in the year of the Lord’s nativity 393, in the sixth indiction.

In the second year of Duke Dagobert, Caesar Valentinian, having sent messengers to the people of the Franks in Germany, demanded the tribute imposed the previous year. To him the dukes and people of the kingdom sent back word through the same messengers as follows: the everlasting freedom of the Franks [unclear] to impose tribute on nations

Hinc ortum est odium francorum in treuiros propter quod postea rheno transmisso, in regione treuirorum hye mare coeperunt, &amp; omnia deuastare. ¶ His autem peractis, Quintino utile uisum est, si exercitum omen treuiorum traducerent in franciam, imparatosqꝫ subita irrup tione praeoccuparent. Sed Nanneno consilium Quintini non pla cuit, qui francos in solo proprio ad resistendum esse non dubitabat audentiores. as he was accustomed with the rest, not to pay. But you, who, when the strength of the Franks was absent, fought against an unarmed few, and conquered by deceit, not by courage, if you trust that you have the right of exacting tribute from the Franks, come whenever you wish, and by the sword we shall show that we are most free and always have been, and that you are a slave. By this we make you certain, lest you send anyone to us unarmed concerning this matter, since indeed we strive rather to give up life than to lose liberty.

When Valentinian had received this message, he wondered at the constancy of the Franks, and said to those standing around: “Frank, Frank, you are a hard people, to be named rather from ferocity than from liberty.” And the matter rested in the current year, because at that time the Roman commonwealth was suffering many varied hostile incursions from different nations.

But in the following year Valentinian, deceived by the counsel of his own men, again sent to the Franks Sisinnius, a count of the court, so that he might induce them by good persuasions to the payment of tribute and to the very firm friendship of the Romans. But the Franks, not forgetful of those things which they had previously sent back in answer to Valentinian, and also wishing to avenge their most beloved king Marcomir, slew with the sword the count sent to them, together with the whole company which he had brought, in contempt of Valentinian and of all the Romans.

After this the Franks, having gathered a very great army of their men into one body, under the leaders Sunno and Genebald, whom the Gauls called Gundebaud, crossed the Rhine with force and, bursting into the borders of the Romans and laying everything waste, struck fear even into the people of Cologne. For they strove to subject to their dominion everything that lay between the rivers Rhine, Meuse, and [Tabula?]. But afterward, when the incursion of the Franks became known at Trier, Nannenus and Quintinus, chiefs of the Treveri, who, like the people of Cologne, followed the Roman side, gathered an army and determined to make a movement against them. For meanwhile the Franks, after the region of the Gauls had been ravaged and many of them killed, sent the spoils back to their native seats with part of the army, while they proceeded farther.

When Nannenus and Quintinus, chiefs of the Treveri, had come with an army, the Franks, as we have said, in good number and already laden with plunder, had crossed the Rhine, intending to return to their comrades in order, with all their strength, to lay waste what remained untouched among the Gauls. A great confusion overtook the Franks because of the ill-considered and insufficiently cautious division of the army.

For the first seats of the Franks were, as we have often said, around the borders of the mouths of the Rhine, where now are Holland, Zeeland, the people of Utrecht, Guelders, and the Frisians. A part of these afterward acquired the name Westphalians, that is, western Gauls, by comparison with the others, who received the name Eastphalians. And the eastern ones had [unclear] in the region of Münster, they said. The Franks had on the east the Saxons, Teutons, Germans, and Marcomanni; to the south the people of Cologne and the Gauls; to the west the Tungri and Morini, who inhabited the maritime regions; and to the north the Scots, Arcadians, Dacians, and also the sea.

The Franks, scattered, are cut down in turn by the enemy.

Therefore Nannenus and Quintinus, when they had arrived with the army of the Treveri at the places in which the remnants of the Franks had remained, awaiting the return of their companions, drew up the battle line and pursued the fugitives as far as the Carbonarian Forest, forcing them to withdraw, after no small number of them had been slaughtered. From this arose the hatred of the Franks against the Treveri, on account of which they afterward crossed the Rhine and began to winter in the territory of the Treveri and to lay everything waste.

When these things had been done, it seemed useful to Quintinus that they should lead the whole army of the Treveri into Francia and forestall them, unprepared, by a sudden incursion. But Quintinus’s plan did not please Nannenus, who did not doubt that the Franks would be bolder in resisting on their own soil. Therefore Nannenus, parting from Quintinus with his men, returned to Mainz.

But Quintinus, persisting in his plan, crossed the Rhine near the fortress of Musium and led out the army, intending to destroy the Franks at the first assault, with a spirit higher and greater than his strength for winning. But the Franks, not sluggish, met the Gauls with a manly encounter, and when battle had been joined many thousands of the Treveri perished, with few saved. In that engagement Heracleus, tribune of the Roman legion, fell, and almost all who had been in command of the soldiers perished with him by the missiles and sword of the Franks. For, with the exception of a few to whom dark night and the woods offered safety and the opportunity of hiding, the whole army of Quintinus perished by sword, bow, and marsh.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 394, in the seventh indiction, the emperor Valentinian died by a noose at Vienne, a city of Gaul, through the deceit and severity of Arbogast, master of the soldiers; and a certain Eugenius, a Roman, by the plotting of the same Arbogast, seized the rule of the Gauls and reigned for three years. Afterward, when war was joined with the emperor Theodosius, he was slain by him.

The Franks, having heard of the death of Caesar Valentinian, resolved to cross the Rhine and invade Gaul. Arbogast, understanding their plan, forestalled them: in the depth of winter, when the Rhine was frozen, he led an army across at Cologne Agrippina and began to lay waste with hostile incursion the Franks nearest the Rhine.

Against him, in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s nativity, 394, the leaders of the Franks moved a powerful army; engaging the enemy, they killed more than twelve thousand Gauls and put the rest to flight with Arbogast.

After this, in the year of the Lord 497, the emperor Theodosius came from the East into Gaul with a great army against Eugenius. When Eugenius learned this, he was afraid; and coming to the Rhine, with great prayers and promises he implored the aid of the Franks and Saxons, which nevertheless he could not obtain. Therefore Theodosius, coming into Gaul, joined battle with Eugenius, and, having won the victory, slew him with many others. But Arbogast, the instigator of all evils, in despair, killed himself with his own sword.

Eugenius led an army against the Franks at Cologne.

The Franks kill twelve thousand Gauls.

Theodosius fought against Eugenius.

Eugenius is slain by Theodosius in battle.

[Valentinian?] the emperor died by a noose. Eugenius usurped the empire in Gaul.

The Franks win a victory against the Romans.

Quintinus leads forces against the Franks.

Vuandalī ānis. xxx in hispania māserūt Inter Alaricum et amp; Stiliconem pugna. Alarici mala de Honorio suspitio. Stilicho comes ab Honorio interficit̉. Roma capit̄ &amp; sub uertitur ab Alarico rege gothorum. Franci sub ducibus occupauerūt galliā. Franci regē vuanda lorum cum .xx. mil. occidunt. Respendial rex ala norū in hispania. ture hostis Carocus, fine miseratiōe crudeliter occidit. Ab urbe me tensiū progressus interiorē galliā homo truculētus intrauit, &amp; post multaꝝ desolatiōes urbiū, arelatēse postremo ciuitatē obsedit ubi a milite quodā nomine Mario captus, &amp; uinculis constrictus, pom̄s ciuitates, quas deuastauerat circumductus est cū ludibrio, &amp; uitā nimis impiam digna morte finiuit. ¶ Vuandali aūt, qui remanserant in gallia cū alanis, regē postne cē Caroci suꝑ se cōstituerūt godgisith, hominē sceleribus famosum ¶ Alaricus etiam rex vuisogothorum, cum exercitu magno deua stans italiam, Honorio cesari demandauit ut uel secum bello con grederetur, uel gothis in regno suo locum aptum concedat cū pace manendi. Honorius uero non ausus dimicare cum Alarico, delibe ratione cum suis pręhabita, gallias alioqui furore multaꝝ gentium agitat as, gothis inhabitandas concessit. ¶ Vuandalī autem, qui remanserant in gallijs, audientes gothos aduentum, quamuis ex una essent natione scanziana procreati, ni hilominus timore perterriti, galliam desererunt, &amp; cū alanis sue tijs hispaniaꝝ partē occuparūt ubi annis ferme trigīta cōmoratio po stea in Affricā nauigauerūt, &amp; Hipponam urbem destruxerunt. ¶ Alaricus uero permissione Honorij Caesaris galliam petiturus cū suis, italia digreditur super quē comes Stilicon, romani ductor exercitus, in festo dominicę resurrectionis nihil mali suspicantem non iussus irruit, eumqꝫ ad pugnam inuitum prouocauit. Et primo quidem impetu uictor extitit, in secundo congressu uictus salutem fuga querere cōpulsus fuit. Alaricus rex, qui hoc factū Honorij sub ordinatione credidit, mox foedus qđ cum eo fecerat rupit, itinereqꝫ mutato in italiā reuertitur, &amp; omnia circunquaqꝫ Honorij partium depopulatur. ¶ Honorius uero Caesar intelligens comitem Stiliconem tantos esse causam malorū, eū cepit, &amp; cū Euchario filio capite truncauit. ¶ Alaricus autem rex urbem romam cepit, ędificia multa subuer ti, &amp; ciues in rebus grauiiter lesit. A sanguine tamen et amp; hominum cęde tēperauit, &amp; fugientibus ad sanctorum basilicas pepercit. Die tertia discessit sua sponte a roma, nauigaturusqꝫ in siciliā naufragiū pertulit, &amp; non multo post infirmatus grauister, subito uitam cum morte commutauit. ¶ Dum hęc agerentur in italia per gothos, franci tempus adessera ti, quo sibi galliam subiicerent uniuersam, contractis copijs magnū adunauerunt exercitum, &amp; sub ducibꝰ Faramundo Marcomiro, Sunnone, Priamo, &amp; Antenore, fines gallicanos ingressi, primo Vuandalīs congrediuntur, qui gallias denuo incursabant, quorū regem godgisith (quem nonnulli godogisilium nuncupant) cum uigintimillibus occiderunt. ¶ Et nisi Respendial rex alano rum, vuandalis ex hispania ubi tunc regnabat tempestiue uenisset in auxilium, omnes fuissent a francis occisi.

Theodosius, victorious, died on his return at Milan; his body was brought back to Constantinople and buried with due honor. After him his two sons succeeded in the empire: Arcadius in the East, and Honorius ruled among the Romans.

In the following year, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 388, in the eleventh Roman indiction, Dagobert died, interrex of the Franks, son of the late most noble king Clogio, brother of King Marcomir.

Genebaldus. Genebaldus, the elder son of the aforementioned duke Dagobert, succeeding first in the government of the kingdom of the Franks, presided over the people and the dukes for twenty-one years. Yet he neither wrote himself king nor was called king by others, but, content with the title of duke, usurped nothing of royal dignity for himself. He had two brothers, Marcomir and Sunno, who, together with the other dukes of the Franks, faithfully administered the commonwealth of the people, its wars, and its affairs by common vote.

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 403, in the second Roman indiction, Marcomir, duke of the eastern Franks, died. He was a vigorous man but a pagan, dwelling among the Suebi at Würzburg among the [Dorigi?], and was buried according to his ancestral superstition on the mountain called Frankenberg.

To him in the Peapolitan duchy of the Franks succeeded his elder son, named Faramund, a prudent, bold, strong, warlike man, who presided over his people for fifteen years. Afterwards, as we shall say, he was elected king of the Franks by the unanimous consent of the dukes and nobles of the people.

After this, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 410, in the eighth Roman indiction, while the Franks, from hatred of the Romans and Gauls, looked the other way, Carocus, king of the Vandals, came out from the Scanzian islands, or, as they are now called, the Gothic islands, with an innumerable multitude of people. He made his way through Germany and Saxony and, with the consent of the Franks, crossed the Rhine and entered Gaul; after ravaging the region round about, he grievously afflicted the natives of the land.

He had a mother, on whose nod he depended, who said to him: “If you seek an eternal name, listen to and follow my counsel. Destroy all the buildings that former kings and princes constructed; kill the people whom they spared. For you will not be able to construct better or more beautiful buildings than those they constructed long ago; nor, by piety, moderation, or clemency in sparing those whom you have conquered, will you make for yourself a glorious name.”

Using the wicked counsel of his impious mother, Carocus crossed the Rhine and wiped out, burned, and utterly destroyed the city of Mainz on this side of the Rhine, together with all its inhabitants. Then he attacked Worms, and afterwards Speyer, with similar fury; after killing all the citizens whom he found, he overthrew them.

Moving from there, he besieged, captured, and destroyed the very ancient city of the Treveri on this side of the Moselle, which was scarcely breathing a little after the slaughter by the Franks. From Trier he moved to the city of Metz, which, when the wall had miraculously fallen by divine agency, he captured and overthrew, all its inhabitants being killed. For all people of both sex and age whom the most savage [unclear] found on his way—

Carocus, king of the Vandals. The Vandals ravage Gaul. Carocus is captured. The Vandals and Alans were in Spain. Alaric, king of the Visigoths, devastates Italy. [unclear] the enemy Carocus cruelly killed without mercy. Advancing from the city of the people of Metz, this savage man entered the interior of Gaul, and after the desolation of many cities he finally besieged the city of Arles. There he was captured by a certain soldier named Marius, bound in chains, and led around with mockery through the cities which he had devastated; and he ended his excessively impious life by a fitting death.

The Vandals, however, who had remained in Gaul with the Alans, after the death of Carocus set over themselves as king Godgisith, a man notorious for crimes.

Alaric also, king of the Visigoths, devastating Italy with a great army, sent word to Caesar Honorius that he should either engage him in battle or grant the Goths a suitable place in his kingdom where they might remain in peace. But Honorius, not daring to fight with Alaric, after first taking counsel with his men, granted the Gauls, which were otherwise being shaken by the fury of many peoples, to the Goths to inhabit.

The Vandals, however, who had remained in Gaul, hearing of the arrival of the Goths, although they had been born from one Scanzian nation, were nevertheless struck with fear, abandoned Gaul, and with the Alans their allies occupied part of Spain. After remaining there for almost thirty years, they later sailed into Africa and destroyed the city of Hippo.

But Alaric, by the permission of Caesar Honorius, intending to seek Gaul with his men, departed from Italy. Count Stilicho, commander of the Roman army, attacked him on the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection when he suspected no harm, without being ordered, and provoked him unwillingly to battle. In the first assault indeed he was victorious; in the second encounter he was defeated and was compelled to seek safety in flight. King Alaric, who believed that this deed had been done by Honorius’s arrangement, immediately broke the treaty which he had made with him, and, changing his route, returned into Italy and laid waste everything round about belonging to Honorius’s party.

But Caesar Honorius, understanding that Count Stilicho was the cause of such great evils, seized him and beheaded him together with his son Eucharius.

King Alaric then captured the city of Rome, overthrew many buildings, and gravely injured the citizens in their possessions. Yet he restrained himself from bloodshed and the slaughter of men, and spared those who fled to the basilicas of the saints. On the third day he departed from Rome of his own accord; and, intending to sail into Sicily, he suffered shipwreck, and not long afterward, being gravely ill, he suddenly exchanged life for death.

While these things were being done in Italy by the Goths, the Franks, thinking that the time had come for them to subject all Gaul to themselves, gathered forces, assembled a great army, and, under the dukes Faramundus, Marcomirus, Sunno, Priam, and Antenor, entered the Gallic territories. First they engaged the Vandals, who were again raiding Gaul, and killed their king Godgisith, whom some call Godogisilus, together with twenty thousand men.

And unless Respendial, king of the Alans, had come in time from Spain, where he was then reigning, to aid the Vandals, they would all have been killed by the Franks.

In the year of the Lord 419 Genebaldus died, interrex of the Franks, son of Dagobert and grandson of King Marcomir, in the twenty-first year of his rule; after his death the Franks, as we shall say, again had kings.

In that same year, immediately after the death of Genebaldus, the nobles and elders of the Franks gathered together and held mature counsel among themselves, judging it useful that, after the custom of the ancients, they should appoint for themselves one king from among the dukes. And the proposal seemed good in the eyes of all; and the following dukes assembled, for the sake of this matter, at another diet: namely Pharamundus, duke of the eastern Franks; Duke Marcomir and Duke Sunno, brothers of the eastern Pharamundus; Duke Clodius, son of Pharamundus; Duke Dagobertus, son of Marcomir; Duke Nicanor; Duke Pharabertus; Duke Richimer; Antenor, duke of the Menipolitani; Duke Priamus, his brother; Bertheri, a Gallican duke; Heribert, an island duke; Duke Sunno and Duke Richer, sons of the late Genebaldus, duke and interrex of the Franks; Duke Diocles; and Duke Meroveus. There were also present some of the priests and wise men of the Franks: Salegasthald, chief priest of Jupiter; Gasthald; Herahd, master of letters; Vuisogasthald, priest of Diana; Rutvuicus; Adelhardus; Richeri; and many others, both from the common people and from the nobles.

All these, after sharing among themselves the counsel of mature deliberation, at last with unanimous consent elected Pharamundus, duke of eastern Francia at Wurzburg, as king of the Franks. He had been the son of Duke Marcomir, who died, as we said above, in the year of the Lord 404; this Marcomir was the son of Clodius, who was the son of Dagobert, who was the son of Genebaldus, first duke of the eastern Franks and brother of King Marcomir; their father was Clogio, king of the Franks, who, as we said above, died in the year of the Lord 478.

Pharamundus, therefore, son of Marcomir, great duke of the eastern Franks, elected king by the common vote of the nobles in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s nativity, 419, in the second Roman indiction, on the twenty-fourth day of the month of April, in the fifty-sixth year of his age, reigned over the Franks for seven years: a man esteemed in his generation, but not a Christian.

He soon entrusted the duchy of eastern Francia to his brother Marcomir to govern; Marcomir ruled it energetically for eighteen years. His lineage and successors in the duchy, continuing in order down to the last duke Hetanus and to Charles the Great, son of Pippin, we have described above, when we set down the genealogy of the first duke.

In the third year of his reign, King Pharamundus of the Franks, in order to restrain by laws a people uncultivated in its customs and fierce in spirit, summoned certain nobles of the kingdom to him and began to hold mature counsel concerning the establishment of new ordinances.

Genebaldus, duke or interrex, dies.

63
Clodius Régis Pharamundi filiùs, eodem anno patri succedens, regnauit annis uiginti princeps magnanimus, fortis, & bellicosus qui gallos et romanos sua fortitudie potenter contriuit, & francorũ regni terminos longe ac late per galiam extendit, cunctifqꝫ per totam europam nationibus propter suam potentiam metuendus fuit. ¶ Qui statim in principio regni sui cunctis per edictũ francis mandauit longas nutrire comas quatinus agallis, quos uel expugnaturi essent, uel iam prius secum habitare deuictos, frací primo fecernerentur contuitu. Quapropter deinceps et ipse rex Clodus crinitus seu capillosus est dictus qui comam et barbam nutriuit prolixam. Gallos aūt a se deuictos, in signum seruitutis, coman detondere mandauit. Ex quo subinferre licebit, quod frāci germani gallos seruituti subegerunt, non galli neque alia queuis natio unquā superauerē Germanos. Manifestū est em̄, Hunibaldo testante, quod frāci ex eo tempore quo Germaniam sunt primo ingressi, usque ad mortem regis Clodoui qui primus fidem christi suscepit (uti dicemus) per annos nō minus nongentos quadraginta sub regibus et regulis quadraginta septem semper et fuerūt et manserunt liberrimi, nec ulliunꝗ̃ uel ad momentum seruierunt. Post uero Clodoneum quod liberi permanserint usque in presentem diem omnes frāci tam illiq́ ui sunt in Gallia, quam isti qui in Germania remanserunt, cum notū sit historiarū sine liuore peritis, probatiōe opus est nulla. ¶ Clodus rex Francorum anno regni sui octauo qui fuit domini cęnatiuitatis quadringente simus tricesimus quartus indictiōe Romanorum secunda contractis copijs exercitum mouit in doringiā Frāci, quod longe supra diximus, sub Franco rege ante chrī natiuitatem tricelimo septimo cum dorigis, saxonibus, theutonibus atque germanis perpetuum contraxerant foedus, quod usque ad obitum regis Marcomiri per annos ferme.CCCC.XXX.inuiola biliter seruatum est ab omnibus.Marcomiro autem rege francorū a Valentiniano caesare (ut prius est dictum) āno dn̄i. CCC.XCIII. occiso,dorigi et saxones cum Germanis et theutonibus a societate francoꝝ recesserunt rebus non satis prouide sub ducibus actis. ¶ Huius occasione disfidij,rex Clodus doringiam potenter intra uit regē uicit et gentē,eosque tributū Francis dare annuū,&amp; uiuncētiū deinceps obedire mādatis coartauit, ut ꝗ liberore sub iure foederis antiqui socij manere cōtempserāt eore serui,subditi et tributarij esse cogerent̃.Simile Germanis postea contigit atque Saxonibus, ꝗ rupto societatīs foedere deīceps frācos nō amplius(ut prius)senserūt amicos sed reges et amp;dn̄os. ¶ Exide rex Clodius rheno simul et amp; mosatrāsmissis expeditiōe mouit ī Gallia oemque regionē tūgore deuastās et amp;potēter obtinēs,frācor regno subiugauit,atque p confirmatiōe no ue possessionis olim amisset, sunc uero receptę, ibidem aliquandiu consedit,inde usque ad tabulam procedens omnia recepit. QVADRAGESIMVS QVARTUS Clodus crinitus regnauit annis uiꝑiti. Franci ut liberi comam nutriebant. Galli seruì comam detondebant. Non francos galli, sed gallos frāci sibi subiecerunt. Franciom̄s tam gallicani q̃ germanici semper liberrimi. Clodus rex exercitum mouit Francorum in doringiam. Dorigi a francorū societate recedunt. Franci doringiam suo regno subijcītut Dorigi francorū seruituti suij ciuntur. Franci gallos serui. tuti sue subijciunt.

He corrected the ancient laws. For the constitutions of the old kings the condition of the times did not admit in every respect, although, through the varied unrest of the nation over many years, they had fallen not only into disuse but also wholly into oblivion and contempt; and for this reason it seemed altogether necessary either to alter them by correction or to abolish them by novelty.

Four lawgivers of the Franks.

Salagastus.

Vuesogastald.

Vuyndegast.

Basogasthald.

The laws of the Franks, having been established, are approved by King Clodio.

The Vandals, with the Alans and Suevi, lay waste Spain.

Whence the Vandals are. The Alans. The Suevi. The Lombards. The Normans, etc.

The holy priest Jerome wrote many things.

Jerome, stricken with asthma, dies.

Saint Alban, priest, is martyred at Mainz.

Pharamund, king of the Franks, dies.

But in that assembly of the Franks there were many men prudent in their generation; from their number four of the more distinguished were chosen, to whom the king, together with the nobles, entrusted full power to frame laws. Their names were said to be these: Salagast, Vuesogast, Vuyndegast, Basogast. The first of these built a village beside the banks of the river Main, which he named Salagastat after himself; Vuyndegast, however, in eastern Francia founded a village of his own name, Vuyndesheim.

Therefore these four, coming together in one place for three assemblies, and carefully considering the origins of the cases, issued a new volume of legal constitutions, striking out a judgment on each matter. From the more principal author, Salagast, who was the chief priest of Jove, it received the name of the Salic law; to it King Clodoveus later added a chapter of interpretation.

In the same year the Vandals, Alans, and Suevi, having divided the region of the Spains among themselves into three parts for habitation, being separated into three kingdoms, clashed with one another in internal war. The Vandals, Alans, Suevi, Swedes, Goths also, Lombards, and Normans are alike in origin as far as concerns the first homeland of their nation, having arisen from the borders of Germany, from the Scandinavian islands, which are now called Gothia under four or five divisions, from the beginning of their migration.

In the third year of Pharamund, king of the Franks, the blessed Jerome, an illustrious priest for fifty-six years, having published his books, worn out by a severe asthmatic ailment and so cast down in his chest that he could not rise from bed unless he grasped with his hands a rope which hung from a beam for this purpose, died at Bethlehem, in the ninety-first year of his age, on the last day of September.

In the sixth year of Pharamund, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 425, in the eighth indiction of the Romans, Saint Theonestus, bishop of Philippi in Greece, driven from his church by the violence of heretics, came into Italy and then into the borders of Germany with Alban the priest, Ursus the deacon, and Abraham the subdeacon. Of these Alban suffered at Mainz for the faith of Christ.

Pharamund, king of the Franks, dies in the seventh year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 421, in the ninth indiction of the Romans.

64
Franci exploratores mittunt in galliam. Burgūdiones in provincia lugdunensi. Exploratorū uisa et audita per galliam. Clodius rex uerbarum notauit. Franci expeditionē mouerūt in galliam. Franci romanos milites apud Tornacū occiderunt. Frāci magnam gallicie partem sibi subiuergarunt. ¶ Clodius crinitus rex francorum auxilium regnum ualde. Nomina populoꝝ qͦs Clodius subiectit. Clodius rex franco-rū augustus moritur. QVADRAGESIMVS QUINTVS Meroueus regnauit annis .XII.. ¶ Post hęc anno suo undecimo indictione romanorū quinta Clo- dius rex francorū consyderans romanorū potestatē haud parū des- fecisse, misit exploratores in ulteriorem galliam, ut sitū terrę, fortitu- dinē gentis, urbiumqƺ ac munitionū custodiā diligent̓ explorarēt, sibiqƺ renunciare studerent quantotius. Eo tempore burgūdiones habitant in prouincia lugdunensi, & gothi ī aquitania qui cū his- spanis et gallis terram occupabant. ¶ Reversi exploratores ad Clodium retulerūt regiones esse optimas, fructiferam penitus terram, situm quoqƺ amoenissimum, gen- tem inermem, pauidam, inualidamqƺ, & romanorū in urbibus paruā esse custodiā. Quibus auditis rex Clodius, cui nihil plus animo fuit quam nomen, gloriamqƺ francorū dilatare, & regnū, magnū suobꝝ contraxīt exercitū, & mouens ultra flumen quod tabula nominat̉ uersus mare in galliam urbem cameracensem obseredit, & cepit, ro- manis quos in ea reperit cunctis militibus occisis. ¶ Inde mouens per carbonarium nemus ad tornacensem urbē iter festinus direxit, que ciuitas romanorū fuit presidio munita. Roma- ni uero milites qui erant in pręsidio cum audissent francorum ad- uentum, contra eos extra urbem processerunt ad bellū, in quo usqƺ ad unum omnes a francis fuerunt occisi, ut nec unus quidem remā serit ex cunctis, qui ceterorum interitus nunciū detulisset romanis. Vrbem uero turnacensem cum omni regione sibi subiecerunt. ¶ Deinde progressi ulterius francia morinos, tarauanos, & quicquid reliquū fuit galliarū, usqƺ ad mare, in suam receperūt omnimodam potestatem, possidentqƺ uniuersa usqƺ in presentem diē, quem roma- ni deinceps nec recuperauerunt, imino nec recuperare poterunt in sempiternum. Aruit em̄ roma quem dudum floruit. Clodius uero insignis francorum rex posteaꝗ regni terminos ma- gnifice dilatauit, omnemqƺ terram galliarum que fuit inter rhenum ab oriente, & mare merinum ab occidente, britanicum ab aquilonem, usqƺ ad sequanā uersus meridiem hoc est batauos, monapios, tungros, tarauanos, morinos, ambiones, cameraceses, tornacenses, atrebateses, beluaceōses, & quicquid his regionibus interiacet, ultraqƺ Sequanam usqƺ ad ligerim francorum regno potenter fecisset subiectum. Moritur anno regni sui uicesimo, dominice uero nativitatis .CCC.CXLVI.indictione.XIIIII.. Meroueus Clodij memorati regis maior natus filius, patri succedens, regnavit super francia annis duodecīs princeps potentia, fortitudine, magnitudineqƺ rerum gestarum nulli praecedentium regum inferioris qui romanum contriuit imperium, & patris uestigia gloriosa imitatione secutus, regnum francorum id paucis, quibus regnauerat annis, non mediocriter augmentauit. Clodius rex francorum in Gallia et Britania regebus suis operaverat. Meroueus successor eius continuans hęc magnanimos actos, sed permutans eū ut regnaretur in Francia, quamque postea mortuus est. Meroueus autem successor eius Remigius, qui postea duxerat in Germania, et postea regnabat in Britannia, ubique opera suae memoria habebunt. Clodius autem postea duxerat pro Romana causa in Germania, et postea ad Galliam regressus, ibidem regnavit, et postea mortuus est, cum filio suo Clovis, qui postea regnabit in Francia. Quod autem fuerit merito Clodii, vel si fuit, nec modo possumus certe judicare, sed sufficit exemplum huiusmodi, quo magistrum pater, dummodo potest, filium sui educet et educitur, et si filius ejus bonam partem faciat, patrem ei gratiarum habere videtur. Et sic etiam Clodius, dummodo poterat, filium suum, Merouem, educere et educit, et si Meroues bona partem fecit, Clodius ei gratiarum habuit. Meroueus rex francorum magnanimis actis operaverat, et postea mortuus erat, ut supra diximus. Postea duxerat Remigius in Germania, et postea in Britannia, et postea regnavit in Francia. Et postea mortuus est Remigius, et postea duxerunt pro Romana causa in Germania Gaisericus, et postea ad Galliam regnabat, et postea mortuus est, cum filio suo Clovis. Quod autem fuerit meritum Gaiserici, vel si fuit, non modo possumus certè judicari, sed sufficit exempla huiusmodi, quod magistri pater dummodo potent, filium sui educunt et educuntur, et si filii ejus bona partem faciant, patrem ei gratias habebunt. Et sic etiam Gaisericus dummodo potuerat, filium suum Clovidem educere et educit, et if Clovis bona partem fecit, Gaisericus ei gratias habuit. Clodius rex francorum merito operaverat, et postea moritur, ut supra diximus. Meroueus rex francorum operarum magnanimitatis memorie reperietur, et postea mortuus esset, ut supra dictum est. Postea duxerant pro Roma Gaisericus, et postea in Gallia regnavit, et postea morierunt, cum filio suo Cloviis. Quod autem fuisset merito Gaiserici vel si fuisse, non modo possemus certe iudicare, sed sufficietur exempla hujusmodi, que magistrum pater dummodo potens, filium suis educet et educit, et si filii eius bona partem faciant, patronis ei gratiarum habebunt. Sic etiam Gaisericus dummodo poterat, filiem sui Clovidem educere et educi, et si Clovis bona partem fecisse, Gaisericus ei gratiarum habuerit. Clodius rex Francorum merito opera factas habebatur, et postea moribundus esset, ut supra dicitur. Et postea duxerant per Romam Gaisericus, et postea Gallicia regnabat, et postea morierant, cum filio suo Cloviss. Quod autem fuerat merito Gaiserici vel si fuerat, non modo possumus certo judicari, sed exempla huiusmodi quod magister pater dummodo potent, filium suos educet et educit, et qui filii ejus bonam partem fecerint, patrem eis gratias habuerint. Sic etiam Gaisericus Dummodo poterat, filios sui Clovidem educere et educiri, et si Cloviis bona partem fecisset, Gaisericus eis gratiarum habuisset

Clodius, son of King Pharamund, succeeding his father in the same year, reigned twenty years, a high-minded, brave, and warlike prince, who by his valor powerfully crushed the Gauls and Romans, and extended the boundaries of the kingdom of the Franks far and wide through Gaul, and because of his power was feared by all the nations throughout all Europe.

He, immediately at the beginning of his reign, commanded all the Franks by edict to grow long hair, so that from the Gauls, whom they were either going to attack or who, already conquered, were dwelling with them, the Franks might be distinguished at first sight. For this reason thereafter King Clodus himself was called “the long-haired” or “the hairy,” for he grew his hair and beard long. But the Gauls conquered by him he ordered to have their hair cut off, as a sign of servitude. From this one may infer that the Frankish Germans subjected the Gauls to servitude, and that neither the Gauls nor any other nation ever overcame the Germans. For it is clear, as Hunibald bears witness, that from the time when the Franks first entered Germany until the death of King Clodoveus, who first received the faith of Christ, as we shall say, through not less than nine hundred forty years, under forty-seven kings and petty kings, they always were and remained entirely free, and never served anyone even for a moment. But after Clodoneus, that all the Franks remained free down to the present day, both those who are in Gaul and those who remained in Germany, since it is known to those skilled in histories without envy, needs no proof.

Clodus, king of the Franks, in the eighth year of his reign, which was the four hundred thirty-fourth year from the Lord’s birth, in the second indiction of the Romans, having gathered forces, moved his army into Thuringia. The Franks, as we said far above, under King Franco, in the thirty-seventh year before the birth of Christ, had made a perpetual treaty with the Thuringians, Saxons, Teutons, and Germans, which was kept inviolate by all for almost 430 years, until the death of King Marcomir. But after Marcomir, king of the Franks, was killed by the emperor Valentinian, as was said before, in the year of the Lord 393, the Thuringians and Saxons, together with the Germans and Teutons, withdrew from the alliance of the Franks, affairs having been conducted not sufficiently prudently under the dukes.

On account of this breach, King Clodus powerfully entered Thuringia, defeated the king and the people, and compelled them to pay annual tribute to the Franks and thereafter to obey the commands of the victors, so that those who had scorned to remain free allies under the law of the ancient treaty were forced to be their servants, subjects, and tributaries. The same later happened to the Germans and Saxons, who, after breaking the treaty of alliance, thereafter no longer found the Franks friends, as before, but kings and lords. Then King Clodius, after crossing both the Rhine and the Meuse, moved an expedition into Gaul, and, devastating and powerfully occupying the whole region of Tongeren, subjected it to the kingdom of the Franks; and for the confirmation of the new possession, which he had formerly lost but now recovered, he settled there for some time. Then, advancing as far as [Tabula?], he recovered everything.

65
Omnes enim galliarum fines, quos pater francorum adiunxerat re gno,cunctis regni sui diebus non solum subditione sua continuit, sed etiam romanis ubilibet inuentis, uel occisis, uel fugatis, termi- nos acquisitę possessionis longe lateqꝫ mirum inmodum dilatauit. ¶ Anno regni sui octauo, terręmotus poene fuerunt affidui, &; fi- gna in caelo plura, &; metuenda sint ostensa. Nam aduesperascẽte quadam die, coelũ rubẽs ut ignis ab aquilone apparuit, intermistis per ignem ruborem lineis quibusdam clarioribus, in hastarum similitudinem deformatis. Eclipsin luna patitur cometes horrendę magnitudinis apparuit, &; alia multa sunt uisa prodigia, que nõ fu¬ isse penitus ociosa declarant mala subsecuta. ¶ Sequenti etenim anno qui fuit regis Merouei nonus. &amp; domi- nicę natiuitatis, CCCC.LIII. indictione romanorum sexta. Attila rex hunorum Vualimirus rex ostrogothorum. Ardaricus rex gepi darum, &; alię gentes aquilonares in unum conspiranets, a pano¬ nię finibus egrediuntur, &; imperium occidentale simul &; regnũ francorum in partibus gallicanis cum quingentis millibus pugna torum inuadunt strages ingentes conficiunt nemini parcunt. ¶ Et primo quidem per uniuersam galliam furor eorum in tantũ permittente deo deseruit, ut nulla munitione firmitas aut fortitudo, ci¬ uitatem, oppidum ul̃ castellum ab eorum infestatione posset defen dere. Contra quorum insolentiam. Meroueus rex francorum. The odoricus quoqꝫ rex Vuisogothorum. &amp; Aetius romanorum patri tius cum aliarum diuersarum gentium copijs militaribus processe- runt ad bellum apparatu communi, cum quibus in campis dimica¬ uere cathalaunicis, a mane usqꝫ ad noctem. &amp; franci uicerunt hostẽ cum adherentibus socijs licet Attila non fuit omnino deletus, ¶ Cesa sunt in eo pręlio centum octoginta millia pugnatorum, in¬ ter quos etiam cecidit Theodoricus rex Vuisogothorum, uir belli¬ cosilsimus. Retrocedentibus francis, simul &; ceteris qui conuene¬ rant in hunos, Attila rex sumpta militia in patriarcham redijt, vt exerci¬ tu reparato surorem continuare posset incoeptum, &amp; galliam cum italia in desolationem reducere. ¶ Sequenti nanqꝫ anno ingressus italia rex Attila, omnes poene ciuitates eius, aut diripuit, aut funditus euertit. Ad quem Leo papa primus pontificalibus uenit indutus, &amp; non solum urbi populoqꝫ salutem impetrauit, sed etiam ut relicta italia abiret, obtinuit. Interrogatus uero a suis cur placidus extiterit, respon debat se illum non fuisse reueritum, sed senem quendam ueneran- dum aspectu, iuxta eum stantem, qui gladio euaginato mortem re¬ gi minabatur, si pontificem uel cõtristaret, uel negaret omne quod postularet. The Franks send scouts into Gaul. The Burgundians in the province of Lyon. What the scouts saw and heard throughout Gaul. King Clodius took note of their words. The Franks launched an expedition into Gaul. The Franks killed the Roman soldiers at Tournai. The Franks subjected a great part of Gaul to themselves. Clodius the long-haired, king of the Franks, greatly increased the kingdom. The names of the peoples whom Clodius subjected. Clodius, king of the Franks, dies [unclear]. The Forty-Fifth: Meroveus reigned twelve years.

After these things, in his eleventh year, in the fifth indiction of the Romans, Clodius, king of the Franks, considering that the power of the Romans had declined in no small degree, sent scouts into further Gaul, so that they might diligently investigate the situation of the land, the strength of the people, and the guard of the cities and fortifications, and take care to report back to him as quickly as possible. At that time the Burgundians were living in the province of Lyon, and the Goths in Aquitaine, who, together with the Spaniards and Gauls, occupied the land.

When the scouts returned to Clodius, they reported that the regions were excellent, the land wholly fruitful, the situation also very pleasant, the people unarmed, fearful, and weak, and that the Roman guard in the cities was small. When he had heard this, King Clodius, who had nothing more in mind than to extend the name and glory of the Franks, and their kingdom, gathered a great army of his men, and, moving beyond the river which is called Tabula toward the sea into Gaul, besieged and took the city of Cambrai, killing all the Roman soldiers whom he found in it.

Then, moving through the Carbonarian Forest, he hastened on his way to the city of Tournai, which city was fortified by a Roman garrison. But the Roman soldiers who were in the garrison, when they had heard of the arrival of the Franks, advanced against them outside the city for battle; in that battle they were all killed by the Franks to the last man, so that not even one remained of all of them to carry news of the others’ destruction to the Romans. They subjected the city of Tournai, with the whole region, to themselves.

Then, advancing further, the Franks brought the Morini, the Taravani, and whatever remained of the Gauls as far as the sea under their complete power, and they possess all these things down to the present day, which the Romans afterward neither recovered nor indeed will be able to recover forever. For Rome has withered, though once it flourished.

But Clodius, the distinguished king of the Franks, after he had magnificently enlarged the boundaries of the kingdom, and had powerfully subjected to the kingdom of the Franks all the land of the Gauls which lay between the Rhine on the east, the southern sea on the west, the British sea on the north, as far as the Seine toward the south, that is, the Batavi, Menapii, Tungri, Taravani, Morini, Ambiani, people of Cambrai, people of Tournai, Atrebates, Bellovaci, and whatever lies between these regions, and beyond the Seine as far as the Loire, died in the twentieth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 446, in the fourteenth indiction.

Meroveus, the elder-born son of the aforementioned King Clodius, succeeding his father, reigned over Francia for twelve years, a prince inferior to none of the preceding kings in power, courage, and the greatness of his deeds; he crushed the Roman empire, and, following his father’s footsteps in glorious imitation, not moderately increased the kingdom of the Franks in the few years in which he reigned.

King Clodius of the Franks had carried out his works in Gaul and Britain under his kings. Meroveus, his successor, continuing these magnanimous deeds, but changing him so that he might be ruled in Francia, and afterward he died. But Remigius, successor of Meroveus, who afterward had led in Germany, and afterward reigned in Britain, everywhere they will have the memory of his work. But Clodius afterward had led on behalf of the Roman cause in Germany, and afterward, having returned to Gaul, reigned there, and afterward died with his son Clovis, who afterward will reign in Francia. But what may have been of the merit of Clodius, or whether it was, we cannot now judge certainly; but an example of this kind suffices, whereby a father as teacher, so long as he is able, educates and is educated by his own son; and if his son does a good part, he seems to give thanks to the father for it. And thus Clodius too, so long as he was able, educated and does educate his son Meroveus, and if Meroveus did a good part, Clodius gave thanks to him.

Meroveus, king of the Franks, had performed magnanimous deeds, and afterward was dead, as we said above. Afterward Remigius had led in Germany, and afterward in Britain, and afterward reigned in Francia. And afterward Remigius died, and afterward Gaiseric and afterward [unclear] led on behalf of the Roman cause in Germany, and afterward he reigned in Gaul, and afterward died with his son Clovis. But what may have been the merit of Gaiseric, or whether it was, we cannot now certainly judge; but examples of this kind suffice, that fathers as teachers, so long as they are able, educate and are educated by their own son, and if their sons do a good part, they will give thanks to the father for it. And thus Gaiseric too, so long as he was able, educated and does educate his son Clovis, and if Clovis did a good part, Gaiseric gave thanks to him. Clodius, king of the Franks, had acted meritoriously, and afterward dies, as we said above.

Meroveus, king of the Franks, will be found in the memory of works of magnanimity, and afterward was dead, as was said above. Afterward they had led on behalf of Rome, Gaiseric, and afterward he reigned in Gaul, and afterward they died with his son Clovis. But what may have been of the merit of Gaiseric, or whether it had been, we cannot now judge certainly; but examples of this kind will suffice, that a father as teacher, so long as he is able, educates and does educate his sons, and if his sons do a good part, they will give thanks to patrons for it. Thus Gaiseric too, so long as he was able, educated and was educated by his son Clovis, and if Clovis had done a good part, Gaiseric would have given thanks to him. Clodius, king of the Franks, was held to have meritorious works performed, and afterward was dying, as is said above. And afterward they had led through Rome, Gaiseric, and afterward he reigned in Galicia, and afterward they died with his son Clovis. But what may have been of the merit of Gaiseric, or whether it had been, we cannot now judge certainly; but examples of this kind, that a father as teacher, so long as they are able, educates and does educate his sons, and those sons of his who have done a good part have given thanks to their father for it. Thus Gaiseric too, so long as he was able, educated and was educated by his sons Clovis, and if Clovis had done a good part, Gaiseric would have given thanks to them.
