For all the territories of the Gauls which the father of the Franks had added to the kingdom, throughout all the days of his reign he not only kept under his own rule, but also, with the Romans wherever they were found either killed or put to flight, he extended the bounds of the possession he had acquired far and wide in a remarkable manner.

In the eighth year of his reign earthquakes were almost continual, and many fearful signs were shown in the sky. For on a certain day, as evening was coming on, the sky appeared in the north red as fire, with certain brighter lines interspersed through the fiery redness, deformed into the likeness of spears. The moon suffered an eclipse; a comet of dreadful magnitude appeared; and many other prodigies were seen, which the evils that followed declare not to have been at all idle.

For in the following year, which was the ninth of King Meroveus and, from the Lord's Nativity, 453, in the sixth indiction of the Romans, Attila king of the Huns, Vualimirus king of the Ostrogoths, Ardaricus king of the Gepids, and other northern peoples, conspiring together, set out from the borders of Pannonia and invaded both the western empire and the kingdom of the Franks in the Gallic regions with five hundred thousand fighting men; they wrought immense slaughter and spared no one.

And first, indeed, throughout all Gaul their fury, God permitting it, raged to such an extent that no strength or firmness of fortification could defend a city, town, or castle from their assault. Against their insolence Meroveus king of the Franks, and Theodoric also, king of the Visigoths, and Aetius, patrician of the Romans, advanced to war with the military forces of various other peoples, by common preparation; with them they fought in the Catalaunian fields from morning until night. And the Franks with their allied companions defeated the enemy, although Attila was not wholly destroyed.

In that battle one hundred eighty thousand fighting men were slain, among whom Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, a most warlike man, also fell. When the Franks, together with the others who had assembled against the Huns, withdrew, King Attila, taking his army, returned into [unclear], so that, after repairing his army, he might be able to continue the fury he had begun and reduce Gaul together with Italy to desolation.

For in the following year King Attila entered Italy and either plundered or utterly overthrew almost all its cities. Pope Leo I came to him dressed in pontifical vestments, and obtained not only safety for the city and people, but also that he should depart, leaving Italy. When he was asked by his men why he had become mild, he replied that he had not revered him, but rather a certain old man, venerable in appearance, standing beside him, who with a drawn sword threatened death to the king if he should either grieve the pontiff or deny anything that he asked. Not long after, King Attila, glutted at his wedding, died from a stroke of apoplexy.

He kept Gaul powerfully under his authority.

The city of the Treveri is captured by the Franks and possessed by them.

The emperor Avitus was staying among the Treveri.

Lucius, a senator of the Treveri, handed the city over to the Franks.

Avitus violated the wife of Lucius.

The Franks are summoned to Trier by Lucius.

The city of the Treveri had for many years been subject to the Romans.

The kingdom of the Franks grew greatly over 900 years.

The Franks, by continuing wars, at last conquered.

The kingdom of the Franks greater than all the kingdoms of all Europe.

In the eleventh year of Meroveus, king of the Franks, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 457, in the tenth Roman indiction, the Franks took the city of the Treveri on the following occasion; Attila, king of the Huns, had captured it in war a few years before and had crushed it with grievous devastation. After the death of Valentinian, whom the friends of the patrician Aetius had killed in the same year, and who after Theodosius had reigned with Marcian, Avitus was appointed emperor by the Romans; under him the city of the Treveri was captured.

At that time there was in the city of the Treveri a certain senator named Lucius, who had a wife judged by very many to be most beautiful; Avitus was wasting away in shameful love for her. For this reason, feigning illness, he lay down on his bed and, as though to obtain relief from his sickness, ordered all the senatorial women of the city to come to visit him in succession. Among the others came the wife of Lucius, suspecting no evil; Avitus at once violated her. When the crime had been committed, the woman returned weeping to her husband’s house. On the next day Caesar Avitus rose from his bed, healthy in body but polluted in conscience by the crime, and said to Lucius when he met him: “You have beautiful baths indeed, Lucius, but you wash in cold water,” hinting at the foul, unnatural discharge of his wife. But Lucius understood the figure, took it grievously, and, messengers and letters having been sent in the utmost secrecy to the Franks, promised that if they came as quickly as possible, he would hand over the city of the Treveri into their power without doubt, delay, or difficulty.

For up to that point the Treveri, for many years past, had sided with the Romans and their kings with stubborn attachment. But the Franks, not forgetful of the slaughter and wrongs which they had once suffered from Nannenus and Quintinus, princes of the Treveri, at the Carbonarian Forest in the time of Duke Dagobert, the interrex, immediately gathered forces and hastened gladly to the destruction of the Treveri. When the city had been captured, the Franks plundered everything and subjected it to their kingdom.

In these times the kingdom of the Franks gradually took on great growth and extended its borders in many ways throughout the Gauls. Hence the kings of the nation, who from their first entrance into Germany had held seats around the Rhine, where Holland now is, with the peoples who are called Gelderlanders, Westphalians, Clivenses, and Frisians, for almost eight hundred and seventy years, at [Neopagus?], Duisburg, and in the other places and castles on this side of the Rhine, transferred the dwelling-place of their habitation into the Gauls, rarely resting from wars, until at last they subjected all Germany, Gaul also, and at the same time Italy, to the kingdom of the Franks.

And so the kingdom of the Franks, which took its beginning from one small people, through much labor, through most bloody wars, through the very great bloodshed of kings, dukes, nobles, soldiers, and commoners, over about nine hundred years at last grew immeasurably; it took on growth beyond all the kingdoms of all Europe, so that it ruled with power over many kingdoms and peoples, and from many kingdoms there was made one which, gathered by the sword, for the honor of the conqueror, would be called, and was, by the name of the Franks

Hildericus ꝓfugus de doringia reuocatur in regnum. manorum quintadecima. Hildericus industria &; fide Vuinibaldi amici sui, qui fuit unus ex potentioribus regni principibus, ex do¬ ringia reuocatus in regnum francorum, omniū fauore procerū &; gentis in regnum paternū restituitur, &; Aegidius cunctis odiosus inde fugatur. Et regnauit deinceps Hildericus modestissime adhuc annis uiginti duobus. Cunqꝫ audisset Basina uxor Basani regis doringoꝝ, quod Hildericus esset a francis restitutus in regnum, dimisso uiro suo secuta est eum in galliā, nimio eius amo re concitata, quem̄ ex diuturna familiaritate cohabitandi apud dorin gos contraxerat. Hildericus uenientem hilari uultu admittens, sibi ut notam desumpsit uxorē, Basani regis a quo triennio beningne fuerat hospitio receptus male humanitatem hanc remunerans. Instante autem prima nuptiarum nocte, Basina monuit Hilderi cum paulisper differre concurritū, forescꝫ cubiculi obseruare, &; que tertio uiderit in atrio portenta renunciare uaticinantī sibi per omnia fideliter. Mulieri credulus rex ut mandauit obsequitur, obseruatisqꝫ tertio ędibus, ad eam reuersus est dicens primo se uidiffe in atrio pa latij rhinocerotas id est unicornes, leones quoqꝫ &; leopardos. Secū do lupos &; ursos fuentes, seqꝫ mutuo insectantes. Tertio uidit ait canes plures, sed exiguos, qui sese mutuo dente lacerabant, &; mor debant infesto, sed quid significent tu dicito. Ad hec mulier Saga regi sic ait. Generabimus ecce sobolem, ua rijs moribus cum tempore diuersam. Prima em̄ quem nascetur ex no¬ bis erit multum generosa, quem nobilitate sua leonibꝰ fit comparā da, &; unicornibus generolis. Ex prima generatione cum tempore surget secunda, quem more luporum contempta nobilitate, rapinas &; oppressiones pauperū exercerabit. Generatio posthanc tertia, quem &; ultima erit ex nobis, more canū se mutuo lacerabit, mordebitqꝫ, &; collidet, donec postremo innouissimis diebus regnum deficiet. Concepit eadem nocte mulier, &; peperit filium, nomine Clodone um ut dicemus. Sequenti anno qui fuit dominice natiuitatis quadringētesimus sexagesimus tertius. Hilderico natus est filius nomine Clodoneus, qui patri successit postea in regno francorum, &; primus fidē christi suscepit. ut infra dicemus. Eodem ferme tempore Hildericus francosum rex, contracto magno pugnatorū exercitur bellum mouit contra gentem alemannorum, qui habita bant inter italiam &; sueuiam ubi iam sunt urbes, curienlis, &; sedu nensiualensisqꝫ. Congressione facta superati sunt alemani, &; sub tributo francorum redacti. His quoqꝫ temporibus mortuo Vtherpendragon rege britanię, quem nunc anglia dicit̉, sub limatus fuit in regno eius filius, nomine Arcturus, de quo non solū historia britonum, narrante Galfredo monemutense, sed etiam uo ces populorum anglie miranda personant, usqꝫ in presentem diem licet plura magis sint fabulosa, quam conformia ueritati. Qui Ar¬

From this it is plainly clear that, just as the Franks who remained with the Germans use the language and customs of the Germans, so also those who entered Gaul with the kings and remained with the Gauls changed both their customs and their manner of speaking together with their settlements; and those whom nature had made Germans from the beginning of their birth, change of place in the midst of the Gauls likewise made Gauls in speech and customs. Indeed, when they were in Troy, they practiced Trojan customs and speech; among the Scythians likewise Scythian ones; in Germany they learned and kept German ones, and in Gaul Gallic ones. So too Aeneas, coming from the Trojans into Italy with his people, gradually forgetting his native speech, began to use the customs and language found at Rome.

After this Meroveus, king of the Franks, seized by sickness, died in the pagan worship of idols, as all his forebears had done, in the twelfth year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord’s nativity 458, in the eleventh indiction. The son of King Meroveus, succeeding his father in the kingdom of the Franks, reigned twice through a varied change of affairs. For first after his father he reigned only one year; then, because of his insolence and debauchery, as we shall say, he was deprived of the kingdom and fled into Thuringia. After him the Franks set over themselves as king a certain Aegidius, a Roman; when he had been driven out after three years, Hilderic was recalled from Thuringia into Francia and reigned twenty-two years. And the whole time of his reign, from his first establishment after his father down to his death, came to twenty-six years; yet he reigned only twenty-three, since Aegidius, as we have said, occupied the kingdom for three years while he himself was in exile in Thuringia with King Basinus.

After only one year had been completed in the kingdom, the nobles of the kingdom, conspiring against him, wished to kill him, because, living too insolently and wantonly, he had defiled by his foul conduct many of their daughters and wives and those of the nobles. When he learned this, he fled with a few men into Thuringia, and remained with Basinus, king of the Thuringians, his kinsman, for three years. He withdrew, however, after being deprived by the Franks, in the year of the Lord 459, in the twelfth indiction.

After his departure from the kingdom, in that same year, the princes of the Franks at once set over themselves as king a certain Aegidius, a Roman prefect at Soissons, who occupied the kingdom of the Franks for three years while Hilderic was in exile. He, continually raging against the chief princes of the kingdom, slaughtered many, having no reasonable cause apart from empty suspicion. Therefore the rest, fearing that similar things would at some time threaten them, unanimously arranged a conspiracy against the tyrant, judging that it would be more tolerable to suffer that man to rule the kingdom who abused the daughters and wives of his subjects than to endure longer that man who thirsted for nothing more than the blood of princes.

In the year, therefore, of the Lord’s nativity 462, in the [unclear] indiction. The kingdom of the Franks today is and remains divided in two. The Franks are more often reckoned with the peoples among whom they were. Meroveus, king of the Franks, dies. The forty-sixth. Hilderic reigned twenty-three years. Hilderic, an insolent and debauched king. Hilderic lived twenty-six years in the kingdom. King Hilderic, in fear of the Franks, flees into Thuringia. Aegidius the Roman is made king by the Franks. Aegidius, excessively cruel, is deposed. Between two evils one is more tolerable than the other.

Omnes posthec urbes munitiones italię, nullo resistente penitus obtinuit, quietiffime possedit, impositoqꝫ caipti suo regni diademate annis quatuordecim in italia pro suo libito regnavit, postea tamen aregothorum peremptus fuit. ¶ Hildericus rex francorũ congregato suorũ exercitu maximo, ꝑ uniuersam galliam anno dominicę natiuitatis. CCCC.LXXV. potenti manu discurrit, omnia que restabant suo regno subiecit, cõtra uenire audentes occidit, dedicatione uero spontanee facietes cũ gratia suscepit. Multos in eo tumultu romanorum occidit, ab eorum domino galliam liberauit. ¶ Eodem tempore franco coloniã agrippina de potestate romano rũ in manu ualida eripientes, etiam suo dominio subdiderũt. Deinde Moguntiam, Vuormatiam, spirã, nõdiu post argentinã, cum oppidis munitionibus uniuersis per omnem regionem cifrhena nam a Constantia ciuitate alemanię usqꝫ ad mare, ac deinceps per morinos omnem galliam usqꝫ ad ligerim in suam potestatẽ nullo resistente redegerunt. ¶ In principalioribus aut ciuitatibus ex genere francorum regio posuerunt duces, qui sub nutu potestate Hilderici regis succelforum, eius populum regerent, secundũ leges patrias iustitiã fingulis administrarent. Hilderic, a fugitive, is recalled from Thuringia to the kingdom.

[unclear] the fifteenth. Hilderic, through the diligence and loyalty of his friend Winibald, who was one of the more powerful princes of the kingdom, was recalled from Thuringia to the kingdom of the Franks, restored to his paternal kingdom with the favor of all the nobles and of the nation, and Aegidius, hateful to all, was driven from it. And thereafter Hilderic reigned very moderately for another twenty-two years.

And when Basina, wife of Basanus, king of the Thuringians, had heard that Hilderic had been restored by the Franks to the kingdom, she left her husband and followed him into Gaul, stirred by excessive love for him, which she had contracted from long familiarity in living together among the Thuringians. Hilderic, receiving her as she came with a cheerful countenance, took her as his wife, as one known to him, ill repaying this hospitality to King Basanus, by whom for three years he had been kindly received as a guest.

But as the first night of the marriage approached, Basina advised Hilderic to postpone intercourse for a little while, to watch the doors of the bedchamber, and to report faithfully to her as she prophesied what prodigies he saw in the courtyard on the third occasion. The king, trusting the woman, obeyed as she commanded; and after watching the buildings for the third time, he returned to her, saying that first he had seen in the courtyard of the palace rhinoceroses, that is, unicorns, and also lions and leopards. Secondly, wolves and bears raging and pursuing one another. Thirdly, he said, he saw many dogs, but small ones, which tore one another with their teeth and bit fiercely; but you tell me what they signify.

To these things the woman, a prophetess, spoke thus to the king: Behold, we shall beget offspring, diverse in character in the course of time. For the first generation that will be born from us will be very noble, such that in its nobility it is to be compared to lions and to noble unicorns. From the first generation in time a second will arise, which, after the manner of wolves, with nobility despised, will practice robberies and oppressions of the poor. The third generation after this, which will also be the last from us, will after the manner of dogs tear, bite, and strike one another, until at last, in the final days, the kingdom will fail. That same night the woman conceived and bore a son, named Clodoveus, as we shall say.

In the following year, which was the four hundred sixty-third from the Lord’s nativity, a son was born to Hilderic, named Clodoveus; he afterward succeeded his father in the kingdom of the Franks, and was the first to receive the faith of Christ, as we shall say below.

At about the same time Hilderic, king of the Franks, having gathered a great army of fighters, made war against the people of the Alemanni, who dwelt between Italy and Swabia, where now are the cities of Chur, Sitten, and the Valais. When battle was joined, the Alemanni were defeated and reduced under tribute to the Franks.

In these times also, when Uther Pendragon, king of Britain, which is now called England, had died, his son, named Arthur, was raised up in his kingdom. Concerning him not only the history of the Britons, as Geoffrey of Monmouth relates, but also the voices of the peoples of England proclaim wonders down to the present day, although many things are more fabulous than in accord with the truth. tributum olim eis impositum soluere contē nerent,&amp; eius matrem Basinam non solum de adulterio,sed etiam de furto calumniarentur manifeste.Veniens itaqꝫ in regionem do ringorum omnia ferro deuastauit et amp; igne,regem uicit,&amp; ad soluti onem tributorum coegit.

Arthur was a prince magnificent beyond measure.

Arthur, strong in great uprightness of character, prudence, gentleness, and at the same time humanity, took every care to show himself lovable and venerable to all, because, together with virtue of soul, he also abounded in wondrous liberality toward everyone, and especially toward churchmen, on whom, for the love of Christ, he bestowed many little gifts and also presents.

King Arthur expelled the Saxons and Picts from Britain.

He expelled the Saxons and Picts from Britain, and powerfully subjected the Scots, the Irish, and the Orcadians to his kingdom. When the kings of Dacia and Norway heard this, they came of their own accord and submitted themselves to his lordship.

Merlin.

Marvelous things concerning this Arthur’s birth, and likewise his future deeds, Merlin, the prophet of the English, foretold to his father Uther Pendragon; we made mention of these in the first volume of the Annals.

Odoacer the Saxon came into Gaul.

In these same times Odoacer, by nation a Rugian, or a German Saxon, armed with a multitude of Turcilingi, Heruli, and also Suetii, or those whom we now call Swedes from the island, set out from almost the farthest borders of Saxony and came into Gaul, and entered the city of Orleans as victor. Afterwards he also received Angers into his power by the surrender of its citizens.

The war of the Franks with Odoacer.

Against him Childeric, king of the Franks, led out his army on the following day, joined battle, killed Count Paul, obtained the city, and put Odoacer with his army to flight.

Odoacer, overcome by the Franks, proceeds to Italy.

Odoacer, making peace with King Childeric, left Gaul and entered Italy intending to conquer it. He compelled Orestes, the patrician of the Romans, who did not dare to meet him in Liguria, to flee back; and when Orestes was hiding in the city of Ticinum, which is now called Pavia, he besieged, captured, and killed him.

Odoacer reigns in Italy for fourteen years.

After this he obtained absolutely all the cities and fortifications of Italy, with no one resisting, and possessed them in complete quiet. Placing the diadem of the kingdom on his own head, he reigned in Italy according to his own will for fourteen years; afterwards, however, he was slain by the king of the Goths.

The Franks, after killing the Romans, subjugated all Gaul to themselves.

Childeric, king of the Franks, having gathered a very great army of his men, traversed all Gaul with a powerful hand in the year of the Lord’s birth 475, subjected to his kingdom everything that remained, killed those who dared to oppose him, but received graciously those who voluntarily made surrender. In that tumult he killed many of the Romans and freed Gaul from their dominion.

The Franks, taking Cologne from the Romans, subjected it to themselves.

At the same time the Franks, seizing Cologne Agrippina from the power of the Romans with a strong hand, also subjected it to their own lordship. Then Mainz, Worms, Speyer, and not long afterward Strasbourg, together with all the towns and fortifications throughout the whole Cisrhenane region from the city of Constance in Alemannia as far as the sea, and thereafter through the Morini all Gaul as far as the Loire, they brought under their power, with no one resisting.

Here the petty kings of the Franks multiplied. Sigebert, petty king of the Franks at Cologne.

But in the more important cities they placed dukes from the royal stock of the Franks, who, under the command and power of King Childeric and his successors, were to rule his people and administer justice to individuals according to the laws of the fatherland. Of these, at Cologne they appointed a petty king named Sigebert; at Cambrai, [Riacharius?]; among the Morini,

¶ Anno regni sui undecimo rex Clodoueus contractis copijs, aduersus alaricum regem occidentalium gothorum duxit exercitum quem decímo lapide ab urbe pictanorum sibi congręssum cũ pluri bus occidit, cuius et thesauros omnes, & ciuitatem ipsam suo re gno adiecit. ¶ Anno regní suí quintodecimo, qui fuit dn̄icę natiuitatis.CCCC.XCIX.indictione romanorum septima,cum alemāni rursus in superbiam erecti, francis nec subiacere uellent,nec amplius dare tributumClodoueus ingentem suorum conuocauít exercitũ,& mo uit contra alemannos fortem expeditionem ad pręlium.Inito certamine acriter ancipitiqꝫ marte diu fuit pugnatum, & plures utrobiqꝫ ceciderunt. ¶ Postremo diuina ordinante prouidentia pugnantibus fortiter alemānis franci paulatĩ ceperunt deficere,cunqꝫ iam ꝓpe uideret᷑ , ut fugerent,rex perfusus lachrimis apud se tacitus orauit'diccẽs.Do mine iesu christe,quem uxor mea filium predícat eße dei, & omia postulata posse dare in te fideliter credenti hus,si dederis mihi uicto riam de his inimicis meis hodie,credã in te, atqꝫ in nomine tuo baptifarme faciam' & ero nomini tuo fidelis seruus atqꝫ deuotus,q̃ diu uixerõ. ¶ Cunqꝫ sic orans manibus et oculis in coelũ eleuatus,subgemifice ret christi affuit repente auxilium quo presente in fuga m conuer tuntur alemanni,& qui prius ut murus pugnabant,immobiles subitoto nunc fugiunt quemadmodum solent pauentissime mulieres. King Riuacharius. [unclear] Carocus, king of the Morini. Heribertus, king of the Treveri. Godegisilus, king of Metz. Arbogast, king of Mainz. All under one king of the Franks. The Lombards first occupied the Rugi. Childeric, king of the Franks, dies. The forty-fourth. Clovis reigned thirty years, the first Christian. Clovis, king of the Christians, burned churches. Queen Clothild, wife of King Clovis, a Christian. The Franks made war on the Thuringians and overcome them.

Carocus among the Treveri and Mosellans, Heribertus in the principate of the city of Metz, Godegisilus among the people of Mainz, Arbogast, and others in other cities, they appointed as vicars of the kingdom, according to the custom of the ancient Franks; yet King Clovis later had almost all of them killed because of his ambition for monarchy.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 479, in the second indiction of the Romans, in the times of the aforesaid Childeric, king of the Franks, after Odoacer’s departure from the Rugi, the Lombards invaded Rugium. At that time a fifth king, named Gudeoch, ruled over them, and they dwelt in that kingdom for some time.

But Childeric, king of the Franks, after he had performed many deeds bravely, died in the completed twenty-third year of his reign, but the twenty-sixth interrupted year, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 484, in the seventh indiction of the Romans. Clovis, son of King Childeric by Basina, when he was twenty-one years of age, succeeded his father and reigned thirty years: fifteen of these he spent as a pagan, like all the kings of the Franks before him, in vanity, and the remaining fifteen, reborn in the faith of Christ, he passed faithfully. He was a prince outstanding in form and distinguished in courage of mind; and soon at the beginning of his reign he drove out the son of the former Roman duke Aegidius, named Syagrius, who held rule over Soissons, and added the city to the kingdom of the Franks.

Proceeding from there, he took the city of Reims, over whose church at that time presided Saint Remigius, a most learned bishop; he plundered all the churches both there and elsewhere, burned many, and divided the booty among the soldiers according to law. Whatever of Roman jurisdiction existed in all Gaul, Clovis in a short time subjected wholly to the dominion of the Franks, just as it remains up to the present day. He took as wife Clothild, daughter of Hilperic, king of the Burgundians, whom Gundebald, the king, his brother, had slain; and his wife, that is, Clothild’s mother, was a faithful Christian woman, who diligently admonished the king to believe in the Lord Jesus and to renounce the vain worship of idols. Although he despised this at first, nevertheless, after fifteen years had passed in his reign, and after obtaining victory over the Alemanni, as we shall say in its place, he afterward believed in Christ.

In the ninth year of his reign, King Clovis made war on Thuringia, because they both disdained to pay the tribute formerly imposed on them, and openly accused his mother Basina not only of adultery but also of theft. And so, coming into the region of the Thuringians, he devastated everything with sword and fire, defeated the king, and compelled them to the payment of tributes.

72
Franci omnes pene chrisidē suscipiunt. Reges proceres frācorum multas construūt ecclesias. Clodoneus mulsos confanguineos francoꝝ reges occidit. Sigebertus rex colonię dolo clodonei īterficitur a filio. Clodoneo credulus iuuenis paternū aspirat ad regnum. Ludouicus qui partrem occidit submittit. Ludouicus patricida regē inuitat. Parricida machinati one Clodonei regis perimitur. Rex Clodoneus uenit coloniā et amp; admittitur. Et reliquum populum diebus postea sequentibus uniuersum pon̄tifices sacerdotes dn̄i cum ingenti letitia baptizabāt, gratias omnipotentis dei miserationibus agentes qui per suam gratiam, ut pa cem daret ecclesię, gentem ferocissimam iugo fidei subiecit. Magna deinceps pro christi honore facta sunt non solum ꝑ Clo doneū, sed multo magis per successores eius frācorū reges, ecclesię constructe fundata seruientiū deo plura per germaniam italiam galliā coenobia diuiniqꝫ cultus ministeriū cum tempore multiplici terfuit augmētatū. Clodoneus aūt rex, si homo fuerit in subditos pientissimus, in suos tamen confanguineos nimiū legitur extitisse crudelis, quippe qui plures nobilissimos de antiqua regū francorū propagine ortos, reges, duces principes crudeliter infidiose fecit occidi, ut regnum solus haberet. Verū ut paucos ex multis posteritati comēdemus, amor nos impellit historię ueritatis. Regnabat eo tempore apud Coloniā agrip pinam homo senex de regū frācorū semine procreatus, nomie digebertus quem Clodonei pater Hildericus, post aquisitas colonias illic uicarium regni posuerat. Is filium habebat nomine Ludouicum cui rex Clodoneus in astutia dolo sic scripsit. Pater tuus iā senex est, regno inutilis, qui si moreretur, tibi cū amicitia nostra regnū illius proueniret, non alteri. Iuuenis regni cupiditate seductus, patrem deliberauit occidere. Cum autrex Sigebertus die quadā nihil mali suspicatus de colonia egrederetur, rheno transmisso, per buroniam syluam uenationē ageret cum paucis, claro meridie dormientē in tentorio immissis super eum percussoribus patrem filius, tanquam eius regnū posses furus iuxta Clodonei promissum fecit occidi. Cede īmmo parricidio, nequissime peracto. Ludouicus regi scriptur Clodoneo. Pater meus est mortuus, ego thefauros eius pe nes meteneo cum regno. Mitte ergo uiros, quicquid tibi ex thefauris patris mei placuerit, bona tibi uoluntate trāsmittam. Cui rex clodoneus rescripsit. Gratias ago bone uolūtati tue, rogo ut ueni entibꝰ nostris patefacias cuncta, tu regnū patris cum amicitia nostra solus de cętero iam possessurus. Venientibus autem legatarijs Clodonei regis. Ludouicus pa tris thefauros ostendit qui dum uaria conspicerent atqꝫ diuersa, iuuenis ait. In hanc pater meus thecam nummos aureos confueuit repone̓re. Immitte unus astantium inquit manum tuam usqꝫ ad fundum, ut probes si omnia sint aurum. Quod cum fecisset, esset ualde decliuus, unus ille qui iusserat, eleuata manu securim in eius cerebrū uibrauit, statim in eodem loco mortuus est. His nequiter peractis, rex Clodoneus uenit ad Coloniam, qua sinescius scelerum, conuocato uniuerso ciuitatis populo dixit.

In the eleventh year of his reign King Clovis, having gathered his forces, led an army against Alaric, king of the western Goths; when Alaric met him at the tenth milestone from the city of Poitiers, he killed him together with many others, and added all his treasures and that very city to his own kingdom.

In the fifteenth year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 499, in the seventh Roman indiction, when the Alemanni, again raised up in pride, would neither be subject to the Franks nor any longer pay tribute, Clovis summoned a great army of his men and launched a strong expedition against the Alemanni for battle. Once the contest had begun, the fighting was fierce and long with the fortune of war undecided, and many fell on both sides.

At last, by the ordering of divine providence, while the Alemanni were fighting bravely, the Franks gradually began to give way; and when it already seemed almost certain that they would flee, the king, bathed in tears, prayed silently within himself, saying: “Lord Jesus Christ, whom my wife proclaims to be the Son of God, and able to grant all things asked by those who faithfully believe in you, if today you give me victory over these enemies of mine, I shall believe in you and shall have myself baptized in your name, and I shall be a faithful and devoted servant to your name as long as I live.”

And while he was praying thus, with hands and eyes raised to heaven, and sighing deeply, the help of Christ suddenly came to him; and when it was present, the Alemanni were turned to flight, and those who before had fought immovably like a wall now suddenly fled just as the most terrified women are accustomed to do. In that battle the king of the Alemanni fell, with many others. But when the Franks did not cease to pursue the fleeing Alemanni more insistently, they cried out to King Clovis: “Do not pursue us any further, most victorious king, because we are now yours; we promise that from this time onward we shall serve you forever.” Moved by these pleas, he forbade the pursuit; and, after receiving the Alemanni in surrender, he returned to Gaul.

When he had come to the palace, on the advice of Queen Clotild he called to him Remigius, the most holy bishop of the church of Reims. Having been more fully instructed by him in the Christian faith, in a public assembly, while all the leading men of the Franks listened, he offered himself with the greatest reverence and humility for the holy mystery of baptism. The most learned bishop said: “Gently bow your neck, Sicamber. Worship what you burned. Burn what you worshiped.” From this it is clear that the Franks had somewhat earlier been called Sicambri, not among the Scythians but among the Germans. Clovis, therefore, the first of all the kings of the Franks, received the faith of Christ, and was baptized by Saint Remigius in the thirty-sixth year of his age, the fifteenth of his reign, and the year of the Lord’s Nativity 499, in the seventh Roman indiction.

On the same day, after the king, three thousand of the courtly princes and nobles of the Franks were baptized. The Thuringians are compelled to pay tribute to the Franks. The Franks kill the king of the Visigoths in war. The Franks waged war against the Alemanni under Clovis. Clovis vows that he will become a Christian if he wins. With Christ’s help invoked, the Franks overcame the Alemanni. The king of the Alemanni is slain by the Franks. The Alemanni submit to the [dominion?] of the Franks. Clovis receives the faith of Christ from Remigius. King Clovis is baptized by Saint Remigius the bishop. Three thousand of the chief men of the Franks are baptized on the same day.

73
Audite ciues optimi, nefandum quod breui contigit malū Ludo- uicus filius parentis mei Sigeberti, patrem suum fallis circumuenit sermonibus, quod ego infidiar erius uitę. Cumqꝫ ille per buroniā syluam fugeret, immissis super eum latrunculis, genitorem suū in- terfecit. Ipse quoqꝫ dum thesauris incubaret, a quo nescio percussus interijt. Sed in his ego nequaquā sum conscius. Nec em̄ possum fan guinem parentum meorum effundere, cum fit nefas. ¶ Sed quia sic ista contigerunt, do uobis confiliū, si uidetur accep- tum, conuertimini ad me, ut sub mea sitis defensione. At illi mani- bus &; uocibus plaudentes, eum more gentis erectū clypeo, regem super se constituerunt. Et sic regnum Sigeberti cum omnibus the- sauris eius in suam accepit potestatem Prosternebat enim deus quo tidie hostes eius sub manibus ipsius &; augebat regnum illius ual- de, eo quod ambularet recto corde in uia mandatorum dei. ¶ Regem etiam Cararicum, &; filium eius dolo cepit quos primo tondens, alterum presbiterum, alterum uero diaconū ordinari fe- cit, quorum thesauros cum regno sibi subiiciens ambobus postea fecit amputari capita. ¶ Riuacharium quoqꝫ regem apud Cameracum francis imperan- tem, &; nimis petulanter luxurioseque uiuentem, una cum Richario fratre eius, proditorie captos, a bello fugientes propria manu secu- ri percutiens occidit. ¶ Lingomirum etiam fratrem eorum apud cenomanniam regnā tem, simili crudelitate fecit occidi. Quibus mortuis regna eorū cum thesauris sibi usurpauit. Interfecit &; alios reges francoꝝ plures, qui omnes de sanguine parentū eius fuerant procreati maxime de quibꝰ suspiciose nimis metuebat, ne sibi pręriterent regnum nemini parcens eoqꝫ modo regnū suū ex- tinctis poene cognatis omnibus per totam galliā dilatauit. Sed Clo- doneum laudet Hunibaldus quantum uoluit, quasi bene in his fe- cerit, ego in hac parte laudare nequo parenticidam, &; qui tot in- nocentes necauit. ¶ Nam die quadā coram multis aulicis suis dixiffe fertur de his parentibus suis atqꝫ cognatis, quos ipse perdide rat. Vę mihi quia tanq̄ peregrinus inter extraneos solus remāsi, &; neminē habeo de parentibus siue cognatis meis hodie amplius ui- uentē qui me inaduersitate si superuenerit in aliquo polsit adiuura- re, ut amicum solet amicus. Hoc autem dicebat in dolo, putans ali- quē excircunstantibus pro consolatione responsurū, ecce illū uel il- lum ex tuis ad huc habes iuuentutem, ut qui supereffent ex cogna- sis etiā quantocius occiderent &; ipsi. ¶ Anno regni sui .xvij. rex Clodoneus ad instantiam Clotildis reginę continuam, mortē parentum suorum crudelem depatruo uindicari cupientis, bellum indixit Gundebaldo regi burgundionum, quo superato burgun- diā tributu &; subiectioni francorum ascripsit. Expurgatio regis Clodonei fictitia. Colonienfes Clodo neū ꝓ rege suscipiūt Cararicus &; filius eius reges a Clodo- neo fraudenecati. Riuacharius rex frā- cię cameracenfis cū fratre occiditur. Lingomirus rex frā- ciae cenomanice ab eo interficitur. Plutes fuerūt reges frācorū his tpibus. Iniuria parentum re- gnare crudelitas eft. Verba regis Clodo- nei in dolo prolata sunt. Nemo dubitat ma- lum hominem, Bellum francorum contra borgūdiōes. M A C B I D E F G H K J O P Q S T V X Y Z

Almost all the Franks receive the faith of Christ. The kings and nobles of the Franks build many churches. Clodoneus killed many kinsmen, kings of the Franks. Sigebert, king of Cologne, is treacherously killed by his son through Clodoneus. The credulous young man aspires to his father’s kingdom. Ludovicus, who killed his father, sends word. Ludovicus the parricide invites the king. The parricide is destroyed by the contrivance of King Clodoneus. King Clodoneus comes to Cologne and is admitted.

And in the days that followed, the bishops, priests of the Lord, baptized all the rest of the people with great joy, giving thanks for the mercies of almighty God, who through his grace, in order to give peace to the Church, subjected a most fierce people to the yoke of faith.

Thereafter great things were done for the honor of Christ, not only by Clodoneus but much more by his successors, the kings of the Franks: churches were built, several monasteries of those serving God were founded throughout Germany, Italy, and Gaul, and the ministry of divine worship in time was increased manifold. But King Clodoneus, though he was a man most dutiful toward his subjects, is nevertheless read to have been exceedingly cruel toward his own kinsmen, since he caused many most noble men, sprung from the ancient stock of the kings of the Franks, kings, dukes, and princes, to be cruelly and treacherously killed, so that he alone might hold the kingdom.

But that we may commend a few out of many to posterity, love of historical truth impels us. At that time there was reigning at Cologne Agrippina an old man, born from the seed of the kings of the Franks, named Sigebert, whom Clodoneus’s father Hilderic, after Cologne had been acquired, had placed there as vicar of the kingdom. He had a son named Ludovicus, to whom King Clodoneus wrote thus in cunning and deceit: “Your father is now old, useless for the kingdom; if he were to die, his kingdom would come to you, with our friendship, and not to another.”

The young man, seduced by desire for the kingdom, resolved to kill his father. And when King Sigebert one day, suspecting no evil, went out from Cologne, crossed the Rhine, and was hunting with a few men in the forest of Buronia, the son, as though he would possess his kingdom according to Clodoneus’s promise, had assassins sent against him and caused his father to be killed while he was sleeping in his tent at bright midday.

After the murder, indeed the parricide, had been most wickedly carried out, Ludovicus wrote to King Clodoneus: “My father is dead; I have his treasures in my possession along with the kingdom. Send men, therefore, and whatever pleases you from my father’s treasures, I will send to you with good will.” King Clodoneus wrote back to him: “I give thanks for your good will; I ask that you reveal everything to our men when they come, since you alone are henceforth to possess your father’s kingdom with our friendship.”

When the envoys of King Clodoneus came, Ludovicus showed them his father’s treasures. While they were inspecting various and diverse things, the young man said: “In this chest my father was accustomed to store gold coins.” “Put your hand in,” one of those standing by said, “all the way to the bottom, so that you may test whether it is all gold.” When he had done this and was bent far down, the very man who had ordered it raised his hand and swung an axe into his brain; he died at once in that same place.

When these wicked deeds had been done, King Clodoneus came to Cologne, and, as if unaware of the crimes, summoned all the people of the city and said:

“Listen, excellent citizens, to the unspeakable evil that lately occurred. [Chloderic?], the son of my kinsman Sigebert, ensnared his father with false words, saying that I was plotting against his life. And when he was fleeing through the [Buconian?] forest, robbers were sent against him, and he killed his own father. He too, while he was brooding over the treasures, was struck by someone I know not and perished. But in these matters I am in no way privy to the crime. For I cannot shed the blood of my kinsmen, since it is a sin.”

But because these things had so happened, “I give you counsel, if it seems acceptable: turn yourselves to me, so that you may be under my protection.” And they, applauding with hands and voices, set him up on a raised shield according to the custom of the nation, and appointed him king over them. And thus he received into his own power the kingdom of Sigebert with all his treasures. For God daily laid his enemies low beneath his hands, and greatly increased his kingdom, because he walked with an upright heart in the way of God’s commandments.

He also deceitfully seized King Chararic and his son; first tonsuring them, he had one ordained priest and the other deacon. Subjecting their treasures together with the kingdom to himself, he afterwards had both their heads cut off.

[Ragnachar?] also, the king ruling the Franks at Cambrai and living far too wantonly and luxuriously, together with Richarius his brother, were treacherously captured while fleeing from battle; striking them with an axe by his own hand, he killed them.

He also had [Rignomer?], their brother, who was reigning at Le Mans, killed with similar cruelty.

When these men had died, he usurped their kingdoms with their treasures for himself. He also killed many other kings of the Franks, all of whom had been begotten from the blood of his own kin, especially those of whom he was suspiciously very much afraid, lest they take the kingdom away from him; sparing no one, and in this way, when almost all his kinsmen had been extinguished, he enlarged his kingdom throughout all Gaul. But let Hunibald praise Clodoneus as much as he wished, as though he had done well in these matters: I, in this respect, cannot praise a parricide, and one who killed so many innocent men.

For on a certain day, in the presence of many of his courtiers, he is said to have spoken about these relatives and kinsmen of his, whom he himself had destroyed: “Woe to me, because, like a foreigner among strangers, I remain alone, and today I have no one of my relatives or kinsmen still living who could help me in any way in adversity, if it should come upon me, as friend is accustomed to help friend.” But he said this deceitfully, thinking that someone from among those standing around would answer by way of consolation: “Behold, you still have this man or that man from among your own [unclear],” so that those of his kinsmen who survived might themselves also be killed as quickly as possible.

In the seventeenth year of his reign, King Clodoneus, at the continual urging of Queen Clotild, who desired the cruel death of her parents to be avenged upon her paternal uncle, declared war on Gundebald, king of the Burgundians. When he had been defeated, Clodoneus assigned Burgundy to the tribute and subjection of the Franks.

Clodoneus, king of the Franks, dies.

Clodoneus, king of the Franks, after his realm had been extended throughout all Gaul and a great part of Germany, and after many things had been bravely accomplished in war and peace, at last died in the thirtieth year of his reign, the fifty-first of his age, and the year of the Lord’s nativity 514, in the seventh Roman indiction. He was buried at Paris in the church of Saint Peter.

He left four sons: Lotharius, Theodoricus, Clodomirus, and Hildebertus, who divided their father’s kingdom in equal portions. But because several kings were subsequently born from these men, and because at one time the kingdom of the Franks was subject to a single monarch, while at another time it was divided into several parts and ruled by many, we have judged it worth the effort to continue in order, marked chapter by chapter in red, the names of those kings who carried the sequence of the royal stock in a direct line down to Hildericus, the last king. For among the sons of Clodoneus, Lotharius was not the firstborn; rather Theodoricus was the elder by birth. Clodomirus was born second; Lotharius himself, by whom the genealogy of the kings is continued, was born third.

After King Clodoneus died, Hunibald also completed his history of the origin of the Franks, divided into eighteen books, comprising a period of no fewer than nine hundred and fifty years, in which there were forty-seven kings from Marcomirus, son of Antenor, who first led the people from the borders of Scythia to the mouths of the river Rhine in Germany, down to the death of King Clodoneus. What follows in this second volume of our annals we have taken from authors whose names are these.

Einhardus, abbot of Saint-Amand; Flodoardus, priest of the church of Reims; Richerus, monk of Reims; Gregorius, archbishop of Tours; Lampertus, abbot in Hasungen; Regino, abbot of Prum; Eghardus, first abbot in Vraugia; Lampertus, monk of Hersfeld; Freculfus, formerly a monk, bishop of Lisieux; Strabus, monk of Fulda; Vuindekindus, monk in Corvey of Saxony; Rupertus, monk of Saint Alban near Mainz; Ioannes, monk of the same monastery; Adelbertus, monk of the monastery of Saint Vincent at Metz; Meginfridus, monk of Fulda; Golftherus, monk of Saint Matthias, in the deeds of the Treveri; Marianus Scotus, monk of Fulda; Sigebertus, monk of Gembloux; Richardus, monk of Cluny; Rupertus Ganguinus also, formerly minister general of the Order of the Holy Trinity; Ado, bishop of Vienne; Galfridus Brito; Saxo Dacus; Ptolemaeus of Lucca, a Saxon by country, in the Rudimentum novitiorum; Vuernherus, Carthusian monk of Cologne; Gotfridus of Viterbo; Rupertus, Premonstratensian canon; Hartmannus Schedel from Nuremberg; Iacobus of Bergamo, hermit of Saint Augustine; Marcus Antonius Sabellicus. From the aforementioned and various other writers of histories I wrote the two volumes of our annals that follow, not without the greatest labor, because there is much diversity among historiographers, not only in the years,

but also in the deeds and names of persons, which has increased my labor not a little, since quite often something is ascribed to one person which another did or said, and something that was done in another year is narrated as having been done in this one, and a deed which was done in this way by one is said by another to have been done otherwise.

Since, therefore, it is not within my powers to reconcile so great a discordance of histories, I follow the judgment of those whom I find to have differed less from one another, which could be observed not uniformly in every case, but in certain cases.

Therefore the third-born son of King Clodoveus, from whom the line of the kings of the Franks descending in direct succession continued down to Hilderic, the last of the stock of Faramund, reigned after his father in Soissons, a city of the Franks, for fifty years; and when his brothers and all their sons had died, he finally recalled into one monarchy the kingdom that had been divided into four parts. Each of his brothers reigned for a time in his own place.

There is great disagreement among the historians.

Trithemius follows those less discordant.

The Forty-Eighth.

Lotharius reigns for fifty years.

¶ For Theodoricus, the first-born of King Clodoveus, whom he had begotten not by Queen Clotildis, but before his marriage to her by a certain concubine, received in the division of the kingdom of the Franks Austrasia, in which is the city of Metz, together with the other cities belonging to it; and at that time it was called the kingdom of Austrasia, or of the Austrasians, in which he reigned for twenty-three years. After him Theodobertus, his son, reigned over the Austrasians for twenty-two years. When he too had died, his son Theodobaldus reigned over the people of Metz for nine years; and when he had departed this life, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 560, in the eighth Roman indiction, without children, his uncle Lotharius, named above, received the kingdom of the Austrasians, or of the people of Metz.

Theodoricus reigned over the Austrasians for twenty-three years.

Theodobertus reigns after his father for [fourteen?] years.

Theodobaldus reigns for nine years.

¶ Clodomirus, however, the third son of Clodoveus, but the first-born by Queen Clotildis, reigned at Orléans in Gaul for seven years; and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 521, after he had killed Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, with his wife and sons, and had again engaged with his brother Godemarus, he was killed by him. He left three young sons, Theodobaldus, Guntherus, and Clodoaldus; after their father’s death, the most pious grandmother Clotildis, living at Tours, raised them with herself like a mother. But a few years later, Lotharius and Hildebertus, kings and brothers of the aforesaid Clodomirus, having summoned to themselves their nephews Theodobaldus and Guntharius, and in their ambition for rule devising wicked things, killed them with their own hands. But the third, changing nobility destined to perish into divine servitude, became a cleric.

Clodomirus reigned at Orléans for seven years.

The three sons of King Clodomirus of Orléans are named.

The impious kings killed their nephews.

He wrote the Rule of monks. The Order of Saint Benedict is instituted. The Cistercian. Also the Celestines, Wilhelmites, Mount Olivet, the Slavs, Vallombrosa, Saint Paul, the Humiliati. The expedition of the Franks into Thuringia. The final destruction of the kingdom of the Thuringians by the Franks.

With the brothers and their sons and grandsons dead, or cruelly killed, Lothar alone obtained the monarchy of the whole kingdom of the Franks, and thereafter, after all his brothers, reigned still for five years.

In the second year of King Lothar, Sigismund, king of Burgundy, who had built the monastery of the Agaunensian martyrs, killed his son Sigeric, having followed the wicked counsel of that boy’s stepmother. Led to great penitence, he devoted himself wholly to the holy martyrs of Agaunum; and that he was worthy of pardon is attested by frequent miracles after his death, for in his honor health is granted to those suffering from fever.

In the fourth year of King Lothar, Theodoric, king of Austrasia, his brother, having been asked by Ermenfrid, king of the Thuringians, under the promise of half his kingdom, treacherously killed the brothers Bertharius and Balderic on the road, while they were returning toward Thuringia, suspecting no evil, from the city of Metz, to which they had come for the sake of greeting him. But when the crime had been carried out, and Theodoric sought from Ermenfrid the half of the kingdom of Thuringia promised to him, the latter neither gave what he had promised nor sent a fitting reply to the petitioner, deceived by the counsel of his wife, who was the sister of that Theodoric and of Lothar. This matter afterward, as we have said in the first volume of the Annals, brought on the final destruction of all Thuringia and extinguished there the royal name and title. In the same year the holy virgin Brigid, dying in Scotland, ascended to Christ.

In the seventh year of Lothar, king of the Franks, Boethius, the Roman consul, worn down by long imprisonment, was killed by Theodoric, king of the Goths, who, after Odoacer had been slain, was occupying Italy; he wrote many useful works for the faith of Christ. Father Benedict, our holy lawgiver, also flourished in these times in Italy, the first founding abbot of the monastery of Cassino, who was the prince of all western monks. To them he handed down a rule of life outstanding in every discretion, and a lucid teaching of words, made honorable by his deeds, is called by the name of Saint Benedict himself. The Order of Cistercian monks also professes the same rule. The Order of Saint William. The Order of Mount Olivet. The Order of the Slavs. The Order of Vallombrosa. The Order of Saint Paul the First Hermit. The Order of the Humiliati, together with certain others which, for the sake of brevity, we have passed over here. The life of this saint the divine Pope Gregory set forth.

In the tenth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 524, the seventh indiction of the Romans, when the king of the people of Metz sought satisfaction from Ermenfrid, king of the Thuringians, for the murder of his brother, as we have said, and did not obtain it, he was roused to anger. Having called to his aid his son Theudebert and his brother Lothar, kings, he moved an expedition into Thuringia, captured King Ermenfrid with his wife and children, and subjected the whole kingdom to himself.

78
Lotharius monar- chiā solus obtinuit. Lotharius rex gra- num filium igne cre mauit. Lotharius rex fran- corum moritur. Cenobiū sancti me- dardi construirur fuessionis. Monasteriū sancti Germani de pratis fundatur. QVADRAGESI- MVVS NONVS. Hilpericus regnauit annis.XXIIIII. Biennio prius rege nauit fuessionis. Andouera hilperici regis uxor. Fredegundis reginae deceptrix. Concinnatrix doli regem alloquitur. Hilpericus audoue ram repudiat ut cō- matrem. consurgunt, auxliumqꝫ ferētibus doringis qui et ipsi grauiter fere bant iugū francoꝝ omne tributū pari constantia negabāt. Lotharius rex, mor¬ tuo iam Hildeberto fratre, cunctisqꝫ alijs, tam nepotibus quam fra¬ tribus suis, uel interfectis, uel naturali fine consumptis, monarchiā totius regni francoꝝ solus obtinuit annis quinqꝫ. ¶ Anno regni sui.XLIX.Lotharius rex francobꝰ, Granū filiū diu rebelle, multa in regno malafacientem,cum in britanniā nouā (quę olim armorica dicebat̉) fugisset ad Conobrū britanię ducem cū exercitu persecutus est facta cōgressione.Conobrū duce inter fecit britaniā obtinuit filiū cepit quē cū uxore filiabus cōsum¬ ptū ignibus,in cinerē redegit. ¶ Anno sequenti,regni uidelicet eius quinquagesimo,dominicę uero natiuitatis.D.LXIII.indictione romanoꝝ . Lotharius ipse rex francorum moritur ,filios relinquens quatuo,r,Heribertū Gunthramū,Sigebertum, Hilpericū q regnū inter se rursum di¬ uisere paternū.Memoratus rex Lotharius abbatia sacti medardi no- quamen sis tornacensis primi ep̄i,apud fuessionas construxit in quam ei usdē sancti corpus a tornaco translatum cum summa reue¬ rētia honore collocauit. ¶ Hildebertus autrex,frater eius, cōstruxit abbatiā sancti Germani de pratis,in qua stolā sancti Vin¬ centij martiris cum eius dalmatica reposuit.Sed ordo nūc postulat compendij,ut divisionem regni prosequamur. From that time the Thuringians did not have a king of their own.

And Radegund, among the other captives, daughter of Bertharius, once king, whom, as we have said, his brother Ermenfrid had caused to be killed through Theodoric king of the Metensians, King Lotharius joined to himself in marriage. She shone with great holiness, and afterward, becoming a nun, was radiant with very many signs and miracles. Concerning this destruction of the Thuringians, Fortunatus the archbishop wrote more fully in verse and in prose.

In the twelfth year of his reign, Lotharius king of the Franks, with his brother Hildebert, besieged Autun, a city of Burgundy, and, after King Godomar had been put to flight, powerfully subjected the whole province of the Burgundians to his rule.

In the year [unclear] of the reign of Lotharius king of the Franks, he powerfully wrested from the hand of King Athalaric whatever his grandfather Theodoric, king of Italy, had possessed in Gaul.

In these days Saint Nicetius flourished, formerly abbot of the monastery of Limoges, archbishop of Trier, a man of many virtues in Christ, whose deeds are extant. Theodoric king of Austrasia, who ruled over the Metensians, the people of Trier, Liege, Cologne, Mainz, and all those dwelling this side of the Rhine, brought many clerics from among the Arvernian citizens, whom he ordered to be enrolled for service to the Lord in the church of Trier.

In the twenty-sixth year of King Lotharius, in the ninth indiction, King Hildebert, with his brother’s son Theodobert, rose against that same Lotharius, his brother. But his mother Clotild, by prayers before God, acting so that there should be no war among her sons, they were restrained by a dreadful storm; and since not even a sign of so great a terror appeared over Lotharius, Hildebert, compelled by manifest necessity, withdrew from his brother in peace.

In the twenty-eighth year, Lotharius and Hildebert, the aforementioned brothers, after besieging the city of Caesaraugusta in Spain, when the citizens prayed to God and carried around the tunic of the holy martyr Vincent, received from them as a gift the stole of that martyr himself, and returned in peace, after the greater part of Spain had been acquired by war. At the same time Saint Maurus and Faustus, disciples of the divine Benedict, flourished in Gallic France, distinguished in conduct, learning, holiness of life, and miracles.

In the fortieth year of Lotharius king of the Franks, and in the year 554 of the Lord’s nativity, in the second Roman indiction, Queen Clotild died, formerly the wife of the great Clovis, king of France, with whom she also was buried at Paris in the church of Saint Peter. In the same year Bucellinus and Amingus, dukes of the Franks, having joined battle with Narses the Roman patrician, were both killed by him, together with not a few others.

For these were the two dukes Bucellinus and Amingus, who seven years earlier had entered Italy with Theodobert, king of the Franks, with a strong force, and did not cease to disturb it with various warlike assaults. From there, sailing into Sicily, they subjected it to the tribute of the Franks, and, after many spoils had been gathered, rebellion [unclear]

In the forty-third year of his reign, Lotharius king of the Franks, having gathered his forces, moved into Saxony. For the Saxons, until then tributary to the Franks, into rebellion

fraudulentia deceptrix fredegundis a rege Hilperico in uxore affusit̉, de qua genuit regni sui paterni (ut dicemus postea) successorē. ¶ Heribertus autem, Lotharij maior natu filius, in diuisione mo narchię regni francoꝝ Neustriam accepit, sedem regni sui parisijs tenens, &; regnauit annis nouem, nihilqꝫ memoria dignū agēs moritur anno dn̄i D.LXXIII, indictione romāoꝝ undecima, regnū fratribus dimittens. Gunthramus, Lotharij regis secundo natu filius, aurelianis regnauit annis triginta tribus, princeps ī sua conditione optimus, sed uxorem nequissimā assecutus, nomīe austrigildem, quę inter plura que patrauit mala, cū infirmaretur ad mortem, &; a medicis iuuari non posset, callida regem persuasione circumuenit ut unius petitionis effectū ei se concessuꝝ indubitant̓ iuramento firmaret. Prius ergo quā moriar, īquit, medicoꝛū meorū, qui me suis medicamentis inaniter cruciauerūt, amputarī facias capita me uidente. Quid plura? Qui medicos introducāt illico mit tuntur, quibus reginae thalamū ingressis, lamīa dixit. Ha uos non medici, sed mendaces, qui me uestris medicamentis ante tēpus mo ri compellitis, eam uobis remunerationē paraui, ut ante me ad mor te complulsi tranfeatis. Mox ut libidinē Lictor impiae mulieris satia ret, duorū medicoꝝ innocentium capita ipsa inspectante ac ridente bestia, iussus amputauit. Rex aūt Gunthramus obijt anno domini D.XCVII indictione romanoꝝ quintadecima. Sigebertus autē, tertio natus Lotharij regis filius, regnauit metis in austrasia super Treuiros, quoqꝫ londienses, colonienses, moguntinos, &; reliquas urbes, &; prouincias cisrihenanas annis. XIII. Vxorem habuit hispaniam, nomine Bruniam (quam scriptores Brunihildē frequentius appellare consueuerunt) decem regum interfecticē quae francis usqꝫ adeo exosa, ut Sibyllae in ea uaticinium impletum uideretur dicentis. ¶ Veniet Brunia de partibus hispaniae, ante cuius conspectū gen tes &; reges peribunt, ipsa uero calcibus equorū peribit. Genuit aūt ex ea Hilpericus filium, nomine Theodobertum qui regnauit posteum annis uno uiginti, &; moritur āno domini. D.XCIX. Cuius filius, nomine Theodoricus, succedens, regnauit annis. Contra quoꝝ insolentiam sigebertus rex frater regis hilperici H iij Hilbertus regnauit annis.IX. Hildebertus re.neu strie ocio deditus. Gunthramus regnauit aurelianis annis XXXIII. Regina crudelis memoria indigna. ¶ Medici capitibus truncantur persuasione ruginę. Gunthramus rex moritur. Sigebertus regnauit in austrasia. Brunichildis uxor sigeberti crudelis. Vaticinium sibyllae de brunihilde regīa Theodoricus rex austrasiae filius eius. Tres filii Theodori ci &; basthardi. Huni dorigiā uastantes eadimtur a francis.

Lotharius alone obtained the monarchy. King Lotharius burned Chramn, his son, with fire. Lotharius, king of the Franks, dies. The monastery of Saint Medard is built at Soissons. The monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Pres is founded.

The Forty-Ninth. Chilperic reigned twenty-four years. Two years earlier he reigned at Soissons. Audovera, wife of King Chilperic. Fredegund, deceiver of the queen. The contriver of the deceit addresses the king. Chilperic repudiates Audovera as his co-mother.

They rise up, and the Thuringians too bring aid, who themselves also bore the yoke of the Franks with great hardship and, with equal firmness, refused every tribute. Therefore Lotharius, coming into Saxony with a great army, subdued the Saxons in a severe battle.

In the forty-fifth year of his reign, Lotharius the king, now that his brother Childebert was dead, and all the others, both his nephews and his brothers, had either been killed or consumed by natural death, alone obtained the monarchy of the whole kingdom of the Franks for five years.

In the forty-ninth year of his reign Lotharius, king of the Franks, pursued with an army Chramn, his son, long rebellious and doing many evil things in the kingdom, when he had fled into New Brittany, which was formerly called Armorica, to Conobrus, duke of Brittany. When battle was joined, he killed Duke Conobrus, obtained Brittany, captured his son, and, consumed by fires together with his wife and daughters, reduced him to ashes.

In the following year, that is, the fiftieth of his reign, but the year of the Lord’s nativity 563, in the twelfth indiction of the Romans, this same Lotharius, king of the Franks, dies, leaving four sons, Charibert, Gunthram, Sigebert, and Chilperic, who again divided their father’s kingdom among themselves. The aforesaid King Lotharius built the abbey of Saint Medard, formerly the first bishop of Noyon and Tournai, at Soissons, into which he translated the body of the same saint from Tournai and placed it with the highest reverence and honor. But King Childebert, his brother, built the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Pres, in which he deposited the stole of Saint Vincent the martyr together with his dalmatic. But the order of the abridgement now requires that we pursue the division of the kingdom.

Chilperic the Younger, son of Lotharius king of the Franks, is therefore placed by us before his brothers in this abridgement of the kings, because through him the line of kings descending in straight order is continued down to Childeric. He reigned in the city of Soissons two years before the death of his father, and, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-two years. And thus the whole time that he reigned was twenty-four years. The name of his first wife was Audovera, by whom he begot two sons, Clovis and Merovech, both of whom, killed in adolescence by the deceit of their stepmother, as we said in the first volume, perished.

When Audovera had given birth to an infant while the king was absent, since no one who would raise the boy to be baptized from the sacred font was at hand, the queen mother herself, deceived by Fredegund’s wicked counsel, fulfilled the office of co-mother, and raised from baptism the infant whom she had borne. Fredegund, the contriver of the deceit, joyfully announcing this to the king when he soon came, said: “You will not have Audovera as wife henceforth, O king; she preferred to be your co-mother rather than your spouse. Now I am yours.” For this reason King Chilperic repudiated Audovera his wife, asserting that by decree of the canons it was forbidden him to have his co-mother as wife. Seduced by such cunning through Fredegund, the queen is thrust into a monastery, her

Sueui saxones recufabant admittere. Bellum inter saxões fit et sueuos. Vnde nomen uuestualen qui et longobardi apd'ptolomeum. sub cuius regno continebantur dorigi, produxit copias, bellũ cõmisit,multa hunorum millia prostrauit ceteros in fugã cõuertit Interea dum Sigebertus occupatur in doringia cũ hunis, frater eius rex Hilpericus fraternel charitatis oblitus, terminos regni eius hostili deuastat incursu, atqꝫ remensem obsidet urbem, eamqꝫ in deditionem accepit. ¶ Eodem anno haste in aere sunt uisę,ac militū acies, simul conflationum strepitus auditi, primo tēdentes irruptionem longobar doꝝ ī italiā, de quibus Gregorius papa magnus in homilia loquit̉. ¶ Nam anno sequenti,dñieę uidelicet natiuitatis.D.LXVIII.indictione romanorum prima.rex longobardoꝝ Alboinus pannoniam,in qua cum sua gente prius confederat,hunis longobardoꝝ commendauit amicis, assumptis in auxilium saxonibus,marcomannis,alijscꝗ gentibus uicina,cum omni populo suo ear partem italię occupauit,quę nomīe gẽtis,lōgobardia uocat̉ usqꝫ inpresens ¶ Eodem anno Sigebertus rex francoꝝ qui metis habitabat in austrasia frater Hilperici, terrã perlustrans saxonię habitat oribus ua cuam qui cum longobardis (sicut diximus) abierant in italiā ne penitus in solitudinem redigeretur,eam sueuis tradidit incolendã.ltaqꝫ saxones cum longobardis in italiâ, sueui habitauerūt in sax onia quatuordecim annis, quibus euolutis, cũ se uiderent saxones ultimo loco mancipiorum consuetudinem inter longobardos,in saxoniam redire consultant. ¶ Anno igitur dominicę natiuitatis.D.LXXXII.indictione romanorum quintadecima saxones qui cum longobardis erāt in italia,non ferentes ultra uuinulorum (sic enim prius uocababantur lon gobardi) superbiam dominationem iniquam,cum liberis uxoribus,conductu Sigeberti regis francoꝝ,per galliam australiā ad coloniam agrippinam reuersi sunt,ubi rheno trāsmisso priores repetiuere saxonię sedes,quas dimiferant. ¶ Sueui autem quibus rex donauerat Sigebertus ad inhabitandum,primo saxonibus negabant introitum, secundo tertiam eis partem restituere confenferunt. Verum saxonibus non partem, sed totam reposcentibus, mediam sueui regionem obtulerunt.Saxones in sententia maniere constantes,non partem non mediū terrę sed integrum totum repetentes. ¶ Postremores ferro cõmittitur, nimis acriter pro sediū possessi one ab utroqꝫ exercitu pugnatur.Tandem uicti sunt sueui eorum plusq̄ uiginti millia in eo certamine gladio saxonũ perierunt.Et ita saxones terram,quam uuinulorum persuasionę satis in consulte dimiferant,bello recuperauerunt anno post exitū quartodecimo, sueuis alijs occisis,alijs expulfis. ¶ Exeo tempore saxones memorati, de lōgobardia in germaniā reuerfentes,dicuntur vuestualen idest occidētales galli,usqꝫ in presentem diem,cum tamen ueri sint saxones atqꝫ germani.Vrbem cõ

deceitful Fredegundis, by fraud, was taken by King Hilperic as his wife; by her he begot, as we shall say later, the successor to his fatherly kingdom.

Heribert, however, the eldest son of Lotharius, in the division of the monarchy of the kingdom of the Franks received Neustria, holding the seat of his kingdom at Paris; and he reigned nine years, and, doing nothing worthy of memory, died in the year of the Lord 573, in the eleventh indiction of the Romans, leaving the kingdom to his brothers.

Gunthramus, King Lotharius’s second-born son, reigned at Orleans for thirty-three years, a prince excellent in his own condition, but he obtained a most wicked wife, named Austrigildis. Among the many evils she perpetrated, when she was sick unto death and could not be helped by the physicians, she circumvented the king with crafty persuasion, so that he confirmed by an undoubted oath that he would grant her the fulfilment of one request. “Before I die,” she said, “have the heads of my physicians, who have tormented me in vain with their medicines, cut off while I am watching.” What more? Those who were to bring in the physicians were sent at once; when they entered the queen’s chamber, the witch said: “Ha! You are not physicians, but liars, who by your medicines force me to die before my time. I have prepared such a reward for you that, compelled to die, you shall pass over before me.” Soon, to satisfy the lust of the impious woman, the executioner, as ordered, cut off the heads of the two innocent physicians while that beast herself watched and laughed. King Gunthramus died in the year of the Lord 597, in the fifteenth indiction of the Romans.

Sigebert, however, the third-born son of King Lotharius, reigned at Metz in Austrasia over the people of Trier, and also those of [unclear], Cologne, Mainz, and the other cities and provinces on this side of the Rhine, for thirteen years. He had as wife a Spaniard named Brunia, whom writers have more often been accustomed to call Brunihildis, the murderess of ten kings, who was so hateful to the Franks that the prophecy of the Sibyl seemed to be fulfilled in her, saying:

“There will come Brunia from the regions of Spain; before her sight peoples and kings will perish, but she herself will perish by the heels of horses.” Hilperic begot from her a son named Theodobert, who afterward reigned twenty-one years and died in the year of the Lord 599. His son, named Theodoricus, succeeding, reigned sixteen years; at the instigation of his grandmother Brunichildis he expelled Saint Columbanus from Gaul in the year of the Lord 614, and died shortly afterward, leaving three sons, as is read, bastards. The eldest, Sigebert, was put to flight in battle by Lotharius, son of the aforesaid king, and thereafter appeared nowhere. Corbus, the second-born, was killed by the same Lotharius. But Meroveus, the third-born, whom the same Lotharius had raised from the sacred font, he preserved alive. Brunihildis, however, the murderess of ten kings, he put to death.

In the third year of King Hilperic, the Huns, having gone out with a great army, began to ravage the regions of the Franks in Thuringia in hostile fashion. Against their insolence King Sigebert, brother of King Hilperic,

Vrbem suessionis, regni sedem hilperici fratris occu- pat. Anno regis Hilpericí nono indictione roma- norum sexta moritur frater eius Heribertus, rex francorum, qui re- gnabat in neustria urbe parrhifiorum sine liberis. ¶ Anno Hilperici regís francoꝝ decimo. under whose reign the Thuringians were contained, brought forth his forces, joined battle, laid low many thousands of the Huns, and put the rest to flight. Meanwhile, while Sigebert was occupied in Thuringia with the Huns, his brother, King Chilperic, forgetful of brotherly charity, laid waste the borders of his kingdom with a hostile incursion, and besieged the city of Reims, and received it in surrender.

In the same year spears were seen in the air, and battle-lines of soldiers, and at the same time the din of clashes was heard, first portending the incursion of the Lombards into Italy, concerning whom Pope Gregory the Great speaks in a homily. For in the following year, namely the year of the Lord’s nativity 568, in the first Roman indiction, Alboin king of the Lombards entrusted Pannonia, in which he had formerly dwelt with his people, to the Huns, friends of the Lombards, and, taking as allies Saxons, Marcomanni, and other neighboring peoples, occupied with all his people that part of Italy which, from the name of the people, is called Lombardy down to the present.

In the same year Sigebert king of the Franks, who lived at Metz in Austrasia, brother of Chilperic, surveying the land of Saxony, empty of inhabitants who had gone with the Lombards, as we have said, into Italy, lest it be reduced utterly to solitude, handed it over to the Suevi to inhabit. And so the Saxons lived with the Lombards in Italy, and the Suevi in Saxony, for fourteen years. When these had passed, since the Saxons saw themselves among the Lombards in the lowest place, in the condition of slaves, they took counsel to return to Saxony.

Therefore in the year of the Lord’s nativity 582, in the fifteenth Roman indiction, the Saxons who were with the Lombards in Italy, no longer enduring the pride and unjust domination of the Winili, for so the Lombards were formerly called, returned with their children and wives, under the conduct of Sigebert king of the Franks, through southern Gaul to Cologne Agrippina. There, after crossing the Rhine, they sought again their former seats in Saxony, which they had left behind.

But the Suevi, to whom King Sigebert had given them to inhabit, at first denied the Saxons entry; secondly, they agreed to restore to them a third part. But when the Saxons demanded back not a part but the whole, the Suevi offered half the region. The Saxons remained constant in their judgment, demanding back not a part, not half of the land, but the entire whole.

At last the matter was committed to the sword; the fight for possession of the settlements was waged very fiercely by both armies. At length the Suevi were defeated; more than twenty thousand of them perished in that battle by the sword of the Saxons. And thus the Saxons recovered by war the land which, by the persuasion of the Winili, they had left quite imprudently, in the fourteenth year after their departure, some of the Suevi being killed, others expelled.

From that time the aforesaid Saxons, returning from Lombardy into Germany, are called Westphalians, that is, western Gauls, down to the present day, although they are nevertheless true Saxons and Germans. The city

they built in the middle of their region a new [city], which they called Milan, in memory of the other one in Lombardy; in it there is now the episcopal see of the church of Münster. Hence some writers also called these Saxons, or Westphalians, Lombards, because they cast off their customs and rites in Saxony.

In the fifth year of King Chilperic, the king of Austrasia, his brother, remembering the injuries which he had received from him when, in the preceding year, absent from the kingdom, he was fighting with the Huns in Thuringia, gathered a great army and advanced against him to war. He occupied the city of Soissons, the seat of his brother Chilperic’s kingdom. He condemned his son Theodebert, when captured, to exile; he defeated Chilperic himself in battle and put him to flight; and all the things which he had previously taken away he recovered again for himself, and he usurped a great part of his kingdom.

In the same year King Sigebert took as wife Bruna, or Brunhild, daughter of Athanagild, king of the Visigoths, as was said above, who was reigning in Spain.

In the seventh year of Chilperic, king of the Franks, the Huns again devastated Thuringia; by magic arts they accomplished great things. Against them Sigebert, king of the Franks, advanced to battle. By their enchantments he had almost been deceived and defeated, but, prudently invoking the name of Christ, he stood firm, fought manfully, and finally conquered; and when a treaty had been concluded, the Huns returned to their own lands.

In the following year the Winili, who are the Lombards, after the city of Pavia had been taken by surrender after a siege of three years, in a short time gained almost all Italy except Rome and Ravenna, and, with no one resisting them, held dominion powerfully everywhere. In the ninth year of King Chilperic, in the sixth indiction of the Romans, his brother Charibert died, king of the Franks, who reigned in Neustria, in the city of the Parisians, without children.

In the tenth year of Chilperic, king of the Franks, Alboin, king of the Lombards, was killed by a certain armor-bearer of his on the following occasion. In the five hundred and seventh year of the Lord’s nativity, in the tenth indiction of the Romans, in the times of Lothar, great king of the Franks, this same King Alboin had a war with Chunimund, king of the Gepids, in which sixty thousand men fell on both sides. There Alboin killed Chunimund and had a drinking-cup fitted for himself from the shell of his head, which he was especially accustomed to use on the festive days of birthdays. He also took his daughter captive as his wife. And when, in the aforesaid year of Chilperic, on a certain solemn day, having become rather merry among the cups, he offered his wife her father’s brain, saying [unclear] For two years after he had died, the Lombards were under dukes for ten years.

Chilperic, king of the Franks, in the thirteenth year of his reign, in the tenth indiction of the Romans, too treacherously presses, harasses, and disturbs Sigebert his brother, king of the Franks in Austrasia, through his son Theodebert.

Monasteriū tamen sancti patris nostri benedicti abbatis in monte cassino intrantes spoliauerunt, & destruxerunt, eo dem tempore monachis romam fugientibus. ¶ Anno Lotharij regis frācoꝝ decimo indictione quintadecima, obijt Ganthramus rex francorū filius Lotharij magni secundo genitus, & nepos Clodouei regis ano regni sui.
