Whence, in the following year, the fourteenth of King Hilperic, and the year of the Lord’s nativity 578, a cruel war arose between them, in which Theodobert, son of Hilperic, was killed, and many of the Franks were slain on both sides.

After this, the Franks over whom Hilperic ruled, holding their own lord in hatred, resolved by common counsel to set over themselves as king his brother Sigebert, who seemed to be of a gentler disposition. When Fredegund, the wife of Hilperic, learned this, she sent two boys and treacherously caused King Sigebert to be killed in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s nativity.

In the following year Hilperic, king of the Franks, compelled Brunhild, the widow of his brother Sigebert, to go into exile with her sons. Almost all the Franks labored under hatred of this woman; although she made excessive use of much insolence, nevertheless she honored the churches of God. She also built several monasteries, and in various places established from the foundations new buildings of different kinds and of admirable workmanship.

In the seventeenth year of Hilperic, king of the Franks, the dukes of the Lombards began to lay waste the borders of the Gauls. The Franks met them with a great and strong multitude of forces, and fought several battles with them with doubtful fortune, sometimes defeated, and sometimes also victorious. In the end, however, the Franks triumphed.

Hilperic, king of the Franks, in the twenty-third year of his reign after his father, at the contrivance of his wife Fredegund, was killed in the year of the Lord’s nativity 587, in the fifth indiction of the Romans, leaving behind one only son, named Lothar the Younger, an infant of four months, who succeeded in the kingdom. The son of the husband-slaying Fredegund, when he was an infant of four months, was put in his father’s place and reigned forty-four years, beginning under the guardianship and direction of his mother. In the second year of his reign, Antharius, king of the Lombards, after the dukes had been driven out, took as wife Theodelinda, daughter of Garibald, king of Bavaria; to her, as to a woman of singular devotion, blessed Pope Gregory afterward sent the four books of the Dialogues.

In the fifth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, in the tenth indiction of the Romans, Saint Gregory the First, pope, formerly a monk and deacon, was ordained at Rome. He wrote, said, and did many things for the honor and benefit of the holy Church.

In the same year also, when Antharius, king of the Lombards, had died without children, the Lombards, having granted Queen Theodelinda the choice of selecting a husband for herself and a king for Italy, chose Agilulf as king for themselves and at the same time as her husband; thereafter he ruled energetically over the Lombards for twenty-five years.

In the eighth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, in the thirteenth indiction of the Romans, Garibald, king of the Bavarians, died, the father of the aforementioned Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards. After him Hildebert, king of the Franks, appointed as king of Bavaria a certain duke named Thassido, born of the race of the Franks, who overcame the Forabos, who are Slavs but later were called Bohemians, in war.

Theodoricus rex coloniam fratre interfecto ingreditur. Theodoberti regis perempti tres filij. Eiusdem filia una speciosissima. Brunihildis nepotes suos peremit. Sigebertus filius re- gis fugit ad oriētales Sigebertus fit dux alemānoꝝ heluetio rum. Theodoricus rex austrasię moritur. Lotharius fit mōar- cha regni totius frā corum. Brunichildis decem regum interfectrix occiditur. Lotharius monar- charegnū commisit comitibus. Vuernherus maior domus. Harpo comes bur- gundię constituitur Factus itaque uictor in sanguine fratris truculentus rex Theodori cus, coloniā intrauit cū pace, ipsamque urbē et ciues cū uniuerso fra- tris austrasiorū regno in deditione accepit, qui et ipse tanden uene- no Brunichildis auię (quemadmodū suo loco dicemus) interijt he redibùs priuatis. Theodobertus aut̄ rex miserabili forte peremptus, tres filios et unā (ut legitur) speciosissimā filiā reliquit Sigebertū uidelicet. Gunthramū, & Lothariū. Nomē filię nusꝗ repi Rex uero Theodoricus, coloniā ingressus, prescriptos duos iu- niores fratribus filios Gunthramū Lothariumque, & sororem eorundē ad ciuitatē metēsem misit captiuos, quibus crudelis auia Brunichil- dis occurrens nimioque succensa furore in odiū genitoris occisiꝛ sup eos irruit, & nepotes adhuc paruulos manu propria interfecit, quae Sigebertus autem, na tu maior Theoberti filius quo rūdam auxilio ciuiū submissus per murū secretissime rheno tre nemisso ī habitu scholaris aufugit, ueni ensque in franciā orientalē, apud cognatos suos godfridū, & eius fili um genebaldū tertiū, duces francoꝝ, circa menū et uuirciburg prīcipantiū aliquot annis latuit incognitus. Qui tandē post obitu regis Theodoricj, principum interuentu, ducatu in alemanía superiore, quęnunc dicitur heluetia donatione regis lotharij accepit sed neque nomē regiū, neque diadema portare more parentū suorū permiffus est. Et manfit sub ditio ne regim franccorum. Filium genuit nomine patris sui. Theobertum. Anno regis Lotharij. XXXI. dominicę uero natiuitatis sexcen tesimo decimo octauo īdictione romanoꝝ sexta. Theodoricus rex austrafię uenero Brunichildis auię sue metis interijt anno regni sui nonodecimo. Cuius regnū Lotharius, hilperici filius iam dictus, ac cepit, & fic iuxta uaticiniū, quod ei sanctus colūbanus olim prędix erat, monarchia totius regni francoru euafit, & folus deinceps an- nis. XIII. regnauit Contraque filij regis Theodorici Brunichildis instinctu mouē tes exercitu uicti sunt, & ipsa maloꝝ incentrix omniū Brunichildis capta et cum Eudolina Theodorici regis filia Lothario presentata procerumque condemnata decreto mortis accepithorrendae senten tiam. Nam uno pede et brachio altero mulcta ta, & ad caudā equae indomite colligata, membratim uiolēto extractu discerpta est quā reges decē extinxisse ferebant Lotharius igitur super totius regni francoꝛ quod prius in qua tuorerat diuisum monarchiam sublimatus, cum tam latum domi niū solis inutiliter gubernare non posset prouintias comitibus de antiqua regū prosapia descendentibus cōmendauit. Palatij regalis comitem, sive perfectum constituit Guarnerium, nobilem et ual- de pęminentem uirū. Burgūdiā uero cōmisit cuidā Harponi gubernādam qui et ipse comes erat de francoru regum uefustissimo genere procreatus. Rado comes austra sie constitutus est. Genebaldus dux moguntinus fuit. Marcopolis nūc virciburg dicit̉. Palatinoꝝ comitū Bauarie ducū ori go. Palatinatus baua rię duca tus confugit̉. Sigebertus dux frā corum in alemania fuit. Longobardi frācis tributarij fuerunt. Vuernher maior do mus moritur. Pippinus filius An segili postea maior domus. Linea generationis caroli magni du cum brabantię siml̓ atqƺ bauaria.

In the following year King Agilulf entered, intending to lay waste the borders of the Romans; but through the action of Theodolinda, queen of the Lombards, who was the wife of that same Agilulf, as we have said, not long afterward he made a treaty of friendship with them. Nevertheless, entering the monastery of our holy father Benedict the abbot on Monte Cassino, they plundered and destroyed it, the monks at that same time fleeing to Rome.

In the tenth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, in the fifteenth indiction, Gunthram, king of the Franks, second-born son of Lothar the Great and grandson of King Clovis, died at Orléans in the thirty-third year of his reign, not without a reputation for sanctity. His kingdom passed to his cousin Hildebert by [unclear] of [unclear]. In the following year Richard, king of the Visigoths, entered into a treaty with the kings of the Franks, and took as his wife the sister of the aforesaid King Hildebert. In the same year, on the twenty-first day of the month of November, Saint Columbanus died, abbot, priest, and teacher of the Scots and Picts; he left to his successors many memorials of sanctity, except that, in rustic simplicity, he neither learned nor taught that Easter ought to be celebrated on the Lord’s day, and never on another day.

In the thirteenth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, Hildebert, king of the Franks, died at Orléans. He was the son of King Sigebert, who was the son of Lothar, who was the son of Clovis, the first Christian king. He left two sons, Theobert and Theodoric, who divided their father’s kingdom between themselves; their grandmother Brunichild sowed many kinds of dissensions among them.

Therefore in the year of the Lord’s nativity 605, in the eighth Roman indiction, which was the eighteenth year of the reign of Lothar, Theodobert and Theoderic, the aforesaid brothers, stirred to fury by their grandmother Brunichild, who, as a supporter of Theoderic, labored with incredible hatred against Theodobert, waged a most savage war between themselves, in which more than thirty thousand fighting men fell. Also an angel of the Lord, holding and brandishing a drawn sword in his hand, was seen in the air above the people by many who were present.

At last Theodobert, having been defeated, since he could do nothing else, sought safety in flight. His brother Theoderic pursued him as far as Cologne Agrippina, and along the whole road ceaselessly cut down his soldiers as they fled likewise. But Theodobert entered Cologne and immediately ordered the city gates to be closed.

Theoderic, his brother, pursuing him, as has been said, encircled Cologne with a siege. The citizens, rushing to the walls, asked Theoderic for the terms of peace. He answered them: “You will never have peace from me unless first you cut off my brother’s head and throw it out to me from the wall. But if you refuse to do this, I shall not depart from here until, when the city has been violently taken, I destroy you all with your lord, your little children, and your wives.”

When they heard this, the citizens were exceedingly terrified; and after holding counsel among themselves, at last, lest it happen that all should perish, they cut off the head of King Theodobert, their lord, and threw it out over the wall to the impious Theoderic, as he had ordered, thus purchasing peace disgracefully in the blood of their own king.

The Lombards lay waste the borders of the Romans. The Cassinese monastery is destroyed by the Lombards. King Gunthram of Orléans dies. Hildebert succeeded Gunthram. The Franks enter into a treaty with the Visigoths. Saint Columbanus the abbot died. King Hildebert of Orléans dies. A most savage war takes place between the brother kings of Francia. Thirty thousand Franks perished. An angel was seen in the air with a sword. Theodobert flees from the battle to Cologne. King Theoderic pursues his brother as far as Cologne. The people of Cologne cut off the head of their own king.

Genebaldo eius nominis tertio duci francorꝫ in oriente apud mar¬ copolim quę nunc ab adiacente in monte sanctę marię castello vuir cipurg nominatur. King Theodoric enters Cologne after his brother has been killed.

The three sons of King Theodobert, who had been slain. One very beautiful daughter of the same man. Brunichild killed her own grandsons.

Sigebert, the king’s son, fled to the eastern [lands]. Sigebert becomes duke of the Alemanni and the Helvetians.

King Theodoric of Austrasia dies. Lothar becomes monarch of the whole kingdom of the Franks.

Brunichild, killer of ten kings, is slain.

Lothar entrusted the monarchy of the kingdom to counts. Wernher, mayor of the palace. Harpo is appointed count of Burgundy.

Thus made victor, in his brother’s blood, the savage King Theodoric entered Cologne in peace, and received the city itself and its citizens, together with his brother’s whole kingdom of the Austrasians, in surrender. He too, at last, died by the poison of his grandmother Brunichild, as we shall say in its place, having been deprived of heirs.

King Theodobert, slain by a miserable fate, left three sons and one, as is read, very beautiful daughter: namely Sigebert, Gunthram, and Lothar. I have found the name of the daughter nowhere. But King Theodoric, after entering Cologne, sent the aforesaid two younger sons of his brother, Gunthram and Lothar, and their sister as captives to the city of Metz. Their cruel grandmother Brunichild, meeting them and inflamed with excessive fury, in hatred of their slain father rushed upon them and killed with her own hand her grandsons, still little children, who [unclear].

But Sigebert, the elder son of Theodobert by birth, lowered by the help of certain citizens secretly over the wall and across the Rhine, fled in the dress of a scholar. Coming into eastern Francia, he lay hidden for some years, unknown, among his kinsmen Godfrid and his son Genebald III, dukes of the Franks, who ruled around the Main and Wurzburg. At length, after the death of King Theodoric, through the intervention of the princes, he received by the gift of King Lothar a duchy in Upper Alemannia, which is now called Helvetia; but he was not permitted either to bear the royal name or to wear the diadem according to the custom of his fathers. And he remained under the authority of the kingdom of the Franks.

He begot a son with his father’s name, Theobert.

In the thirty-first year of King Lothar, and in the six hundred eighteenth year of the Lord’s nativity, in the sixth indiction of the Romans, King Theodoric of Austrasia died at Metz by the poison of his grandmother Brunichild, in the nineteenth year of his reign. Lothar, the already mentioned son of Hilperic, received his kingdom, and so, according to the prophecy that Saint Columbanus had once foretold to him, he attained the monarchy of the whole kingdom of the Franks, and thereafter reigned alone for thirteen years.

And on the other side, when the sons of King Theodoric, at Brunichild’s instigation, raised an army, they were defeated; and Brunichild herself, the inciter of all evils, was captured and presented to Lothar together with Eudolina, daughter of King Theodoric. Condemned by the decree of the nobles, she received the sentence of a dreadful death. For, after being mutilated in one foot and the opposite arm, and tied to the tail of an untamed mare, she was torn apart limb by limb by the violent dragging. They said that she had destroyed ten kings.

Therefore Lothar, raised to monarchy over the whole kingdom of the Franks, which had previously been divided into four, since he could not profitably govern so broad a dominion by himself alone, entrusted the provinces to counts descended from the ancient stock of kings. He appointed as count, or prefect, of the royal palace Guarnerius, a noble and very eminent man.

But Burgundy he committed to a certain Harpo to govern; he too was a count born from the most ancient line of the kings of the Franks.

Rado was appointed count of Austrasia. Genebaldus was duke of Mainz. Marcopolis is now called Wurzburg. The origin of the counts palatine and dukes of Bavaria. The Palatinate is joined to the duchy of Bavaria. Sigebertus was duke of the Franks in Alemannia. The Lombards were tributaries of the Franks. Wernher, mayor of the palace, dies. Pippin, son of Ansegil, afterward mayor of the palace. The line of descent of Charles the Great, together with the dukes of Brabant and Bavaria.

He also entrusted Austrasia to Rado, a most noble count; in it were the most renowned cities: Trier, Metz, Liege, Cologne, the Mosellan [unclear], Luxembourgers, Austrasians, [Euphalians?], Namurians, and many others.

To Genebaldus, the third of that name, duke of the Franks in the east at Marcopolis, which is now called Wurzburg from the adjacent castle of Saint Mary on the mountain, he assigned Mainz, Worms, Speyer, and the peoples of those same regions; he founded Frankfurt beside the Main.

But to Pippin, who was the son of Duke Ansegisus, brother of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, and also count of Namur and duke of Brittany, from whom the counts palatine, the counts of the Rhine, and the dukes of Bavaria who live today, eighteen in number, all descended, as I know, apart from the females, on the mother's side, namely from Gertrude, daughter of Henry, count palatine dwelling at Heidelberg, who, having been married to Otto, duke of Bavaria, in the year of the Lord's nativity 1225, joined the principality of Bavaria to the Palatinate; King Lotharius assigned all Lower or northern Francia, that is, the people of Tournai, Arras, the Morini, Terouanne, Cambrai, and whatever lies between them, besides the county of Namur and the duchy of Brabant, which belonged by right to the aforesaid Ansegisus.

To Duke Sigebertus, son of the late Theodobert, king of the Franks in Austrasia, whose head, as we have said, the people of Cologne cut off, King Lotharius, after he was made duke through the intervention of the nobles, entrusted the cities of Alemannia: Chur, Lausanne, Constance, Basel, and the peoples settled around them, the Alemanni, the [Caurici?], and the Helvetii dwelling at the source of the Rhine.

In the thirty-second year of his reign, in the seventh Roman indiction, Lotharius, king of the Franks, remitted to the Lombards, after a treaty had first been made, the tribute of twelve thousand gold florins which they were obliged to pay each year to the Franks.

In the thirty-eighth year of Lotharius, king of the Franks, in the thirteenth Roman indiction, died Werner, count of the palace, or mayor of the palace of the Franks. After him Ansegil, son of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, monk and hermit, previously a married man, was made mayor of the palace of the Franks; with his son Pippin, and Saint Arnulf himself, faithfully assisting him, he held the principate. Pippin, afterward mayor of the palace, who was called the Elder, was the son of the aforesaid Ansegisus, who was son of Saint Arnulf. He was son of Ansegil, or, as others write, of Arnold the Elder. He was son of Ambertus, surnamed Nicanor, born from Blidehild, daughter of Lotharius, the first king of Clovis. That Ambertus was son of Duke Sigebertus.

He was son of Duke Priamus. He was son of Duke Heribertus. He was son of Duke Leontius. He was son of Duke Meroveus. He was son of Duke Diocles. He was son of Duke Sunno. prima quę Bertrudis dicebatur filiũ nomine dagobertum qui successit in regno Prima uxore mortua duxerat secundam nomine Si ghildem que peperit Heribertum. Dagobertus Regis Lotharij maior na tu filius, patri succedens ĩ regno francorum, ãno do minicę natiuitatis pręnorafo, regnauit annis quatuoꝛ decim, & prius in austrasia (sicut dictū est) annis tribus, patre adhuc uiuente, & fic omne tempus quo reg nauit anni fuerunt decem septem. Heribertus autē frater Dagoberti ex patre, sed alia matre natus (ut est dictum) in diuisione regni aquitaniam, tolosam, alias ur bes, quę intra pyreneos montes ligerim continentur, in possessi on em hereditatis accepit, ea uidelicet conditiōne quod in ceteris re gnis frācorum nihil iuris sibi debeat usurpare. Qui sedem regni sui primar iam tolosae constituit. Quarto post hęc anno belli occasione captata uascones in deditionem accepit. Rex Dagobertus monasteriũ sancti Dionysij martiris a funda mentis nouum construxit quod multis praeđjs, rebus, possessio nibus ditauit, licet non sine iniuria quarūdam ecclesiarum quas ui adhibita multis spoliabat ornatibus, tanquam diui Dionysij om̃ia deberentur obsequijs, tam iure quam iniuria conquisita. Templum construxit eiusdem coenobij omnino pulcherrimum, quod argen to solido erat tectum, in quod corpora memorati martiris socio rum eius de catulico uico translata in thecam auream collocauit, ip sofq parietes ecclesiae intrinsecus tapetibus margaritis unionibus decentissime intextis pulcherrime decorauit, locum mona chis incolendum dedit nostri ordinis. Vxorem primo habuit Dagobertus nomine Gertrudem, quam propter sterilitatem repudiauit, superduxitq alterā cui nomen erat Nanthildis. Plurimas deniq pergebat pellicũ cateruę, preter eas quas compluribus in locis comptas reginarum instar ornatas alebat. Obnitebatur tamē eius turpibus factis haud mediocriter pippinus maior domus, siue comes palatinus qui dux brabantię fuerat, si mul namurci comes, nepos sancti Arnulfri ac pater sanctę Ger trudis uirginis monialis niuellis in brabātia, nec usqquaq sine bat regem per tot uitia pro suo arbitrio tam libere defluere. Anno Dagoberti regis secundo qui fuit dominicae natiuitatis sexcentesimus tricessimus tertius uxor eius Nanthildis peperit ei filium qui Sigebertus est nominatus. Hic infans XL die ꝗcū a sancto Amādo epo baptizaretur, tacētibus cūcis ip̄e Amē clara uoce re spondit. Hunc Sigebertum eius patruus Heribertus qui Tholosa regnabat de sacro baptismatis foͤte leuauit. Mortuo autem post ali quot annos rege Heriberto, non diu postea etiã eius filho nomīe I Sichildis mater fuit Heriberti. QVINQVAGE SIMVS PRIMVS. Dagobertus regna uit annis. XVII. But Pippin the elder begot Charles Martel, and he begot Pippin the younger, mayor of the palace of the Franks, and king after Childeric. Thus from King Marcomir the first down to King Pippin, son of Charles Martel, mayor of the palace, and father of Saint Gertrude, there are counted fifty-one generations over the course of one thousand fifty-nine years.

But King Lothar, in the forty-first year of his reign, which was the six hundred and eighth year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the first indiction of the Romans, appointed Dagobert, his son by Queen Bertrada, king of Austrasia, assigning to him Metz, Trier, Cologne, Liege, Tournai, Arras, Tongeren, Therouanne, the Morini, and whatever lay between the western sea, the English sea to the north also, and the Rhine. He earnestly entrusted him to Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, and to Pippin, count of Namur and most noble duke of the Brabantians, to be instructed and guided. Dagobert established the seat of his kingdom, after the custom of the old kings of Austrasia, in the aforesaid city of Metz, and arranged the kingdom of the Franks well, both by himself and through dukes and counts.

In the following year the Saxons, rising in rebellion, refused the customary tribute to the Franks. Therefore King Dagobert, having gathered the forces of his men, moved his army against the rebels and waged war with Berthulf, duke of the Saxons; from the first encounter he was gravely wounded. When his father Lothar, who was then in Ardenne, heard this reported by a swift messenger, he immediately crossed the Rhine at Neuss and hastened to the aid of his son. The battle is renewed, and on both sides the fighting is hard and fierce. At last, however, the Saxons, after their duke Berthulf had been slain by the Franks, were defeated and sought safety in flight.

But King Lothar, pursuing the fugitives with the Franks, laid them low in a pitiable slaughter, sparing no one, but killing with the sword all who exceeded the length of his sword. The people, however, who had remained throughout Saxony he recalled to subjection to the Franks, and imposed on them a tribute of five hundred oxen.

After these things, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 631, in the fourth indiction of the Romans, the aforesaid Lothar, king of the Franks, died in the forty-fourth year of his reign, leaving by his wife

the first, who was called Bertrudis, [bore] a son named Dagobert, who succeeded to the kingdom. After his first wife had died, he had taken a second, named Sichildis, who bore Heribert.

Dagobert, the elder son of King Lotharius, succeeding his father in the kingdom of the Franks in the year of the Lord’s nativity noted above, reigned fourteen years; and earlier in Austrasia, as has been said, three years while his father was still living. Thus the whole time during which he reigned was seventeen years.

Heribert, however, Dagobert’s brother by his father, but born of another mother, as has been said, received in the division of the kingdom Aquitaine, Toulouse, and the other cities contained between the Pyrenees and the Loire, as the possession of his inheritance, on this condition: that in the other kingdoms of the Franks he should claim no right for himself. He established the principal seat of his kingdom at Toulouse. In the fourth year after this, when an occasion for war had been seized, he received the Gascons in surrender.

King Dagobert built the monastery of Saint Dionysius the martyr anew from the foundations, and enriched it with many estates, goods, and possessions, though not without injury to certain churches, which he despoiled by force of many ornaments, as though all things, acquired both lawfully and unlawfully, were owed to the services of blessed Dionysius. He built the church of the same monastery, altogether most beautiful, which was covered with solid silver; into it he transferred the bodies of the said martyr and his companions from the Catulian village and placed them in a golden shrine. He also most beautifully adorned the inner walls of the church with tapestries most fittingly woven with pearls and large pearls. He gave the place to be inhabited by monks of our order.

Dagobert first had a wife named Gertrude, whom he repudiated because of sterility, and he brought in another, whose name was Nanthildis. Finally he kept going to many crowds of concubines, besides those whom he maintained in several places, arrayed and adorned like queens. Yet Pippin, mayor of the palace, or count palatine, who had been duke of Brabant and at the same time count of Namur, nephew of Saint Arnulf and father of Saint Gertrude, a virgin nun at Nivelles in Brabant, resisted his shameful deeds quite considerably, and by no means allowed the king to sink so freely, according to his own will, through so many vices.

In the second year of King Dagobert, which was the six hundred thirty-third year of the Lord’s nativity, his wife Nanthildis bore him a son, who was named Sigebert. This infant, forty days old, when he was baptized by Saint Amandus the bishop, while all were silent, himself answered “Amen” in a clear voice. Heribert, his uncle, who was reigning at Toulouse, lifted this Sigebert from the holy font of baptism. But when King Heribert died after some years, and not long afterward also his son, named [unclear]

With Hilperic, the monarchy of the whole kingdom of the Franks reverted to Dagobert, many always tending toward one, and again, by the plurality of sons, confounding unity.

When King Heribert had died, the Vascones refused to obey and be subject to the Franks; King Dagobert attacked them in war and compelled them to submission.

At the same time [Iudicahel?], who held the duchy of the same Armorican Brittany, terrified by the threat of imminent war, subjected himself and all the people of Armorican Brittany to Dagobert, king of the Franks, and to his successors forever. King Dagobert also attacked in war the Slavs, the Sorbs, who are now called Bohemians; he defeated and overcame them, and made them subject and tributary to the Franks.

If this Dagobert, the great king of the Franks, founded that once distinguished, exempt, and royal monastery of our order in the town of Wissembourg, in the diocese of Speyer, concerning which we have heard many expressing doubt, it seems to me that this was done in the third year after the death of his father, [unclear], since he reigned only fourteen years, although certain uncertain authors seem to have thought otherwise. With this reckoning of times agrees the number of the year of the Lord’s Nativity 634, which was the third year of the aforesaid Dagobert, but the sixth of his reign over Austrasia, and not the twentieth, as we read in the copied letters of that Dagobert himself. How shall we be able to know whether they are true or false, unless we see their archetype? Desiring to untie the knot of this doubt, let us set down a copy of the letters.

Dagobert, by the favor of divine clemency king of the Franks, to all the chief men of his kingdom, indeed to all professing the Christian faith, both future and present. A vow by which anyone has bound himself to God or to his saints cannot be made void without the stain of guilt; and the greater and more worthy is he to whom it is vowed, by so much heavier a judgment will the presumption of one who vows and does not pay be struck. Therefore we too ought and wish to render what we have vowed to the Lord, the terrible God, and to him who takes away the spirits of princes, terrible among all the kings of the earth. How he terrified us with the arm of his power, how, striking and healing, he visited us again, we have judged should be made known to all as an example of correction, especially so that every faithful person, having heard of our peril, may restrain himself from the devastation of the churches of God, and [unclear]; distracted, I neglected the duty of royal office, showing no solicitude or diligence toward those entrusted to me, doing or judging nothing from gentleness or zeal for justice. Among my other transgressions, the destruction of the churches of God [unclear].

King Dagobert enumerates his transgressions.

and I had begun to be the destroyer of those things of which I ought to have been the defender and exalter, fearing neither the eyes of the divine majesty nor the outcry of men. At length the kindness of God, crushing the pride of my obstinate mind with the rod of correction, visited my iniquities, and, when I had been chastened, did not deny me pardon. For, caught up on high and presented before the divine majesty, seated among the choirs of the saints in the guise of one judging, I was gravely and steadfastly accused by the most holy patrons of the churches for ecclesiastical goods seized by robbery by me and consumed, especially by the most holy Mary, mother of God, and by the most blessed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles.

¶ And when, burdened by conscience, I did not dare to defend my offences, at length my special patron, the martyr Dionysius, came to my aid; by his prayers he obtained for me a period of delay of the punishment that was pressing upon me. He himself, as though setting a manner of penance, placed in this my hope of full pardon: if, to the honour of God and of the holy preachers whom I had more greatly offended, I should build a house suitable for divine services. Gladly making this promise, I vowed it, and, dismissed by those above, I returned. Therefore, in sure hope of remission and pardon of our sins, rendering with eager zeal all that we have done, we have built a church in honour of the Holy Trinity, and of holy Mary ever-virgin, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, in the place called Vuyssenburg; and we have determined to exalt it and enrich it with royal munificence. Therefore we give to it, and wish to have been given in perpetuity, from the property of our fisc lying adjacent there, whatever belongs to us, both in villages and in bondsmen, woods, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses; and all these things we transfer by free conveyance to the use of the brethren serving God there under monastic profession. And so that the authority of this our donation may remain stable and firm for all time, we have taken care to note below the boundaries and the names of the surrounding places. Toward the eastern region the march which we have conveyed extends as far as Morchohouen and to Aldenherden, and thence to Goboldefvuege, and thence below Nadumlutra, and thence to Buozdigenhurst, and thence to the boundary which stands on the summit of the valley Iuuenesdal, and thence it leads toward the southern region above Vuarbach, and thence to Bodemloseffaffa, and thence to Sebach, and thence to Kirchdal, and thence to Ingoldesizahe, and thence to the wooded mountains as far as Bedebur. Toward the western region, however, as far as Lutenbach and Bernbach, and thence to Grunenbrunnen, and thence to Otterichescheyt. Toward the northern region as far as Eichenerenberg. But the place itself, which we embrace with singular devotion, now and henceforth we wish to be free from every oppression of servitude, under royal protection, namely in such a way that no public judge, no one from the judicial power, may presume to have any power there, nor to compel the men of that place either to hear cases, or to pay [auffreda?], or taxes. This also we have decreed by equal authority: that no bishop of the city of Speyer, nor any of the other bishops, shall have authority there for ruling, or for conducting any cases whatever; but under the defense of our immunity the father of the monastery, with his brothers, shall freely and quietly possess everything belonging to that place. In addition to this, we grant to the same place a coinage having on it images, letters, and the expressed likeness of the coinage of Speyer, and by the equal gift of our authority we wish it to be valid and firm: that the men of the same church may freely attend to their business throughout our whole kingdom, in such a way, namely, that they pay no toll due. And no judge, or any person of whatever rank, shall presume to inflict any violence upon it in a case of this kind.

Moreover, to the brothers serving God there, so that they may guard the order of holy conduct the more devoutly and tranquilly, we have given free power among themselves of choosing an abbot for themselves. To this abbot, and to all who succeed him, we grant this special privilege of dignity: that he may promote into the order and right of ministerials whomever from the household he shall judge worthy of such honor. All the ministerials of the same church shall also receive their benefice from the gift of the abbot, and shall serve the abbot alone; nor shall the advocate dare to exercise any power over them, unless perhaps, because of some disobedience, the abbot invites the advocate to constrain those ministerials as rebels.

But the rest of the household, at the lawful place and time, three times in the year, ought to assemble at the advocate’s court for the doing of justice, and, if the advocate is present, to pay single denarii for the advocate’s service, excepting those who are in the immunity. But if the advocate is absent from these courts, nothing is owed to him from these denarii, unless he is proved to be in the king’s service. And so that this our tradition, the institution of a dignity of granted right, may remain stable and unshaken forever, we have signed this written charter, strengthened by the addition of our seal. Given, as we did it, in that same monastery, in the month of May, on the eleventh day, in the twenty-third year of our reign, in the name of Christ, happily. Amen. In the year of the Lord 624.

I find nothing in these letters that casts doubt for me upon the foundation mentioned; but because the date of the writing of this page does not agree with the computation of the years of the Lord according to Sigebert, the monk of Gembloux, and also Rupert Gaguin, and many other most diligent writers of histories, I do not know whence this has arisen. For if credit is to be given to the said historiographers, it will be plainly established that Lotharius, the father of Dagobert, was still living among men in the year of the Lord 624, although the son himself asserts that he was dead before he began to found the monastery of Wissembourg. For King Lotharius died, as was said above, in the year of Christ 631, and Dagobert succeeded him at once in the same year and reigned fourteen years. Therefore he who can [unclear] the knot...

[unclear], I cannot persuade myself of anything else, except that King Dagobert founded the monastery of Weissenburg in the third year of his reign, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 634.

At the same time Saint Eligius, powerful at the court of Lothar and Dagobert, kings of the Franks, and a marvelous goldsmith, founded, with both royal and his own expenditures, the abbey of the monastery of our order which is called Solignac; there he himself became a monk and innocently discharged the office of abbot. There also Saint Remaclus, coming from Britain, trained himself under him in Christ’s service.

Saint Dado, also called Audoenus, bishop of Rouen and chancellor of King Dagobert, likewise built within the forest of Brie a monastery of our order, which they call Rebais; over it he appointed Saint Agilus as first abbot, a man lovable to Christ and renowned for many virtues.

In the ninth year of his reign King Dagobert appointed his son Sigebert, a boy of seven years, king over the Austrasians, under the guardianship and direction of Saint Cunibert, archbishop of Cologne, and of Pippin, duke of Brabant and count of Namur.

In the same year, which was the 640th year of the Lord’s nativity, in the thirteenth indiction, Saint Arnulf died: Pippin’s grandfather, from mayor of the palace of the Franks bishop of Metz, and from pontiff a solitary and hermit. Clodulf, ordained bishop of Metz after his father, imitated his holiness.

Doda, formerly the lawful wife of Saint Arnulf before his episcopate, and mother of the already mentioned bishop Clodulf, enclosed at Trier for love of Christ, whom she had chosen as her bridegroom, separated from her carnal husband, shone with holiness.

In the eleventh year of his reign, Dagobert, king of the Franks, led an army against the Wends. The Saxons came to his aid with all eagerness, and when battle was joined the Wends were defeated by the Franks and compelled into servitude to the Franks under tribute. But the Saxons, who annually paid five hundred oxen to the Franks as tribute, having gained the opportunity, approached King Dagobert after the victory and asked that he remit the tribute to them. The king, wishing to return favor for their voluntary service, remitted the tribute.

After this Dagobert, king of the Franks, died on the first day of the month of February, and was buried in the church of Saint Dionysius which he himself had built, in the fourteenth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 645, in the third Roman indiction. The son of King Dagobert, succeeding his father in the kingdom of the Franks, reigned seventeen years. His mother’s name was Nathildis. And his [unclear], named Erckenwald, was born from the most ancient stock of kings.

The opinion of Trithemius on the foundation of the monastery. Saint Eligius, goldsmith and bishop. The monastery of Latiniacum is founded. Saint Remaclus, from monk bishop of our order. The monastery of Rebais is founded.

Sigebert, a boy of seven years, becomes king in Austrasia.

Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, died. Clodulf succeeded his father in the episcopate.

Saint Doda, nun at Trier. The Wends are overcome by the Franks and Saxons. Dagobert remits the tribute to the Saxons. Dagobert, king of the Franks, dies. The fifty-second. Clovis reigned seventeen years. [unclear]

93
Quae tandem cursu presentis stadij sanctissime consummato, migrauit ad dn̄m, in eodem sepulta monasterio sancti Symphoriani martiris, cui deuotissime seruierat. Fuit autem Modoaldus iste (quē alij Rodoaldum scribunt) frater Ithe uxoris pippini senioris, auūculus beate Gertrudis uirginis. Quę ltha fundauit in brabantia monasterium nuellense monialium, in quo cum filia, mortuo Pippino, deinceps omnipotenti deo sanctissime seruiuit. ¶ Modoaldus uero sanctissimus treuiroꝝ praesul, nō diu post obitu sororis, etiam ipse in domino quiescens, iuxta eam in ecclesia sancti Simphoriani sepultus fuerat, qui numeriāus in archiepiscopatu successit. corum dagobertus anno dominicę nativitatís sexcentesimo uicesimo septimo indictione romanorum quintadecima fundare coepit monasterium dolegiēse ordinis sancti benedicti, diocesis treuirobꝫ, consilio auxilio beatí modoaldi archiepiscopi quod Sigebertus rex austrasię, filius eius, consumauit. Et sanctus Pirminius praesul, monachus, posteapulchrius decoravit. ¶ His temporibus in diocesi treuiroꝝ magnę sanctitatis uiri claruerunt, quorum enumbero paulus erat unus, qui super montem gebenam, in opposito ciuitate trans pontem mosellę fluminis, uitam duxit eremiticam, deinde ueniens ad memoratum dolegerentur monastere, monachus factus est, postremo episcopus uiduuenfisis ordinatus, pristinę sancticę normulã in omnibus fideliter custodiuit. Mons gebenna dictus antea, nomen ab eo suscipiẽs, patulimōs (uualgariter paulsberg) nuncupatur, usque in prezentem diem. ¶ Vuandalinus quoque, monachus primum in tholegia, postea eremita in eo loco, ubi nunc oppidum ex eiu nomine cõstat dictum ad sanctum vuandalinum distat uno duntaxat miliario ab ipso monasterio, uir sanctissime conuersationis qui uiuus mortuus usqui multos uerbo exemplo cõuertit ad christum, quem recenseui duo putentur unus. ¶ Fuit alius, quasi eodem tempore, uuandalinus, mo (cursum). nachus prespyter, discipulus sancti Columbani. diui uularici monachi in peregrinatione socius uir sanctus predicator egregius qui multos uerbo et exemplum cõuertit ad chrisium, quem recensesui duo putentur unus. ¶ Ingobertus quoque monachus presbyter Carilephus monachus presbyte Ruolffrichus, Bantus, eius frater Beatus monachus presbyteri Vuołffi laicus, uiri sanctissimi cum alijs multis indiocesi treuiroꝝ his temopribus uitam duxerunt in eremo solitariam ¶ Sanctus quoque Disibotus monachus presbyter in diocesi mungentina, in comitatusepanhemen si duobus a Cruciniaco, uno amonasterio quondam meo spanhein miliaribus, eremiticã ducensuitam, in eo loco prope Sobernheim ubi nahus glanus conflunt monasteriũ cõstruxit monachorum quod eius nomine hodie constat. Monasterij eius parvum hodie cernituruestigium. Sanctus Mododal dus archiep̃s auūculus fuit sctem gertrud. Sactus Modoaldus obijt. Numerianus successit. Doleiense monaste rium nostri ordinis fundatur. Sanctus Pirminus episcopus. Heremite plures in diocesi treuirorúm. Paulus eremita postea monachus po stremo eps uidun. Mons gebenna nunc pauli mona chus eremita. Vuandalinus alius monachus. Vualaricus mona phus. Vuolffricus. Bantus quoque. Beatus eius frater Vuolfiliacus. monachi sancti. Sanctus disibodus monachus ꝓpespann Monasteriu sancki Disiboldi fundatur anno.DC.LX.

Clodoveus reigned in Neustria. Sigibert, his brother, reigned in Austrasia. Saint Amandus, bishop in Maastricht. Pippin, mayor of the palace in Austrasia. Saint Chunibert, archbishop of Cologne, chancellor of the kingdom of Austrasia. Saint Irmina becomes the first abbess in the Horrea at Trier, of our order. The head of Saint Irmina is kept at Spanheim. Saint Modesta. Saint Anastasia. Saint Basilissa, abbesses there. Saint Modoald, builder of many monasteries. The monastery of Saint Symphorian is founded. Saint Severa, abbess of our order near Trier.

Clodoveus reigned over the Franks throughout inner Gaul, namely in Neustria, that is, Paris, Amiens, Beauvais, Blois, Reims, Orleans, Tours, also in Aquitaine, and in the whole kingdom that had been his father’s.

Sigibert, however, his brother, as we have said, reigned in Austrasia: over the people of Metz, Trier, Cologne, Liege, and Traiectum, where Saint Amandus was then bishop; also over the Tongri, Morini, Hollanders, Frisians, Saxons, Sorbs, Thuringians, Bavarians, Suevi, Alemanni, Cisrhenani, the people of Strasbourg, Worms, Mainz, [unclear], and the Burgundians. His mayor of the palace, or prince of the palace, was Pippin the Elder, son of Ansegisus and grandson of Arnulf, count of Namur and duke of Brabant, father of [Grimoald?] and of Saint Gertrude, abbess of Nivelles, in the paternal duchy of Brabant.

The chancellor of Sigibert was Saint Chunibert, archbishop of Cologne. In most of the places or provinces already named, under the rule of King Sigibert and of Pippin, mayor of the palace, there were appointed petty kings, dukes, counts, and prefects, by whose administration the people were governed.

Irmina, a virgin of most holy conduct, was one of the daughters of King Dagobert and the sister of the aforesaid kings. For her, her father, while still living, built in the city of Trier, in his very ancient palace which was called the Horrea, a monastery of maidens under the Rule of Saint Benedict, and a church in honor of blessed Mary ever virgin. In it he placed a congregation of nuns, and gave them this same daughter of his as mother and abbess; she was renowned in life and after death for many virtues and miracles, and her venerable head is kept in the abbey of Spanheim. In the governance of the nuns of the aforesaid monastery, Modesta succeeded this Irmina; she was a pupil of the monastery of Romaric and daughter of the sister of blessed Modoald, archbishop of Trier. After her came Anastasia, and in the fourth place Basilissa; all these have been enrolled among the saints.

At the same time the aforesaid bishop of Trier, Modoald, at whose urging the already-mentioned monastery in the Horrea had been built, also constructed another monastery in an ancient palace situated in the suburbs of Trier. In it he established nuns under the same Rule of Saint Benedict, and set over them Adela, another daughter of King Dagobert.

The same bishop Modoald built a third holy congregation of maidens on the bank of the Moselle, beside the walls of the city of Trier, in honor of the holy martyr Symphorian, under the rule of Saint Benedict. There he appointed his sister, named Severa, as mother and abbess over the nuns; living in all purity of mind and body, she in no way fell short of her brother’s holiness.

Sanctus Remaclus fit ep̄s in traiecto suꝑeriori. Pippinus maior domus namurci com̄is brabantię dux pala¬tinus obijt. Grunualdus fit maior domus ānis .xi.. Hildebertus filius grunvualdi rex. Rathulfus dux dorīgorum superatur. Sanctus Furseus abbas peregrinus. Latiniacum fundat monasterium Foillanus ultanus monachi sancti. Monasterii fossendantur. Duodecim ordinis nostrimonafteria fūdantur. Coenobium stabulēse Malmundarie. Sanctus Remaclus episcopus in mastrichtit monachus stabulensis. Sanctus Lādolinus confessor domini. MONASTERIA Lobiense Alneicēse Vuaslarien̄ Crispin Monasterium floría ceñ fundatur. Corpus sancti Bene dicti abbatis trāsferitur. Anno Clodouei regis francorum primo sanctus Remaclus eccliesietraiectensis ordinatur episcopus uir multe eruditionis, magne sanctitatis. Anno sequenti qui fuit dominice natiuitatis. DCXLVII. īdictione romanorum quinta moritur Pippinus senior comes namurcenfis dux brabantię maior domus palatinus comes Sigeberti regis francorum metis in austrasia regni sedem tenentis pater sancte Gertrudis uirginis relinquens filium Grunvaldum Patri gruvivuald in principatu domus regię successit annis undecim, postea fuit occisus ut suo dicemus loco Is filium habuit nomine Hildebertum de quo etiam dicemus quemadmodum regem fecerit eū domino suo in exilium detrufo. Anno pręnotato Radulfus doringorum dux in superbiam erectus francis negat consuetum soluere tributum Vnde Sigebertus austrasiae francorum rex contractis copijs exercitum mouit in dorīgiam consertisqꝫ manibus ducem uicit ad solutionem tributi coartauit. Eodem anno sanctus Furseus abbas de hibernia pro christiano re peregrinus uenit in gallias a Clodoueo rege susceptus honorifice Latiniacum Cenobium nostrinuncordinis fūdauit monacho sꝗ istituit quē non multo post duo fratres eius Foillanus VItanus monachi pariuoto peregrinationis secuti uerbo exemplouite gallias illustrarunt. Ex quibus Foillanus dono sancte Gertrudisin virginis Fossense monasterium postea fundauit ubi etiam martyrio coronatus indomino quiiescit. Anno regis Clodouei sexto. Sigebertus rex francorū in austrasia de prolis posteritate desperans duodecim ordinis sanctibenedicti monafteria in dei honorem hinc inde construxit cooperante sibi in his maiore domus Grunvualdo sancto Remaclo traiectionium episcopo In quibus Stabulaus Malmundariem eminebātquę sub uno gubernantur abbate Qui Remaclus non multo posti eodem stabulensi coenobio factus est monachus pontificatum curris plenum resignans tandemqꝫ foeliciter quieuit. His etiam temporibus in francia galicana sanctus Landelinusconfessor christíqui morosius quatuor memoratiordinismonafteria construxit Lobiense Aneiense Vuaslariaiense Crispinense ubi corpore in domino quiiescit cum Adoleno Domitianodiscipulis. Eodem tempore coenobiū floriacensefundatur a Leodeboldoabbate ad quod nōmulto post corpus diui patris nostribenedicti abbatis per Agilulfum monachum de montecassinoferturtranslatum eius coenobio (ut supradiximus) per longobardos defolato. His controdicunt itali. Eodem temporercoenobiū floriacenenfundatur a Leodeboldo abbate ad quod nōmultopost corpus diuipatris nostribenedicti abbatise Agilulfum monacchum de montecassinferturtranslatumpt eius coenobio (ut supradiximisper longobardos defolato)His controdicunt itali. Anno Clodoueifeptimo qui fuit dominice natiuitiesexcenti.

After she had at last most holily completed the course of the present race, she departed to the Lord, and was buried in the same monastery of Saint Symphorian the martyr, whom she had served most devoutly. This Modoaldus, moreover, whom others write as Rodoaldus, was the brother of Itha, wife of Pepin the Elder, and the maternal uncle of the blessed virgin Gertrude. This Itha founded in Brabant the monastery of nuns at Nivelles, in which, after Pepin’s death, she thereafter most holily served almighty God with her daughter.

But the most holy Modoaldus, bishop of Trier, not long after the death of his sister, also himself resting in the Lord, was buried beside her in the church of Saint Symphorian; Numerianus succeeded him in the archbishopric. In their time Dagobert, in the six hundred and twenty-seventh year of the Lord’s nativity, in the fifteenth Roman indiction, began to found the monastery of Doleiense of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, by the counsel and aid of the blessed archbishop Modoaldus; Sigebert, king of Austrasia, his son, completed it. And Saint Pirminius, bishop and monk, afterwards adorned it more beautifully.

In these times men of great holiness shone in the diocese of Trier, one of whose number was Paul, who on Mount Gebenna, opposite the city across the bridge of the river Moselle, led an eremitic life; then, coming to the aforementioned monastery [unclear], he became a monk; finally, ordained bishop of Verdun, he faithfully preserved in all things the rule of his former holiness. The mountain formerly called Gebenna, taking its name from him, is called Mount Paul, in the vernacular Paulsberg, down to the present day.

Wendelin also, first a monk in Tholey, afterwards a hermit in that place where now there stands a town called from his name Saint Wendelin, distant only one mile from that monastery, a man of most holy way of life, who, living and dead, converted many to Christ by word and example; whom I have recorded [unclear], lest two be thought one.

There was another Wendelin, at almost the same time, a monk and priest, disciple of Saint Columbanus, companion of Saint Walaric the monk in pilgrimage, a holy man and excellent preacher, who converted many to Christ by word and example; whom I have recorded [unclear], lest two be thought one.

Ingobert also, monk and priest; Carilephus, monk and priest; Wolffrich; Bantus; his brother Beatus, monk and priest; Wolfiliacus, a layman, men of the greatest holiness, with many others, led a solitary life in the wilderness in the diocese of Trier in these times.

Saint Disibod also, monk and priest, in the diocese of Mainz, in the county of Spanheim, two miles from Kreuznach and one mile from my former monastery of Spanheim, leading an eremitic life, built in that place near Sobernheim, where the Nahe and the Glan meet, a monastery of monks, which today bears his name. Today only a small trace of his monastery is seen.

Saint Modoaldus the archbishop was the maternal uncle of Saint Gertrude. Saint Modoaldus died. Numerianus succeeded. The Doleiense monastery of our order is founded. Saint Pirminius, bishop. Several hermits in the diocese of Trier. Paul, hermit, afterwards monk, finally bishop of Verdun. Mount Gebenna, now Paulsberg. Wendelin, monk and hermit. Another Wendelin, monk. Walaric, monk. Wolffrich. Bantus also. Beatus his brother. Wolfiliacus. Holy monks. Saint Disibod, monk, near Spanheim. The monastery of Saint Disibod is founded in the year 660.

Saint Remaclus becomes bishop in Upper Traiectum.

Pippin, mayor of the palace, count of Namur, duke of Brabant, count palatine, died.

Grunuald becomes mayor of the palace for eleven years.

Hildebert, son of Grunuald, king.

Rathulf, duke of the Thuringians, is overcome.

Saint Furseus, abbot and pilgrim.

He founds the monastery of Latiniacum. Foillanus and Ultanus, holy monks.

The monastery of Fosses is founded.

Twelve monasteries of our order are founded.

The monastery of Stavelot-Malmedy.

Saint Remaclus, bishop in Maastricht, a monk of Stavelot.

Saint Landelinus, confessor of the Lord.

The monasteries of Lobbes, Aulne, Waslere, and Crespin are founded. The monastery of Fleury is founded.

The body of Saint Benedict the abbot is translated.

In the first year of Clovis, king of the Franks, Saint Remaclus was ordained bishop of the church of Traiectum, a man of much learning and great holiness.

In the following year, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 647, in the fifth indiction of the Romans, Pippin the Elder died: count of Namur, duke of Brabant, mayor of the palace, count palatine of Sigebert, king of the Franks, who held the seat of the kingdom at Metz in Austrasia, and father of Saint Gertrude the virgin. He left a son, Grunuald. Grunuald succeeded his father in the rule of the royal household for eleven years; afterward he was killed, as we shall say in its place. He had a son named Hildebert, of whom we shall also tell how he made him king after his own lord had been driven into exile.

In the aforesaid year, Radulf, duke of the Thuringians, raised up in pride, refused to pay the customary tribute to the Franks. Therefore Sigebert, king of the Franks of Austrasia, gathered forces and moved his army into Thuringia; and, when battle was joined, he defeated the duke and compelled him to payment of the tribute.

In the same year Saint Furseus, an abbot from Ireland, a pilgrim for the sake of Christianity, came into Gaul. Received honorably by King Clovis, he founded the monastery of Latiniacum, now of our order, and established monks there. Not long afterward his two brothers, Foillanus and Ultanus, monks who followed him with an equal vow of pilgrimage, illuminated Gaul by the word and example of their life.

Of these, Foillanus, by the gift of Saint Gertrude the virgin, afterward founded the monastery of Fosses, where, crowned also with martyrdom, he rests in the Lord.

In the sixth year of King Clovis, Sigebert, king of the Franks in Austrasia, despairing of posterity from offspring, built here and there twelve monasteries of the order of Saint Benedict in honor of God, with Grunuald, mayor of the palace, and Saint Remaclus, bishop of the people of Traiectum, assisting him in these things. Among them Stavelot and Malmedy were pre-eminent, which are governed under one abbot. This Remaclus, not long afterward, was made a monk in the same monastery of Stavelot, resigning the pontificate, full of years, and at last he happily came to rest.

Also in these times in Gallican Francia, Saint Landelinus, confessor of Christ, who in like manner built four monasteries of the aforesaid order: Lobbes, Aulne, Waslere, and Crespin, where he rests bodily in the Lord with his disciples Adolenus and Domitianus.

At the same time the monastery of Fleury was founded by Abbot Leodebold. To it not long afterward the body of the divine father Benedict, our abbot, was brought, translated by the monk Agilulf from Monte Cassino, after his monastery, as we said above, had been laid waste by the Lombards. The Italians contradict these things.

In the seventh year of Clovis, which was the six-hundredth year of the Lord’s Nativity [unclear].

[unclear] and fifty-second. Sigebert, king of the Franks in Austrasia, adopted Hildebert, son of Grunwald, mayor of the palace, as his son, and the kingdom.

In the following year Saint Judoc, son of the king of the Britons, despising kingdom and world, a pilgrim and hermit in the district of Ponthieu, rested in Christ.

In the eleventh year of King Clovis, Sigebert, king of Austrasia, his brother, died, leaving his son Dagobert still very small and entrusted to the faith of Grunwald, mayor of the palace, so that by his help he might be advanced to the kingdom. In the following year Grunwald had him tonsured by Dido, bishop of Poitiers, and sent him to Scotland; and, against his pledge, he raised up Hildebert his own son as king of the Austrasians. But the Franks, grieving over so great a breach of faith by Grunwald, captured him and presented him at Paris for the judgment of King Clovis. Clovis had him bound and made him waste away in prison by a bitter death; and, after casting down his son, he appointed his own younger son Childeric king of the Austrasians, and avenged the wrong done to his nephew.

King Clovis of the Franks, because of an insufficiently reverent contact with the body of Saint Denis, became mad and senseless for two years and died in the seventeenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 662, in the fifth indiction.

The eldest son of King Clovis reigned after his father over the Franks for four years. His mayor of the palace was Ebroin, a man of Gallic cunning, deceitful, ready in counsel for crimes, perverse in action.

From this point the kings of the Franks, down to Pippin, father of Charlemagne, for almost ninety years, degenerating from their forefathers in courage and knowledge, reigned in name alone, doing nothing worthy of the royal office; but all power of governing the kingdom was in the hands of the princes of the court, who had been called mayors of the palace. The kings, however, stayed at home in idleness, doing or arranging nothing, but gave themselves sluggishly to feasting and drinking. Only once in the year, at the Kalends of May, did they come forth in public and show themselves to the people to be seen and greeted, and so returned home.

In these times Queen Balthild, mother of Lothar and formerly the wife left by King Clovis, founded two distinguished monasteries of our order in Gallican France, one of which is called Corbie and the other Chelles; in them many most holy and most learned monks were illustrious.

At the same time also many other monasteries of the aforesaid order of our divine father were built in the Gallican kingdom, among which these are listed: the monastery of Celle, over which [unclear].

The fifty-second. Sigebert, king of the Franks in Austrasia, adopted Hildebert, son of Grunvald, mayor of the palace, as his son, and the kingdom.

In the following year Saint Judoc, son of the king of the Britons, despising kingdom and world, a pilgrim and hermit, rested in Christ in the district of Ponthieu.

In the eleventh year of King Clodoveus, Sigebert, king of Austrasia, his brother, died, leaving his son Dagobert, still very small, entrusted to the loyalty of Grunvald, mayor of the palace, so that by his aid he might be advanced to the kingdom. In the following year Grunvald had him tonsured by Dido, bishop of Poitiers, and sent him to Scotland, and, against good faith, raised up his own son Hildebert as king of the Austrasians. But the Franks, grieving over so great a breach of faith by Grunvald, captured him and presented him for judgment before King Clodoveus at Paris; he had him bound and made him waste away in prison by a bitter death. After Grunvald’s son had been cast down, he made his own younger son Hilderic king of the Austrasians, and avenged the wrong done to his nephew.

Clodoveus, king of the Franks, because of an insufficiently reverent contact with the body of Saint Dionysius, was for two years deranged and out of his mind, and died in the seventeenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 662, in the fifth indiction.

The eldest son of King Clodoveus reigned after his father over the Franks for four years. His mayor of the palace was Ebervuin, whom [unclear] by nature deceitful, prompt in counsel for crimes, perverse in action.

From this time onward the kings of the Franks, down to Pippin, father of Charles the Great, for almost ninety years, degenerating from the solid men in courage and knowledge, reigned in name alone, accomplishing nothing worthy of the royal office; but all power of governing the kingdom was in the hands of the princes of the court, who were called mayors of the palace. The kings, however, remained at home idle, doing or arranging nothing, but sluggishly devoted themselves to eating and drinking. Only once in the year, at the Kalends of May, did they proceed in public and display themselves to the peoples to be looked upon and greeted, and so returned home.

In these times Queen Bechtildis, mother of Lothar and formerly the wife left behind by King Clodoveus, founded two distinguished monasteries of our order in Gallican France, one of which is called Corbie and the other Chelles; in them many most holy and most learned monks became famous.

Childericus, brother of the two preceding kings, who was reigning in Austrasia, after the deposition of Theodoricus, was, by the common election of the nobles, taken up as king and monarch of the whole kingdom of the Franks. He reigned twelve years. His mayor of the palace was Wolfradus, a noble man and powerful in deed and word.

Theodoricus is deposed from the kingdom of the Franks in the first year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 667, in the tenth Roman indiction, and his brother Childericus, who was reigning in Austrasia, is elected by common consent.

Childericus the king is killed together with his wife.

In the ninth year of his reign, King Childericus, through the levity of his own conduct, kindled against himself the hatred of many nobles. Saint Leodegarius, formerly a monk of our order, bishop of Autun, having been driven from his see, he thrust into Luxeuil.

But in the twelfth year of his reign, and in the 679th year of the Lord’s nativity, in the seventh indiction, a certain Frank named Bodilo, whom King Childericus himself had ordered to be bound to a post and flogged, found him out hunting and, by a cruel blow, killed him together with Blithilde, his pregnant wife,

After the killing of King Hilderic, Theodoric, his brother, summoned from the monastery of the holy martyr Dionysius, was restored to the kingdom of the Franks, and thereafter reigned for a second time for fourteen years. His mayor of the palace was Leudesius, son of Erchenvald, appointed for one year by the counsel of Saint Leodegar the bishop, who had then been recalled from the monastery of Luxeuil, and of other leading men.

For in the following year Eberwin, having gone out from the aforesaid monastery, recovered his strength and harried those who had plotted against him with hostile persecution. He fell upon King Theodoric, plundered his treasures and those of the church, slew Leudesius, mayor of the palace, in battle, put the king himself to flight, and, pretending that a certain Clovis was the son of Lothar, formerly king, made him king for himself; and he brought over to obedience to him all whom he could by threats and blandishments, and disturbed the kingdom of the Franks with many upheavals.

In the third year of Theodoric's reign, the holy prelate Leodegar was captured by Eberwin and grievously afflicted together with his brother Gerinus. But Gerinus, not long afterward, was killed at the command of that same tyrant, overwhelmed with stones.

In the sixth year of his reign, Theodoric received Eberwin into favor, and at his persuasion called a synod of bishops. In it, according to Eberwin's judgment, he deprived many of them of their episcopal office, while he condemned others to perpetual exile. Among them Saint Lambert, son of Count Aper, removed from his bishopric of Maastricht, entered the haven of monastic quiet in the monastery of Stavelot, and remained there for seven years.

In the same year Saint Leodegar, bishop of Autun, after being long tortured by Eberwin, after hunger and the squalor of prison, after the tearing out of his eyes, after the cutting of the soles of his feet, after the cutting out of his tongue and lips, by the tyrant's command consummated his martyrdom by the cutting off of his head. Many miracles proved his innocence and merit.

In the eighth year of Theodoric, after the death of Wulfrad, mayor of the palace of the Franks, Pippin, son of Ansegis, held rule in Austrasia together with Duke Martin; Eberwin engaged them and killed Martin.

In the same year Conon was ordained pope at Rome. He ordained Saint Kilian, a Scot by nation and a monk by profession, as bishop, sending him with two monks, Colman the priest and Totnan the deacon, into Germany to preach to the peoples the faith of Christ and the true salvation of souls in him. Coming into eastern Francia, at the city of Wurzburg of the Franks, he for some time devoted himself to the office of holy preaching, where by word and example he called many back to knowledge of the truth. At last, with his aforesaid disciples, he suffered under the secret direction of Geilana, wife of Gosbert, duke of the East Franks, because she feared being separated from her husband when Saint Kilian rebuked him for having her as wife, since his brother had previously had her as wife.

Theodoric reigns for a second time for thirteen years.

Ebroin, mayor of the palace of Neustria, is killed. Waratto, mayor of the palace. A war between Pippin and Giselmar. Bertharius becomes mayor of the palace of Neustria. A war of King Theodoric with Pippin, mayor of the palace. Victory fell to Pippin, who captured the king. Pippin captured King Theodoric. Pippin, mayor of the palace, for twenty-three years. Saint Lambert is restored to his church. Saint Willibrord, abbot, with his twelve monks. Saint Wandregisel flourished and built the monasteries of Fécamp and Fontenelle. Theodoric, king of the Franks, dies. The fifty-sixth. Clovis reigned four years. The two Ewalds, monks, suffered martyrdom in Saxony. Pippin overcame the Frisians in war.

In the ninth year of King Theodoric, Ebroin, mayor of the palace in Neustria, since he did not cease cruelly to oppress the Franks by his tyranny, was killed by a certain Ermenfrid, a noble man; this Ermenfrid soon fled to Pippin in Austrasia, who held the chief office of mayor of the palace. When the most wicked Ebroin had been slain, a certain Waratto was appointed mayor of the palace.

In the following year a battle between Pippin and Giselmar, son of Waratto, was fought at [Nauinucum?]. Not long afterward, when Giselmar had been punished by divine judgment, and Waratto also had died, his son-in-law Bertharius became mayor of the palace. But the Franks, suffering under Bertharius’s estrangement, sought Pippin’s friendship through hostages, promising aid and faithful service if he would take the chief rule from him in war.

In the twelfth year of his reign King Theodoric and Bertharius, his mayor of the palace, declared war on Pippin, who held himself as mayor of the palace in Austrasia against their will. But Pippin conquered in that battle and bound the captured King Theodoric, as he wished, by his own conditions. Bertharius, however, [unclear].

[unclear] Saint Lambert, led out from the monastery of Stavelot, was restored to the bishopric of the church of Maastricht upon the Meuse; he accomplished many useful things in the kingdom of the Franks. And so Pippin subjugated Neustria together with Austrasia to himself; under Theodoric alone he ruled the whole kingdom of the Franks for [unclear] years [unclear].

At that time Saint Willibrord, a monk, came from England into Gallican France with twelve companions of the same profession, and lived in great holiness.

In these same times Saint Wandregisel, who [unclear], nephew through his brother Walgisus of Ansegisel, formerly mayor of the palace of the kingdom of the Franks, built two monasteries of monks under the rule of blessed Benedict in Gallican France, namely Fécamp and Fontenelle, which is now on the borders of Normandy; in these, many very holy and very learned men afterward flourished in the course of time.

Theodoric, king of the Franks, died in the fourteenth year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 693, in the sixth Roman indiction, leaving two sons, Clovis and Childebert, who succeeded each other in turn.

Clovis, the elder by birth of the aforementioned sons of King Theodoric, succeeded him first and reigned over the Franks for four years, with Pippin being mayor of the palace. [unclear] coming from England for love of Christ into Saxony were martyred; they were buried at Cologne [unclear] of Prince Pippin.

Libens pręterissem hanc battologiam imperitorum nisi me scrip- torum meorum defensio compelleret in medium proferre nugaces Scripsimus enim iamdudum, ad instantiam Blasij et Ioannis abba- tum, duo non parue quantitatis uolumina chronicorum siue anna- lium insignis monasterij Hirsaugiensis nostri ordinis quod situm est in diocesi nemetensi, siue spirensi, in quorum primo multis rati- onibus probauimus sufficienter memoratum coenobium sancti pe- tri in erpfurdia non a Dagoberto rege francorum, sed per diuum Vuilhelmum Hisaugienlem abbatem duodecimum primitus esse fundatum. Et quia nunc assertionem hanc nostram magis cognoui mus esse ueram ex confictis ineptissimis litteris quas in predico monasterio erpfurdiaco uidimus nullo munitas sigillo cuiuscūqꝫ legimus sub nomine dagoberti rescripsimus, ne quis falsitatis nos argueret, operepręciũ fore duximus, si earundem litterarum exemplar cum alijs rationibꝰ nostre assertioni coniungamus. Ioānes tritemitis abbas in p̄mo annali um Hirsaugienfis. Probat opinionem erpfurteñ esse falsã. Monasterij sacti petri in erpfurt fundatio. Per fratres de hirsauga facta demonstra- tur. ¶ In nomine sancte et indiuidue trini- tatis. Ego Dagobertus francorum rex, notum facio tam clero quā populo, tā christianis quā paganis quod urbē nostrā nomine Mero uegesburg quę nobis hereditario iure ab ipso auo nostro Meroueo fundatore uidelicet eiudem urbis in thuringia, obuenerat sancto Petro suis monachis deo inibi seruientibus quo ad ipse mons postfundationem monasterij quod in honorem praefati apostoli construxit uocabulum sumpsit, deleto paganico prius nomine aui mei petrimons uocatus cum omnibꝰ seruitijs suis post finem meo um possidendam regali potentia dedimus. Quali autem id dei or- dinatione factum fit, indicabimus. Fuit in p̄dicta urbe iuxta eccle- siam sacti Blasij martyris homo dei nōine Adeo datus rogatu meo amoguntino episcopo Rigeberto inclusus. Qui inclusus ob pericu- lum animę nolens uti communiōe clericorum, uxoribus armis utentium, sępe me rogauit ut de aliquo claustro meo monachū a quo diuinum offitium uerbum uerę fidei audiret cōmunio- nem sacri misterij perciperet sibi euocarem Huius ego ob mu- tuam familiaritatē petitioni annuensi misi ad monasteriorum monacho- rum quod simili modo cōstruxi in Selsenburg uenerabilem se- niorem monachum nomine Truckindum inde euocans, praefato Adeodato incluso doctorē rectorem direxi. Quī eo peruendiens coepit paulatim ex eius doctrina suasione inclulit numerus credē- tium multiplicari tum conuersionē paganorum ad baptismum, tū clericorum laicorum ad monachicum habitum. Hoc ego cerne̓s diuinum in hoc fauorem intelligens tradidi sępe dictam urbem meam cum omnibꝰ sibi pertinentibus sancto petro suis mona- chis ibidem monachiam religionem statuendam abbatia meo auxilio faciendam. Certum est reges francorum eo tem- pore nihil potuisse. Omnis potestas erat penes maiorem do- mus. Nec fecithoc nec po tuit quia maior do- mus dominus fuit; Iͦnnoͤn Iͥnnoͤn Iͣnnoͤn

Fifty-eighth.

He is named Dagobert by more writers than Clovis.

The Franks cast Theudobald, mayor of the palace, down from the principate.

A war between Charles and Daniel Hilperic.

Clovis Dagobert, king of the Franks, dies. Refutation concerning the foundation of the monastery of St. Peter in Erfurt.

In the sixteenth year of Hildebert, king of the Franks, Grimoald, whom Pippin, already weighed down by old age, had appointed mayor of the palace in his place, was killed at Liege, while praying before the altar of St. Lambert, by Ranegarius, an attendant of Radbod, duke of the Frisians.

After his pitiable death, Theudobald, son of Drogo, was made mayor of the palace of the Franks and prince of the court by his grandfather Pippin; in this principate he could scarcely rule for two years, but was cast down by the Franks.

In the following year, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 714, Pippin, son of Ansegisus, mayor of the palace of the kingdom of the Franks, died. He designated as heir of his principate his son named Charles, surnamed Tutides or Martel, born of the concubine Alpaida. But Plectrude, the legitimate wife left by Pippin, seized this Charles, her stepson, assigned him to very close custody at Cologne, and seized the principate with her grandson Theudobald.

Meanwhile Hildebert, king of the Franks, dies in the eighteenth year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 704, in the thirteenth indiction. The son of King Hildebert, succeeding his father in the kingdom of the Franks, reigned four years, or, as others wish, five. Most writers of histories affirm that this man was not named Clovis but Dagobert; whether this diversity occurred by fault of the writers or on any other occasion, we do not know for certain. The greater part, however, call him Dagobert, and he is cast down from the principate. After him the Franks appoint Ragenfrid mayor of the palace.

The Franks, laboring under hatred of Theudobald, conspire together as one; with forces gathered from here and there they move a sufficiently dangerous war against him, in which, after many had been killed on both sides, Theudobald is at last defeated, put to flight, and cast down from the principate. After him the Franks appoint Ragenfrid mayor of the palace.

Meanwhile Charles, son of Pippin, freed from the custody of his stepmother by divine prompting, soon strives to snatch his grandfather's principate from the hand of Ragenfrid; and first, when Radbod, duke of Frisia, was aiding the enemy, he attacked and suffered loss of his army.

In the third year of Clovis or Dagobert of the Franks, Charles, in the district of Cambrai at Vincy, on Palm Sunday, which was the third day before the Kalends of April, engaged Hilperic and Ragenfrid, turned them both to flight, and pursued them as far as Paris. Hilperic, moreover, was by rank a priest, named Daniel, whom the Franks had established as king for themselves in Neustria.

After this Dagobert, or Clovis, king of the Franks, dies in the fourth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord's nativity 711, in the second indiction.

Here it is pleasing to insert the false opinion of certain persons concerning the foundation of the monastery of St. Peter the Apostle in Erfurt, who grant to King Dagobert the great honor of this foundation; but neither time nor reason permits this.

I would gladly have passed over this babbling of the ignorant, had not the defense of my writings compelled me to bring triflers into the open. For some time ago, at the insistence of the abbots Blasius and Johannes, we wrote two volumes, of no small size, of chronicles or annals of the distinguished monastery of Hirsau of our order, which is situated in the diocese of Speyer; in the first of these we proved sufficiently, by many arguments, that the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter at Erfurt was founded originally not by Dagobert, king of the Franks, but by Saint Wilhelm, twelfth abbot of Hirsau. And because we have now learned that this assertion of ours is all the more true from the most foolishly fabricated letters which we saw in the aforesaid Erfurt monastery, secured by no seal of anyone, and which we read under the name of Dagobert and transcribed, lest anyone accuse us of falsehood, we have thought it worthwhile to join a copy of the same letters, together with other arguments, to our assertion.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot, in the first book of the Annals of Hirsau.

He proves the Erfurt opinion to be false.

The foundation of the monastery of Saint Peter at Erfurt. It is shown to have been made by brothers from Hirsau.

Copy of the letters of foundation which are ascribed to Dagobert.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Dagobert, king of the Franks, make known to clergy as well as people, to Christians as well as pagans, that our city, by name Merovegesburg, which had come to us by hereditary right from our grandfather Meroveus himself, namely the founder of that same city in Thuringia, we have given by royal power to Saint Peter and to his monks serving God there, to be possessed after my death, together with all its services; and the very mountain, after the foundation of the monastery which he built in honor of the aforesaid apostle, took its name, the pagan name of my grandfather having first been abolished, and was called Peter’s Mount. But by what ordinance of God this was done, we shall relate.

There was in the aforesaid city, beside the church of Saint Blasius the martyr, a man of God named Adeodatus, enclosed at my request by Rigebert, bishop of Mainz. This enclosed man, because of peril to his soul, was unwilling to make use of the communion of clerics who used wives and arms, and often asked me to summon for him from some cloister of mine a monk from whom he might hear the divine office and the word of the true faith, and receive the communion of the sacred mystery. Assenting to the request of this man, on account of our mutual familiarity, I sent to the monastery of monks which I likewise built in Selsenburg, summoning from there a venerable elder monk named Truckindus, and directed him to the aforesaid enclosed man Adeodatus as teacher and rector. When he arrived there, gradually, by his teaching and persuasion, the number of believers began to be multiplied, both through the conversion of pagans to baptism and of clerics and laymen to the monastic habit. Seeing this, and understanding the divine favor in it, I handed over my often-mentioned city, with all things belonging to it, to Saint Peter and to his monks, for monastic religion to be established there and an abbey to be made with my aid.

His grandfather was not, but the fourteenth king before him.

At that time Erfurt was a small village, not a city.

Rigibertus was bishop of Mainz.

It is certain that the kings of the Franks at that time could do nothing. All power was in the hands of the mayor of the palace.

Nor did he do this, nor could he, because the mayor of the palace was lord.
