Moreover I gave to Saint Peter and his monks, for various uses, the forest which, because of the great number of deer, is called Hirsbrulis, from the southern side of the city toward the east as far as the boundaries of the region of Orlau, which region I handed over in benefice to Pepin, count palatine. I gave nonetheless to the aforesaid monastery the villages made by slaves in the same forest, namely Tuneckdorff, Tugebrachtestet, Tuttelstet, Nevukenrodt, Hochdorff, and several others; and the water Gera, for the monks to catch fish, from the southern part of the city as far as the boundary of the court of my ministerial Gisbotus. I also gave from my court, for the use of the brethren, fifty modii of wheat, one hundred of barley, and as many of oats, and all my other possessions in Thuringia. For the maintenance of this place beloved to me I gave my ministerials with all their offspring and possession, whose names are these: Gisbotus, Eckhardus, Vuolffholdus, Hysen, Egenhen, Vuolffgirus, Omarus, Sigebertus, Theodobertus, Theodoricus, Adelbotus, Adelgerus, Gelferatus, Hingfridus, Huntzelinus, and all the rest, my male servants and female servants in Thuringia. In order that this conveyance to my Lord Jesus Christ may remain firm eternally, we have caused it to be established by our letters, we have requested it to be confirmed by the ban of Rigibert, bishop of Mainz, and we have bound it with our ring and completed it by the display of our seal. Charter at Mainz, on the Kalends of March, in the presence of Bishop Rigebert. The sign of Dagobert, most unconquered king of the Franks. The witnesses of all these matters are these: Pepin, mayor of the palace; his son Charles; Rigibert, bishop of Mainz; Gunthernus, pagan count; Eckebi, count; the whole church in Thuringia around the Rhine in Mainz. These things were done in the seven hundred sixth year of the Lord’s incarnation, in the ninth indiction.

Far be it from me, Trithemius infers, to fight against the truth of this so ancient asserted foundation, if it holds up; but how truth can hold up in it I do not sufficiently see. Therefore I shall also note here briefly what reasons for doubting occur to me, after those, namely, which I wrote for Hirsau.

The first consideration which prevents me from conceding that Dagobert was the founder of the often-mentioned monastery of Erfurt is that the reckoning of the years does not agree; for if this very foundation is ascribed to Dagobert the Great, it contradicts the instrument of the letters no less than the truth of the computed time. For he died in the year of the Lord’s nativity, as we said above, six hundred forty-five, in the third Roman indiction, not less than sixty years before the donation of this document. But if it is attributed to that latest Dagobert, who was Clodoveus, nevertheless a discordance of years follows, because he began to reign in the year of the Lord 715 and died in the year 719. How, then, could he have delivered letters of a foundation of this kind in the sixth year of the Lord?

In the aforesaid instrument of letters the ninth Roman indiction is set down, although it was the fourth and by no means the ninth, as a skilled ecclesiastical computist will plainly find.

The third consideration gives me a strong suspicion of fabrication, because the aforesaid letters of foundation, which the brothers at St. Peter’s in Erfurt display as originals, are protected by no one’s seal, although a hole appears in the parchment, as if the seal had fallen off through excessive age.

The fourth consideration is by no means inferior to the foregoing, because it is found plainly written in the life and deeds of blessed Wilhelm, abbot of Hirsau, that he constructed seven new monasteries of our order, among which the often-mentioned monastery of St. Peter in Erfurt is counted fourth in order. I deliberately pass over several other considerations, lest prolixity create tedium for the reader.

Therefore, just as I wrote and long ago showed by many arguments in that very first volume of my Hirsau chronicles, it was necessary for me to think thus and to prefer to fabrication the truth, which I believe has simply perished.

In the year of the Lord 706 the Roman indiction was the fourth, not the ninth.

In the following year Charles, mayor of the palace of the Franks, launched an expedition into Alemannia and, joining battle with the rebellious Alemanni, emerged victorious. He overcame Lanfrid, their duke, and forced their land into submission.

Lothar, king of the Franks, reigning in name alone, died in the seventh year of his reign, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 726, in the seventh indiction. Theodoric, Lothar’s nephew by his brother, namely the son of the aforesaid King Clovis, whom others called Dagobert, after the death of his uncle and at the same time after the death of Chilperic Daniel the priest, who while Lothar was alive and after his death had acted as king for eight years, was raised by Charles Martel, mayor of the palace, to be king of the Franks, and reigned fifteen years.

In these times there flourished in Gallican Francia Saint Pyrminius, formerly a monk of the monastery of Abbot [Diuinaurus?], bishop of Meaux in the province of Sens, a man admirable for learning and holiness. For the love of Christ, to preach the true faith to the peoples, he came into the regions of Germany, where by word and example he converted many to the worship of truth, and founded several monasteries.

Among these the following are counted as the principal ones and known to us. The monastery of Saint Maurice the Martyr in Dole of Trier, which the great king of the Franks Dagobert, as was said above, once built, he personally visited rather often; for some time he lived there among the brothers, established the conduct of the brothers according to the intention of the Rule of Saint Benedict, and adorned the place.

Likewise the monastery of Schuttern, which is situated three miles above Strasbourg, a city of Alsace, the same Saint Pyrminius founded, just as is found clearly written in the original volume of his Life, which we have in our possession. Nor is it an objection that the brothers of that same monastery, showing no documents of truth, say that Offa, king of England, when he was seeking Rome for the sake of devotion in the times of Saint Gregory the First, pope, was moved by the pleasantness of the place to establish a monastery there; for King Offa and his brother, as we said above under King Hildebert, sought Rome and became monks in the year of the Lord 707, in the fifth Roman indiction. But Saint Pope Gregory, under whom they say that Offa, king of England, came to Rome, had died earlier, in the year of the Lord 605, in the eighth Roman indiction. Sigebert bears witness for our assertion in the chronicles.

The monastery of Gengenbach, in the diocese of Strasbourg, which is one mile distant from Schuttern, the same writer of the Life of Saint Pirmin attests was founded by him.

The same saint founded the monastery which in Latin is called Mauri Monasterium, but in the vernacular Morsmunster, in the diocese of Strasbourg.

Likewise the same saint built the monastery of Neuweiler in the same diocese of Strasbourg; its monks, together with their abbot, in our times withdrew from the order.

There are two monasteries of our order with one name in Bavaria, of which one is called Upper Altha, and the other likewise Altha, but Lower. In the deeds of the dukes of Bavaria we read that Duke Odilo, father of Duke Tassilo, founded Lower Altha. But in the deeds of Saint Pirmin it is said that he built the monastery of Altha in Bavaria, yet it is not there expressed whether Upper or Lower; therefore it is clear that it was Upper.

The blessed Pirmin also built another monastery within the borders of Alsace, if I remember rightly in the diocese of Basel, of the same order of Benedict, which is named Murbach, as is contained in his Life.

He also founded another monastery on an island of the river Rhine, not far from Constance, which is now called Reichenau, in which in the course of time many cloistered men lived, distinguished for learning and holiness. But in these our days it is tossed in great poverty, which once, through extraordinary riches and abundance of goods, was called Rich Reichenau.

He also built from the foundations a new monastery in the town of Amorbach, in the diocese of Würzburg, of our aforesaid order, in which he appointed Saint Amor, his disciple, abbot. And many others which we do not know.

In the fifth year of Theodoric, king of the Franks, died Bede the Venerable, priest and monk in England, a learned and holy man, who wrote many volumes for the usefulness of readers and to the honor of the supreme, undivided deity.

Theodoric, king of the Franks, died in the fifteenth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 741, in the ninth indiction of the Romans. Succeeding him, Childeric, with Charles, surnamed Martel, that is, the Hammer, as mayor of the palace, reigned in name only for nine years. For all power and the resources of the kingdom were in the hands of the mayor [unclear] than that, content with the royal name, with flowing hair and lowered beard, he should sit on a throne and display the appearance of one ruling, hear envoys coming from every quarter, and, as they departed, give them the answers in which he had been instructed.

The monastery of Gengenbach in Alsace is founded.

The monastery of Morsmunster is founded in Alsace.

The monastery of Neuweiler in Alsace is founded [unclear].

Two monasteries of our order of one name in Bavaria.

Upper Altha and Lower Altha are founded.

The monastery of Murbach is founded in Alsace.

The monastery in Greater Reichenau near Constance is founded.

The monastery in Amorbach is founded.

Bede, priest and monk in England, died.

Theodoric, king of the Franks, dies.

The Sixty-First.

Childeric, last king of the Franks, reigned nine years.

The kings of the Franks did nothing except bear the empty name, nor did they have any power in anything.

In the same year Charles Martel died, mayor of the palace of the Franks, duke of Brabant, and count [unclear] of Namur; since he was most warlike and fortunate in all things, he greatly extended the boundaries of the kingdom. He defeated the Saxons, Bavarians, Burgundians, Sorbs, [Bulgarians?] dwelling beyond the Danube, and also the Gascons, Vandals, Goths, Saracens in Spain, Frisians, and many other nations round about; he overcame them by war and the sword. Of his deeds, good and evil, and how he conferred ecclesiastical dignities on his soldiers and despoiled churches, and how for those crimes he was seen after death buried in hell, we have related more fully in the first volume of our Annals, of which this is the compendium.

He left three sons: Pippin, Carloman, and Grifo. Of these, Pippin and Carloman divided the paternal principate between themselves, excluding Grifo, and in this way they ruled over the Franks for four years. But after four years Carloman, moved by the divine spirit, relinquished the whole principate to his brother Pippin, went to Rome, and became a monk on Monte Cassino. Pippin then ruled the principate alone for six years; after King Childeric had been deposed, by common vote he was made king.

Grifo, grieving that he had been disregarded by his brothers, by the counsel of his mother seized the city of Laon and declared war on his brothers. His mother was the stepmother of Pippin and Carloman. They, swiftly gathering their army, surrounded Laon with a siege, captured the city, and held their brother prisoner for four years.

In these times there flourished in the kingdom of the Franks Saint Boniface, English by nation, a monk by profession, by dignity archbishop of the church of Mainz, an apostolic man who by his preaching converted the Thuringians and many others to Christ, for whom later, while preaching in Frisia, he suffered martyrdom.

He founded in the Buchonia forest two notable monasteries of our order, one of which is called Hersfeld in the diocese of Mainz, the other by the river Fulda flowing past it, where he was buried, in the diocese of Wuerzburg.

He also built several convents of nuns, among which there still stands out one of the monasteries in the town of Kitzingen beside the Main, in the diocese of Wuerzburg; over it he placed a holy virgin named Hadelloga, whom he named Thecla, of English origin. Another, near the town of Bischofsheim beside the Tauber, in the diocese of Mainz, over which he placed Saint Lioba, a virgin beloved of God, likewise English by country; of this convent nothing survives today.
